bisettiere.text: The bisettière makes bisette, a fine but coarse lace produced in large quantity for everyday use, notably in lacemaking regions such as Haute-Loire or Normandy. A modest female trade, on the margins of the fine laces intended for a wealthy clientele.

bisouart.label: Bisouart
bisouart.summary: Pedlar of the Dauphiné, an itinerant merchant selling small haberdashery items.
bisouart.text: The bisouart (or bisouard) is a pedlar specific to the Dauphiné, akin to the mercelot who sells haberdashery door to door. An old and obsolete regional term, attested notably in early-20th-century dialect literature.

bistourneur.label: Bistourneur
bistourneur.summary: Veterinary practitioner castrating animals, notably by the method known as bistournage.
bistourneur.text: The bistourneur performs bistournage, a technique for castrating farm animals (bulls, rams) by twisting the spermatic cords without incision, thereby avoiding the infection risks of surgery. The term derives from "bistourner" (to twist), related to "bistouri" (scalpel).

blanchier.label: Blanchier
blanchier.summary: Old form of blanchisseur (launderer), sometimes also denoting a tanner who whitens hides.
blanchier.text: The blanchier is an old form of "blanchisseur", denoting one who bleaches and cares for textile linen. In some records, the term also applies to the tanner-currier who whitens hides (mégissier), the two usages coexisting depending on region and period.

blanchisseur.label: Blanchisseur (launderer)
blanchisseur.summary: Person specialized in washing, bleaching and caring for linen.
blanchisseur.text: The blanchisseur (or blanchisseuse) washes, bleaches and irons the linen of private individuals or institutions, often at a wash-house or river before hanging it out to dry in the open air. A very common trade, especially for women, it was one of the few paid jobs open to working-class women under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century.

blanchisseur_d_eglise.label: Blanchisseur d'église
blanchisseur_d_eglise.summary: Specialist in caring for liturgical linen: albs, altar cloths, surplices.
blanchisseur_d_eglise.text: The blanchisseur d'église specializes in the care of liturgical linens — albs, surplices, altar cloths, corporals and other sacred textiles — which demand impeccable care and whiteness. This specialized trade differs from ordinary laundering by the precious and symbolic nature of the linen treated.

blanchisseur_de_fin.label: Blanchisseur de fin
blanchisseur_de_fin.summary: Specialist in bleaching delicate textiles: lace, batiste, silks.
blanchisseur_de_fin.text: The blanchisseur de fin (or blanchisseuse de fin) specializes in caring for precious and delicate textiles — lace, batiste, fine linen, silks — requiring particular care and skill, unlike the everyday laundering of household linen.

blanchisseur_sur_le_pre.label: Blanchisseur sur le pré
blanchisseur_sur_le_pre.summary: Launderer laying washed linen out on grass, in the open air, to bleach it in the sun.
blanchisseur_sur_le_pre.text: The blanchisseur sur le pré spreads freshly washed linen on the grass of a meadow, exposed to sun and dew, a traditional method that completed the bleaching before industrial chemical products came into use. This open-air practice long characterized the trade before its mechanization.

blasonnier.label: Blasonnier
blasonnier.summary: Craftsman specialized in painting and creating heraldic coats of arms.
blasonnier.text: The blasonnier paints and draws the coats of arms (blazons) of noble families, guilds or towns, on various supports: stained glass, panels, documents. A trade linked to heraldry, often working alongside painters and engravers.

blatier.label: Blatier (grain merchant)
blatier.summary: Merchant of wheat and grain, an intermediary between producers and markets.
blatier.text: The blatier buys and resells wheat and other cereals, often at local markets, acting as an intermediary between peasant producers and urban consumers. This trade, sensitive to famines, was closely watched by the authorities under the Ancien Régime.

bluteur.label: Bluteur (sifter)
bluteur.summary: Mill worker responsible for sifting flour to separate it from the bran.
bluteur.text: The bluteur sifts ("blute") flour as it leaves the mill to separate the fine meal from the bran, using a bolter. An ancillary trade of milling, essential for producing flours of differentiated quality.

bobineuse.label: Bobineuse
bobineuse.summary: Female worker who winds thread onto bobbins used to warp the chains of fabrics.
bobineuse.text: In wool mills, the bobineuse winds thread onto bobbins or spools used to warp the chains of fabrics; the term also denotes a spinner working at home with her spinning wheel.

bocardier.label: Bocardier
bocardier.summary: Mine worker operating the bocard, a machine used to crush ore.
bocardier.text: The bocardier operates the bocard, a mechanical stamping device used to crush and grind extracted ore before its metallurgical processing. A trade linked to mining, present in regions with extractive activity (Massif Central, Pyrenees).

bocqueur.label: Bocqueur
bocqueur.summary: Forest worker felling and cutting wood in bocage areas.
bocqueur.text: The bocqueur (or bocqueteur) fells and cuts wood in the hedgerows and copses characteristic of the bocage landscape, notably in western France. Seasonal work supplementing farming activities.

boeutier.label: Bœutier
boeutier.summary: Old term linked to raising or driving oxen.
boeutier.text: The word relates to raising, trading or driving oxen, likely denoting an ox-drover or a cattle merchant, though the precise sense is not established with certainty in the available sources.

boguier.label: Boguier
boguier.summary: Seasonal worker responsible for husking chestnut burrs.
boguier.text: The boguier processes burrs, the prickly husk surrounding chestnuts, to extract the fruit after harvest. Seasonal trade of chestnut-growing regions (Cévennes, Corsica, Limousin), where the chestnut was a major food resource.

boherdeor.label: Boherdeor
boherdeor.summary: Jouster fighting with a lance at medieval tournaments.
boherdeor.text: The boherdeor is a jouster who fights with a lance at medieval tournaments and jousts, an exercise at once sporting and martial practised by the nobility, sometimes mentioned as an activity or title in old texts.

boisart.label: Boisart
boisart.summary: Maker of household and agricultural implements in wood.
boisart.text: The boisart makes wooden implements for domestic or agricultural use — tool handles, bowls, small instruments. An old regional term, distinct from the boiseur, who works mainly in the forest.

boiseur.label: Boiseur
boiseur.summary: Forest worker handling the felling, shaping and transport of wood.
boiseur.text: The boiseur works wood in the forest: felling, shaping and transporting logs to sawmills or points of sale. The term "boier", a regional variant, denotes the same trade in certain areas.

boisselier.label: Boisselier
boisselier.summary: Craftsman making bushel measures and objects in turned or hooped wood (buckets, measures, boxes).
boisselier.text: The boisselier makes bushels (grain-capacity measures) and other objects in turned, hooped or assembled wood — buckets, small casks, boxes. A trade close to coopering but specialized in smaller pieces for household use.

boitier.label: Boîtier
boitier.summary: Craftsman making boxes and cases, notably for clockwork and goldsmith's work.
boitier.text: The boîtier makes boxes and cases intended to protect or display precious objects: watches, jewellery, instruments. A precision trade, often linked to clockmaking or goldsmithing.

bombeur.label: Bombeur
bombeur.summary: Craftsman specialized in bombage, the technique of shaping glass or metal into a convex form.
bombeur.text: The bombeur performs bombage, an operation that gives a convex ("bombé") shape to materials such as glass (watch glasses, display cases) or certain metal parts, through heating and moulding. The terms "bombagiste" and "bombiste" denote the same specialty.

bonissier.label: Bonissier
bonissier.summary: Craftsman responsible for improving and finishing manufactured products.
bonissier.text: The bonissier carries out the improvement and finishing of products — reworking, quality improvements — in a craft workshop. A rare term whose precise field of application varies by region and trade.

bonne.label: Bonne (maid)
bonne.summary: Female domestic employed in the service of a household ("maid of all work").
bonne.text: The bonne is a domestic employed in a private household for housework, cooking or childcare, either alone or as part of a larger household staff (cook, chambermaid). A very common term from the 19th century to the mid-20th century, denoting both the rural servant and the urban bourgeois domestic.

bonnetier.label: Bonnetier (hosier)
bonnetier.summary: Maker of bonnets, stockings and knitted goods.
bonnetier.text: The bonnetier makes bonnets, stockings and other hosiery items, either machine-knitted or hand-knitted. This textile trade underwent a major boom with mechanization, notably in centres such as Troyes, which became a capital of French hosiery.

boquetier.label: Boquetier
boquetier.text: The boquetier is a merchant selling clogs, distinct from the sabotier, who makes them.

bordeur_de_galetoires.label: Bordeur de galetoires
bordeur_de_galetoires.summary: Craftsman edging galetoires, hand-made textile or decorative pieces.
bordeur_de_galetoires.text: The bordeur de galetoires makes the edging of galetoires, hand-made textile or decorative pieces. A rare regional term, little documented beyond this specific craft.

bordeuse.label: Bordeuse
bordeuse.summary: Female worker who finishes and sometimes decorates shoes.
bordeuse.text: The bordeuse finishes a shoe and sometimes decorates it, a step in the work of an industrial shoemaking workshop.

bordier.label: Bordier
bordier.summary: Small farmer working a modest plot of land, the "borde", often as a tenant.
bordier.text: The bordier farms a small holding, the "borde", generally on a modest tenancy and without owning a full team of draught animals, which places him below the laboureur in the peasant hierarchy. The term "bordager", a regional variant, denotes the same status of small tenant farmer.

bornier.label: Bornier
bornier.summary: Surveyor responsible for measuring land and setting boundary stones marking off properties.
bornier.text: The bornier is a surveyor, responsible for measuring land and marking property boundaries by placing boundary stones, often in the service of a lord, a community, or private individuals in a neighbourly dispute.

bosselier.label: Bosselier
bosselier.summary: Craftsman making embossed metal objects, worked in relief with a hammer.
bosselier.text: The bosselier shapes metal objects in relief (embossed) by hammering, a technique used in goldsmithing or coppersmithing. The spelling "bossellier" denotes the same trade.

boteresse.label: Boteresse
boteresse.summary: Woman carrying loads on her back in a bot, a funnel-shaped basket without a bottom.
boteresse.text: The boteresse carries loads with a bot, a funnel-shaped basket without a bottom carried on the back, unlike the hod. The botty is its male equivalent.

botresse_al_hoye.label: Botresse al hoye
botresse_al_hoye.summary: Boteresse who carries coal delivered by the carter down into the cellars.
botresse_al_hoye.text: The botresse al hoye is a specialized boteresse who carries down into the cellars the coal ("hoye" in Walloon) delivered by the carter, a trade attested in the Borinage.

botteleur.label: Botteleur
botteleur.summary: Farm worker bundling hay, straw or sheaves of grain.
botteleur.text: The botteleur binds hay, straw or sheaves into bundles after the harvest or haymaking, making them easier to transport and store. Seasonal work typical of the countryside before harvest mechanization.

botteleur_de_foin.label: Botteleur de Foin
botteleur_de_foin.summary: Day-labourer bundling hay at haymaking time.
botteleur_de_foin.text: The botteleur de foin is a farm day-labourer employed to bundle hay into bales at haymaking time.

bottier.label: Bottier (bootmaker)
bottier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making made-to-measure boots and tall shoes.
bottier.text: The bottier makes boots and tall shoes covering the leg, often made to measure, unlike the cordonnier, who also repairs everyday footwear. A luxury trade especially valued for equestrian and military footwear.

boucanier.label: Boucanier (buccaneer)
boucanier.summary: Hunter-butcher preparing smoked meat known as "boucané", notably in the Antilles.
boucanier.text: The boucanier smokes and dries meat on a boucan (a green-wood grill), an Amerindian technique adopted by settlers in the Antilles and Saint-Domingue in the 16th–17th centuries. The term later came, by extension, to denote the adventurers and freebooters of the Caribbean, the origin of the English word "buccaneer".

boucher.label: Boucher (butcher)
boucher.summary: Craftsman specialized in slaughtering, cutting and selling meat.
boucher.text: The boucher slaughters livestock (or buys meat already slaughtered), cuts it and sells it retail. An old trade, organized very early into a guild in towns, often hereditary from father to son, and frequently cited in civil records.

boucheur.label: Boucheur
boucheur.summary: Worker responsible for closing and sealing containers or openings.
boucheur.text: The boucheur carries out closing or sealing work, for example corking bottles or sealing casks, depending on the context of the workshop or manufactory. A generic term whose field of application varies by industry.

boucheur_a_l_emeri.label: Boucheur à l'émeri
boucheur_a_l_emeri.summary: Worker who polished the neck of a flask and the barrel of its stopper on a lathe using emery.
boucheur_a_l_emeri.text: The boucheur à l'émeri polishes, using a lathe, the neck of a flask and the barrel of its stopper with emery, so that they fit each other perfectly.

bouchonnier.label: Bouchonnier (cork-cutter)
bouchonnier.summary: Craftsman making stoppers, notably of cork, for bottles and casks.
bouchonnier.text: The bouchonnier makes stoppers intended to close bottles, casks and other containers, traditionally cut from cork. A trade linked to cork-producing regions (southwest France, Corsica) and to the rise of wine bottling.

bouchoteur.label: Bouchoteur
bouchoteur.summary: Mussel farmer exploiting bouchots, poles used to raise mussels.
bouchoteur.text: The bouchoteur raises mussels on bouchots, rows of poles planted in the tidal flat, a technique characteristic of mussel farming on the French Atlantic coast (Bay of Aiguillon, Mont-Saint-Michel).

bouclier.label: Bouclier
bouclier.summary: Craftsman making shields, pieces of defensive armour.
bouclier.text: The bouclier (as an occupational name) makes shields, defensive equipment used until this equipment declined in the face of firearms. A term mainly attested in old records linked to armour-making.

boudainier.label: Boudainier
boudainier.summary: Pork butcher specialized in making black pudding and other pork charcuterie.
boudainier.text: The boudainier (a variant of "boudinier") makes black pudding and other pork charcuterie products, an activity traditionally linked to family pig-slaughtering and village butcheries.

bouffon.label: Bouffon (jester)
bouffon.summary: Professional entertainer employed to amuse a court or a great lord through satire and buffoonery.
bouffon.text: The bouffon entertains a king, a lord or a court with jests, wordplay and satire that was often tolerated despite its boldness, enjoying an unusual freedom of speech. This role, common at European courts from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance, declined as court manners changed in the 17th century.

bougenier.label: Bougenier
bougenier.summary: Maker of arrows for archery or hunting.
bougenier.text: The bougenier makes arrows, cutting and fletching the wooden shafts intended for the bow or crossbow. An old trade linked to weaponry and hunting, now vanished with the decline of the bow as a weapon.

bougeonneur.label: Bougeonneur
bougeonneur.summary: Gardener specialized in disbudding and pruning fruit trees.
bougeonneur.text: The bougeonneur practises disbudding ("bougeonnage"), an operation consisting of removing surplus buds from fruit trees or vines to promote better fruiting. Specialized seasonal work in fruit growing and viticulture.

bouilleur.label: Bouilleur
bouilleur.summary: Distiller, notably of brandy, often a producer distilling his own fruit.
bouilleur.text: The bouilleur distils spirits, in particular brandy, using a still. The "bouilleur de cru" specifically denotes the producer who distils his own harvest (fruit, marc, cider), a particular tax status recognized in France until its gradual abolition in the 20th century.

bouissier.label: Bouissier
bouissier.summary: Craftsman working boxwood, a hard wood used for small turned objects.
bouissier.text: The bouissier shapes objects out of boxwood — combs, buttons, turned pieces — this dense, fine-grained wood being highly prized for small woodenware. A trade linked to regions where boxwood grows, notably Provence and Normandy.

boulanger.label: Boulanger (baker)
boulanger.text: The boulanger kneads, shapes and bakes bread, a staple food of the old diet, in a wood-fired oven that he owns or rents. Organized very early into a strictly regulated guild (price, weight of bread), it is one of the oldest urban trades and one of the most consistently attested in civil records.

boulanger_fournier.label: Boulanger fournier
boulanger_fournier.summary: Baker who owns or runs an oven, where he also bakes bread for other individuals.
boulanger_fournier.text: The boulanger fournier combines the roles of baker and oven-keeper: he owns an oven and bakes in it not only his own bread but also that of residents who have no private oven, for a fee. This role was particularly important in villages subject to the seigneurial monopoly of the manorial oven.

boulinier.label: Boulinier
boulinier.summary: Maritime rope-maker specialized in making bowlines and ship's cordage.
boulinier.text: The boulinier makes maritime cordage, notably bowlines (ropes used to trim the sails to the wind). A trade of naval rope-making, present in the great arsenal ports.

boulonnier.label: Boulonnier
boulonnier.summary: Craftsman making bolts and metal fastening parts.
boulonnier.text: The boulonnier makes bolts and metal fastening parts, an activity that developed with the rise of mechanical engineering and industrial construction in the 19th century.

bouquetier.label: Bouquetier
bouquetier.summary: Merchant or craftsman specialized in composing and selling bouquets of flowers.
bouquetier.text: The bouquetier composes and sells bouquets of flowers, often at markets or in front of churches. An essentially female trade in towns, linked to the flower-selling trade of the fleuriste.

bouracher.label: Bouracher
bouracher.summary: Hosiery worker, employed in making bonnets, stockings and knitted goods.
bouracher.text: The bouracher is a worker employed in hosiery, taking part in making bonnets, stockings or other knitted items, alongside the bonnetier who runs the workshop or business.

bourdier_de_la_garde.label: Bourdier de la garde
bourdier_de_la_garde.summary: Old local title combining a watch or guard function with an office called "bourdier".
bourdier_de_la_garde.text: The bourdier de la garde is a compound title, rare and little documented, combining a watch or guard function ("la garde") with a local office of "bourdier". The precise meaning of this office probably varied between communities and remains uncertain for lack of more detailed sources.

bourdonnier.label: Bourdonnier
bourdonnier.summary: Craftsman making bourdons: pilgrim's staffs, organ pipes or bagpipe drones.
bourdonnier.text: The bourdonnier makes bourdons, a term that, depending on context, denotes the iron-tipped pilgrim's staff, the large organ pipe giving the low note, or the bass reed of the bagpipe. A craft trade linked either to instrument-making or to equipping pilgrims.

bourgeois.label: Bourgeois (burgess)
bourgeois.summary: Free inhabitant of a town enjoying the status and rights of burgher-ship.
bourgeois.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the bourgeois is an inhabitant of a town who has acquired the legal status of burgher-ship, often by payment or by inheritance, giving access to certain rights (exemptions, participation in municipal affairs). The term frequently denotes an urban notable — merchant, officer, property owner — living off his rents or trade, without being noble or a manual craftsman.

bourgeonnier.label: Bourgeonnier
bourgeonnier.summary: Horticulturist practising grafting and plant propagation by budding.
bourgeonnier.text: The bourgeonnier practises budding (or bud-grafting), a grafting technique that inserts a bud of one variety under the bark of a rootstock. A specialized trade of horticulture and fruit growing.

bourgeteur.label: Bourgeteur
bourgeteur.summary: Wool worker working bourget, a coarse woollen fabric.
bourgeteur.text: The bourgeteur is a wool worker who works bourget, a coarse fabric woven from wool tow, used for modest clothing or furnishing fabrics.

bournobile.label: Bournobile
bournobile.summary: Night watchman responsible for watching over a locality during the hours of darkness.
bournobile.text: The bournobile is a night watchman, responsible for patrolling the streets of a town or village to ensure surveillance and raise the alarm in case of danger (fire, intrusion). A modest communal function, now vanished.

bourreau.label: Bourreau (executioner)
bourreau.summary: Officer of justice responsible for carrying out corporal and capital punishments.
bourreau.text: The bourreau, or executioner of high works, carries out sentences pronounced by the courts: capital executions, judicial torture, branding. A hereditary office in many families (the Sansons being the most famous example), the bourreau is at once an indispensable royal officer and a social outcast, marked by infamy and often living apart from the community. "Carnifex" (and its declined form "carnificis") is the Latin equivalent of the term, used in records written in Latin.

bourrelier.label: Bourrelier (harness maker)
bourrelier.summary: Craftsman making harnesses, collars and saddlery for draught animals.
bourrelier.text: The bourrelier makes and repairs harnesses, collars, bridles and other saddlery items intended for draught horses and oxen. An essential trade as long as animal traction dominated transport and farm work, very common in rural records into the 20th century.

bourretaine.label: Bourretaine
bourretaine.summary: Female worker processing bourrette, the part of the silk discarded when unwinding cocoons.
bourretaine.text: The bourretaine, related to the carder of filoselle, processes bourrette, the part of the silk discarded when unwinding cocoons, carding it to spin it into coarse thread.

bourricotier.label: Bourricotier
bourricotier.summary: Person whose trade is linked to driving or raising donkeys and small donkeys.
bourricotier.text: The bourricotier drives or raises donkeys ("bourricots"), used to carry light loads in hilly regions or for small itinerant trade.

bourrier.label: Bourrier
bourrier.summary: Merchant of bourre (waste wool or textile fibre) or, depending on context, a refuse collector.
bourrier.text: The bourrier is a merchant of bourre — waste wool, silk or other textile fibres recovered and resold as stuffing material — or, in some records, a refuse collector responsible for collecting rubbish. The precise sense depends on the local context of the record.

bourriquier.label: Bourriquier
bourriquier.summary: Person practising a transport or trading occupation linked to donkeys ("bourriques").
bourriquier.text: The bourriquier uses donkeys to transport goods or trades in them, an activity close to that of the bourricotier but designated by a different dialectal root depending on region.

bourselier.label: Bourselier
bourselier.summary: Craftsman making purses and coin-purses in leather or cloth.
bourselier.text: The bourselier makes purses intended to carry coin, in soft leather or cloth, often embroidered for a wealthy clientele. A trade close to that of the saddler and glover through the working of fine leather.

bouscatier.label: Bouscatier
bouscatier.summary: Gascon forest worker responsible for clearing and exploiting woodland.
bouscatier.text: The bouscatier exploits and clears woodland, a term derived from the Occitan-Gascon "bosc" (wood), common in southwestern France. He fells, cuts and transports wood to sawmills or points of sale.

bousilleur.label: Bousilleur
bousilleur.summary: Builder using bousillage, a mix of earth and straw pressed onto wattle, in construction.
bousilleur.text: The bousilleur builds walls in bousillage, a mixture of clayey earth and chopped straw pressed by hand onto a wooden frame (wattle), a traditional technique in regions without available stone such as the Landes or Périgord.

bousqueur.label: Bousqueur
bousqueur.summary: Port worker responsible for handling goods on the quays.
bousqueur.text: The bousqueur is a port worker who handles goods on the quays and in warehouses, loading and unloading ships. A physically demanding trade of port areas before mechanization.

boutefeu.label: Boutefeu
boutefeu.summary: Miner responsible for sinking shafts and galleries with explosives.
boutefeu.text: The boutefeu is the miner responsible for sinking shafts and galleries using explosives, a high-responsibility, high-risk post in the mining hierarchy.

boutilier.label: Boutilier
boutilier.text: In Auvergne, the boutilier is the assistant to the vacher (cowherd), responsible for helping him tend and care for the cattle.

boutillier.label: Boutillier (butler)
boutillier.summary: Officer responsible for managing provisions and table service, notably wine, in a great household.
boutillier.text: The boutillier (or bouteiller) manages the provisions and drink service — particularly the wine — in a great seigneurial household, a convent, or at the royal court. The "grand bouteiller de France" was, in the Middle Ages, one of the great officers of the crown, while the term more modestly denoted, in private households, the steward responsible for provisions.

boutillonnier.label: Boutillonnier
boutillonnier.text: In Bas-Poitou, the boutillonnier denotes the basket-maker, a craftsman who weaves willow to make baskets and other utilitarian objects.

boutonnier.label: Boutonnier (button-maker)
boutonnier.summary: Craftsman making buttons, in metal, mother-of-pearl, bone or fabric.
boutonnier.text: The boutonnier makes buttons intended for clothing, in various materials: metal, mother-of-pearl, horn, bone or covered fabric. A trade organized into a guild in several towns, including Paris and Méru, which specialized in mother-of-pearl buttons.

bouvier.label: Bouvier (ox-herd)
bouvier.summary: Driver of oxen, notably harnessed to the plough or cart.
bouvier.text: The bouvier drives and tends draught oxen, used to plough or pull carts before draught horses became widespread. A very common rural trade, especially in mixed farming-and-livestock regions.

bowetteur.label: Bowetteur
bowetteur.summary: Miner sinking bowettes, cross-cut galleries running through rock strata in a mine.
bowetteur.text: The bowetteur sinks bowettes, galleries driven through barren rock to connect seams of coal or ore, a term borrowed from Walloon mining vocabulary also used in the coalfields of Nord-Pas-de-Calais.

boyaudier.label: Boyaudier
boyaudier.summary: Craftsman preparing animal gut for food use (charcuterie) or fine rope-making (catgut cords).
boyaudier.text: The boyaudier cleans and prepares animal gut, used either as casings for charcuterie (black pudding, sausages), or, after twisting, as cords for musical instruments and sports rackets — a specialty sometimes denoted by the related term "boyautier". An unpleasant but indispensable trade, often practised near slaughterhouses.

braconnier.label: Braconnier (poacher)
braconnier.summary: Originally a beater and huntsman's assistant at seigneurial hunts; the sense of "illegal hunter" is later.
braconnier.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the braconnier is a huntsman or beater who takes part in seigneurial hunts, notably by handling scent hounds ("braques"). The modern sense of "one who hunts without right or permit" only gradually took hold as hunting rights were restricted to nobles and then to permit-holders, turning a lawful auxiliary role into a clandestine activity.

braelier.label: Braelier
braelier.summary: Weaver and maker of braies, breeches or trousers of cloth or leather.
braelier.text: The braelier weaves and makes braies — trousers or breeches of cloth or leather worn in the Middle Ages — before this garment was replaced by hose and then breeches.

braisetier.label: Braisetier
braisetier.summary: Merchant or producer of embers and charcoal used for heating.
braisetier.text: The braisetier produces or sells embers and charcoal used for domestic heating and certain craft uses (forge, cooking). A trade linked to forestry exploitation.

brandevinier.label: Brandevinier
brandevinier.text: The brandevinier distils or sells brandevin, an old name for brandy borrowed from the Dutch "brandewijn" (burnt wine). A term mainly attested in the North and East of France, regions in commercial contact with the Netherlands.

brasseur.label: Brasseur (brewer)
brasseur.text: The brasseur produces beer from malted barley and hops, in a brewery that he owns or where he works. A trade mainly established in the North and East of France, regions with a brewing tradition.

brassier.label: Brassier
brassier.summary: Farm day-labourer owning neither land nor draught animals, living solely from the strength of his arms.
brassier.text: The brassier hires out his labour by the day, owning neither land nor a team of animals, unlike the laboureur or even the bordier, who farm a plot of their own. He sits at the bottom of the peasant hierarchy under the Ancien Régime, alongside the manœuvre and the journalier, and made up the bulk of the hired agricultural workforce.

brayeur.label: Brayeur
brayeur.summary: Worker preparing textile fibres (hemp, flax) by breaking before spinning.
brayeur.text: The brayeur breaks hemp or flax stalks with a brake ("braie") to separate the textile fibres from the woody part, a step preceding spinning. Seasonal work in the countryside producing plant textiles (Normandy, Brittany).

brenetier.label: Brenetier
brenetier.summary: Officer or merchant responsible for supplying bran for a lord's hunting dogs.
brenetier.text: The brenetier gathers and supplies bran ("bren"), used to feed the hounds of a seigneurial pack, and also trades in it with other individuals. A modest function attached to the organization of the seigneurial hunt.

brenier.label: Brenier
brenier.summary: Person responsible for the upkeep of a pack of hunting hounds and for handling it during hunts.
brenier.text: The brenier watches over a lord's pack of hunting hounds — feeding, care, training — and handles it during hunting parties. A function close to that of the huntsman, attached to the organization of seigneurial hunting teams.

bresmen.label: Bresmen
bresmen.text: The bresmen is a manservant and porter, a worker responsible for carrying heavy loads in the service of an employer.

breyer.label: Breyer
breyer.text: The breyer is a merchant selling pestles, grinding tools used notably in the kitchen and in various crafts.

brigadier_facteur.label: Brigadier facteur
brigadier_facteur.summary: Departmental postal official responsible for supervising rural postmen.
brigadier_facteur.text: The brigadier facteur is a departmental postal official responsible for supervising and overseeing the rural postmen of his district.

brigandinier.label: Brigandinier
brigandinier.summary: Maker of the brigandine, an armour of cloth or leather fitted with metal plates.
brigandinier.text: The brigandinier makes the brigandine, a cuirass of cloth or leather covered with steel plates themselves covered in skin; the term also came, by extension, to denote the foot soldier wearing this protective garment.

brillanteur.label: Brillanteur
brillanteur.summary: Diamond worker who facet-cuts diamonds to make them more brilliant.
brillanteur.text: The brillanteur is a diamond worker who facet-cuts diamonds, above and below, to maximize their sparkle — the so-called "brilliant" cut.

brilleux.label: Brilleux
brilleux.summary: Poacher trapping birds at night by torchlight.
brilleux.text: The brilleux is a poacher who traps birds at night using a torch, an illegal hunting technique that dazzles the game.

brioleur.label: Brioleur
brioleur.summary: Carrier who took felled wood and bundles out of the forest that woodcutters had cut.
brioleur.text: The brioleur (or porteur de cotrets) carries out of the forest the wood and bundles felled by woodcutters, often on his own back or an animal's, to points of sale or storage. The regional variants "porteur de costraits", "de coustrets" or "de rogatrons" denote the same function.

briqueteur.label: Briqueteur (bricklayer)
briqueteur.text: The briqueteur lays bricks to build or face walls, to be distinguished from the briquetier, who makes them. A building trade linked to regions where brick replaces stone (North, Toulouse, Alsace).

briquetier.label: Briquetier (brickmaker)
briquetier.summary: Craftsman making fired bricks, from clay moulded and fired in a kiln.
briquetier.text: The briquetier moulds clay and fires it in a brickworks to produce building bricks. A seasonal trade tied to local clay deposits, often practised right next to construction sites.

brocanteur.label: Brocanteur (antique dealer)
brocanteur.summary: Merchant of second-hand objects and assorted curios.
brocanteur.text: The brocanteur buys and resells second-hand objects, furniture, curios and knick-knacks, often at the flea market or on a round. An old trading occupation, still very much alive today.

brocheur.label: Brocheur
brocheur.summary: Worker performing brochage — assembling and sewing a book's gatherings before binding.
brocheur.text: The brocheur assembles and sews the gatherings of a book (brochage), an intermediate step between printing and final binding. A book trade distinct from the bookbinder proper, who makes the rigid cover.

brodeur.label: Brodeur (embroiderer)
brodeur.summary: Craftsman decorating textiles by the technique of embroidery.
brodeur.text: The brodeur adorns fabrics with motifs sewn in thread, by needle or by hook, for clothing, household linen or liturgical ornaments. A widespread art trade, notably in religious workshops and at court.

bromurier.label: Bromurier
bromurier.summary: Publisher of postcards and photographs printed by the silver-bromide process.
bromurier.text: The bromurier produces photographic prints (notably postcards) using the silver-bromide process, a technique widespread at the turn of the 20th century with the rise of the illustrated postcard.

bronzeur.label: Bronzeur
bronzeur.summary: Craftsman specialized in working and gilding bronze.
bronzeur.text: The bronzeur works bronze, notably for making or finishing (patina, gilding) art objects, light fixtures or decorative elements. An art trade linked to furniture and statuary, booming in the 19th century.

broqueteur.label: Broqueteur
broqueteur.summary: Farm worker loading sheaves of grain onto carts at harvest time.
broqueteur.text: The broqueteur loads sheaves of grain onto carts at harvest time, using a broque (fork). Seasonal work in the countryside before mechanization.

broquier.label: Broquier
broquier.summary: Small-coopery craftsman making buckets, vats and hooped containers.
broquier.text: The broquier makes small pieces of coopery — buckets, vats, tubs — assembled from hooped staves. A trade close to that of the cooper but limited to smaller pieces.

brossier.label: Brossier (brush-maker)
brossier.summary: Craftsman making brushes from bristles, hair or plant fibres.
brossier.text: The brossier makes brushes for various uses (personal care, housework, industry), setting animal bristles or plant fibres into a wooden support. A trade attested as early as the Middle Ages, organized into a guild in several towns.

brouetteur.label: Brouetteur
brouetteur.summary: Worker transporting materials or goods with a wheelbarrow.
brouetteur.text: The brouetteur transports materials (earth, rubble, goods) by wheelbarrow, on building sites or in towns, before other means of handling became widespread.

bruleur.label: Brûleur
bruleur.summary: Worker whose trade involves a combustion operation: lime, charcoal or other materials.
bruleur.text: The brûleur carries out a controlled combustion operation, for example firing lime in a lime kiln or making charcoal in a stack. The precise sense of the term depends on the local context of the record.

bruleur_de_bateau.label: Brûleur de bateau
bruleur_de_bateau.summary: Probably a worker responsible for caulking boats.
bruleur_de_bateau.text: The brûleur de bateau is probably a worker responsible for caulking boats, a technique involving lightly scorching the hull to make it easier to waterproof.

brunisseur.label: Brunisseur (burnisher)
brunisseur.summary: Craftsman polishing metal or wood by burnishing to give it shine and lustre.
brunisseur.text: The brunisseur polishes a metal (gold, silver, steel) or wooden surface using a hard tool (the burnisher) to tighten the grain and give it a bright shine. A finishing trade used in goldsmithing, clockmaking and cabinetmaking.

brutiste.label: Brutiste
brutiste.summary: Tinsmith making household utensils out of tin-plate.
brutiste.text: The brutiste is a tinsmith specialized in making household utensils (pots, buckets, boxes) out of tin-plate, iron sheet covered with a thin layer of tin. A trade close to that of the coppersmith, who works copper and bronze instead.

buandier.label: Buandier
buandier.summary: Laundry worker working at the buanderie, a communal linen-washing place.
buandier.text: The buandier washes and cares for linen at the buanderie, a communal room or building equipped for washing, often in the service of an institution (convent, hospital, great household). A trade related to that of the blanchisseur, but more specifically tied to the place of work.

bucheron.label: Bûcheron (woodcutter)
bucheron.summary: Forest worker felling trees and cutting timber.
bucheron.text: The bûcheron fells trees in the forest and cuts the trunks into building or firewood timber, using an axe and then a saw. An essential trade of forestry, very common in wooded regions (Vosges, Massif Central, Landes).

bufetier.label: Bufetier
bufetier.summary: Craftsman making sideboards and storage furniture.
bufetier.text: The bufetier (a variant of "buffetier") makes sideboards, furniture intended for storing crockery and household linen. A trade close to the joiner and cabinetmaker.

buffetier.label: Buffetier
buffetier.text: The buffetier makes sideboards and chests, a specialty of cabinetmaking or furniture joinery.

bujourier.label: Bujourier
bujourier.summary: In Saintonge, a potter making bujours, large pots used for boiling laundry.
bujourier.text: In Saintonge, the bujourier is a potter specialized in making bujours, large earthenware vessels in which housewives boiled laundry.

buraliste_des_aides.label: Buraliste des Aides
buraliste_des_aides.summary: Office clerk responsible for collecting duties on foodstuffs and goods.
buraliste_des_aides.text: The buraliste des Aides is an office clerk responsible for collecting and administering the duties, charges and taxes levied on foodstuffs and goods circulating within the territory.

buratier.label: Buratier
buratier.summary: Weaver making burat or bure, a coarse woollen fabric.
buratier.text: The buratier is a weaver specialized in burat or bure, a coarse woollen fabric used for modest clothing and monastic habits.

buvetier.label: Buvetier
buvetier.summary: Keeper of a buvette or a small drinking establishment.
buvetier.text: The buvetier keeps a buvette, a small establishment serving drinks, often near a public place, a festival or a spa. A trade related to that of the innkeeper-tavern-keeper (cabaretier) but denoting a generally more modest business.

cabanier.label: Cabanier
cabanier.summary: Farmer holding a cabane, a small farm in the marshlands of western France (Aunis, Bas-Poitou).
cabanier.text: The cabanier farms a cabane, a modest farm characteristic of the drained marsh areas of Aunis and Bas-Poitou, where the dwelling and the farm share the same name. A status close to that of the bordier or the métayer depending on the region.

cabaretier.label: Cabaretier
cabaretier.summary: Keeper of a cabaret, an establishment serving drinks and sometimes food.
cabaretier.text: The cabaretier keeps a cabaret, a drinking establishment often associated with gaming or popular sociability, to be distinguished from the auberge, which also offers lodging. The variant "cabarotier" denotes the same trade.

cabrolie.label: Cabrolié
cabrolie.summary: Shepherd specialized in keeping and raising goats.
cabrolie.text: The cabrolié keeps and raises goats ("cabres" in Occitan), a pastoral activity distinct from sheep-keeping, practised notably in southern and mountainous regions where goats cope better with difficult terrain.

cabrolier.label: Cabrolier
cabrolier.summary: Driver or maker of cabriolets, light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriages.
cabrolier.text: The cabrolier drives or makes cabriolets, light carriages pulled by a single horse, very fashionable in the 18th and 19th centuries for fast urban travel.

cache_fouan.label: Cache-fouan
cache_fouan.summary: Hunter of moles and other burrowing pests.
cache_fouan.text: The cache-fouan tracks and captures moles ("fouan" in Old French) and other burrowing animals harmful to crops and meadows, using traps. A modest rural trade, sometimes paid by the village community.

cacoletiere.label: Cacoletière
cacoletiere.summary: Woman driving or making cacolets, pack seats or baskets used for transport on mule-back.
cacoletiere.text: The cacoletière is linked to the cacolet, a pack device made of two seats or baskets placed on either side of a mule, used in the Pyrenees to carry travellers, the sick or goods on paths unsuitable for carts.

cadenier.label: Cadenier
cadenier.summary: In shipbuilding, maker of chains, fittings and other metal parts for ships.
cadenier.text: The cadenier makes, in a naval context, chains, fittings and other metal parts used on ships — rigging hardware, anchors, various fittings. A trade linked to ports and arsenals.

cadissier.label: Cadissier
cadissier.summary: Weaver making cadis, a coarse, inexpensive woollen fabric.
cadissier.text: The cadissier weaves cadis, an inexpensive woollen fabric of modest quality, used for popular clothing or lining. This textile, very widespread from the Middle Ages to the modern era, gave its name to the trade.

cadranier.label: Cadranier
cadranier.summary: Maker of clock, compass and measuring-instrument dials.
cadranier.text: The cadranier makes clock dials, compass faces or other measuring instruments, engraving hours or graduations on metal or enamel. A precision trade associated with clockmaking and scientific instrumentation.

cadranier_gnomoniste.label: Cadranier gnomoniste
cadranier_gnomoniste.summary: Specialist in designing and making sundials.
cadranier_gnomoniste.text: The cadranier gnomoniste designs and builds sundials, applying gnomonics, the science of laying out dials according to latitude and orientation. A more learned specialty than ordinary clock-dial making, often practised by scholars or literate craftsmen.

cadre.label: Cadre (executive)
cadre.summary: Employee performing supervisory or managerial functions in a company or administration.
cadre.text: The term cadre denotes, in 20th-century France, an employee holding a managerial, supervisory or technical-responsibility position, distinct from rank-and-file employees. A socio-professional category that emerged with the rise of the large industrial and administrative enterprise.

cagetier.label: Cagetier
cagetier.text: The cagetier makes cages, of wood, wicker or wire, intended for keeping birds domestically. A modest craft trade, linked to the old taste for caged songbirds.

cageux.label: Cageux
cageux.summary: Worker rafting floated timber ("cages") down waterways.
cageux.text: The cageux assembles logs into rafts ("cages") and floats them downstream from logging areas to towns further down, a timber-rafting technique practised notably on the Loire and the Yonne, and as far as Quebec, where the word remains associated with the river log-drivers.

caiffa.label: Caïffa
caiffa.summary: Delivery employee of the Comptoirs Français du Caïffa, a door-to-door coffee and grocery company.
caiffa.text: The caïffa delivers, on a regular round, coffee, chocolate and various grocery products on behalf of the Comptoirs Français du Caïffa, a company founded at the end of the 19th century and remembered in France for its distinctive horse-drawn and later motorized delivery carts, until the mid-20th century.

caillerot.label: Caillerot
caillerot.summary: In the Vendée, a gatherer of fruit (apples, plums, cherries, chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts) resold to merchants.
caillerot.text: The caillerot gathers, in the Vendée, fallen or harvested fruit — apples, plums, cherries, chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts — to resell to local merchants or distillers. A seasonal activity supplementing farm work.

caillouteur.label: Caillouteur
caillouteur.summary: Gunflint cutter, a specialist in cutting flint for weaponry.
caillouteur.text: The caillouteur cuts gunflints (flint) intended to arm the mechanism of flintlock firearms. This craft industry, particularly developed in Loir-et-Cher (the Meusnes area), reached its peak in the 18th and 19th centuries before declining with the advent of percussion weapons.

caissier.label: Caissier (cashier)
caissier.summary: Employee responsible for handling funds in a shop, bank or administration.
caissier.text: The caissier runs the till of a commercial, banking or administrative establishment: receipts, payments, keeping current accounts. A position of trust requiring probity and rigour, common in trade and industry from the 19th century.

calandreur.label: Calandreur
calandreur.summary: Textile worker who presses and glazes fabrics by running them through the calender.
calandreur.text: The calandreur runs fabrics through the calender, a roller machine that presses and glazes them to give a smooth, shiny finish. A finishing step of the textile industry, notably for linens and sheeting.

calculateur.label: Calculateur
calculateur.summary: Person carrying out calculation work, notably accounting or scientific, before the computer era.
calculateur.text: The calculateur carries out calculation work — accounting, astronomical or statistical tables — often in the service of an administration, a bank or an observatory, at a time when this work was entirely manual.

caleconnier.label: Caleçonnier
caleconnier.summary: Craftsman making men's underpants and underwear.
caleconnier.text: The caleçonnier makes underpants, men's underwear, a specialized activity of textile garment-making.

calfat.label: Calfat (caulker)
calfat.summary: Naval worker who makes a ship's hull watertight by driving oakum between the planks.
calfat.text: The calfat (or calfateur) caulks the hulls of wooden ships by packing tarred oakum into the gaps between the planking, thereby ensuring watertightness. An essential trade of shipyards and ports until the decline of wooden shipbuilding.

calicot.label: Calicot
calicot.summary: Originally a merchant or seller of cotton cloth; became, in the 19th century, a popular nickname for the drapery-shop clerk.
calicot.text: The calicot denotes the cotton fabric originating from Calicut, India, and then, by extension, the person who sells it. The term became, in the 19th century, a popular, sometimes derogatory, nickname for a clerk in a drapery or dry-goods shop, popularized after Parisian drapers' clerks distinguished themselves as volunteers during the siege of the Trocadero in 1823.

calicotier.label: Calicotier
calicotier.summary: Maker of calico, plain or printed cotton cloth.
calicotier.text: The calicotier makes calico, a light cotton cloth, plain or printed, produced notably in the textile manufactories of the 18th and 19th centuries.

calier.label: Calier
calier.summary: Maritime worker responsible for handling goods in a ship's hold.
calier.text: The calier works in a ship's hold, loading, stowing and unloading the goods carried. A port trade linked to maritime trade.

calin.label: Câlin
calin.summary: Weaver from the Cholet region, known for its textile industry of handkerchiefs and linen.
calin.text: The câlin practises the trade of weaver in the Cholet area, whose textile industry — notably the famous Cholet handkerchief — made the region's reputation from the 18th century onward.

calmendier.label: Calmendier
calmendier.summary: Weaver making calmande (or calemande), a satin-finished twilled wool fabric.
calmendier.text: The calmendier weaves calmande (or calemande), a twilled woollen fabric, sturdy and satin-finished, used for clothing and furnishings from the 17th to the 19th century. A textile trade related to weaving but specialized in this particular weave.

calottier.label: Calottier
calottier.summary: Craftsman making skullcaps, small round caps covering the crown of the head.
calottier.text: The calottier makes skullcaps, round fitted caps worn notably by clerics, craftsmen, or under other headwear. A trade close to that of the hatter.

calvanier.label: Calvanier
calvanier.summary: Farm worker employed only for the duration of the harvest and threshing, to stack sheaves and thresh wheat.
calvanier.text: The calvanier is a seasonal farm worker, hired only for the duration of the harvest and threshing, responsible for stacking sheaves of grain and threshing wheat. Supplementary labour typical of the great harvests before mechanization.

camelot.label: Camelot
camelot.summary: Itinerant merchant selling small items on the public street or door to door.
camelot.text: The camelot hawks and sells small items, bazaar goods or newspapers, on the street, at markets or door to door, often crying his wares. The term still today denotes a street vendor and, in Quebec, a newspaper delivery boy.

camelotier.label: Camelotier
camelotier.summary: Maker or merchant of camelot, a fabric of goat hair or wool.
camelotier.text: The camelotier makes or sells camelot, a fabric woven originally from goat hair and later from wool, used for hard-wearing clothing. The word gave rise to the term "camelot" later denoting the street vendor, through a shift in meaning from the product sold to the seller.

camerier.label: Camérier
camerier.summary: Ecclesiastical dignitary responsible for serving the papal or episcopal chamber.
camerier.text: The camérier provides the personal service and stewardship of the chamber of a pope, cardinal or bishop, an honorific office of the papal court. The title still exists today in the papal household.

camionneur.label: Camionneur (truck driver)
camionneur.summary: Professional driver of trucks for transporting goods.
camionneur.text: The camionneur drives a truck and handles the road transport of goods, a trade that appeared with the development of the automobile in the 20th century, gradually replacing the carter and the carrier.

campanier.label: Campanier
campanier.summary: Bell-ringer, or person walking ahead of funeral processions ringing a small bell.
campanier.text: The campanier rings the bells of a church, or walks ahead of funeral processions ringing a small bell to announce their passage.

campaniste.label: Campaniste
campaniste.summary: Person responsible for the upkeep of belfries, steeples and bells.
campaniste.text: The campaniste maintains belfries, steeples and the bells installed in them, a trade related to bell-founding and its mechanical maintenance.

campardon.label: Campardon
campardon.summary: Steward collecting the champart, a seigneurial due in kind.
campardon.text: The campardon is a seigneurial steward responsible for collecting the champart, a due in kind owed to the lord on harvests.

cancelier.label: Cancelier
cancelier.summary: In Normandy, maker of fences and trellises.
cancelier.text: In Normandy, the cancelier makes fences and trellises surrounding a house or garden.

canneur.label: Canneur
canneur.summary: Craftsman practising caning, the weaving of rattan strands to seat chairs.
canneur.text: The canneur weaves strands of rattan or rush to seat and back chairs, a technique known as caning. A furniture trade, often complementary to that of the chair-maker.

canonnier.label: Canonnier (gunner)
canonnier.summary: Soldier specialized in serving artillery pieces.
canonnier.text: The canonnier serves in the artillery, responsible for operating and firing cannon, both on land and aboard warships. A rank or role very frequently found in military service records.

canotier.label: Canotier
canotier.summary: Boatman driving a canoe or a light craft.
canotier.text: The canotier drives a canoe, a light rowing or sailing craft, to transport passengers or goods on calm waters. Not to be confused with the hat of the same name, which appeared later.

cantinier.label: Cantinier
cantinier.summary: Person responsible for collective catering, notably within an army on campaign.
cantinier.text: The cantinier keeps a canteen, providing food and drink to a community, a garrison or troops on campaign. The cantinière, a female presence attached to regiments until the early 20th century, held an emblematic role in the French army, selling provisions and tobacco to soldiers and sometimes assisting them in combat.

cantonnier.label: Cantonnier (road mender)
cantonnier.summary: Municipal employee responsible for maintaining the roads of the commune.
cantonnier.text: The cantonnier is a municipal employee responsible for maintaining the roads and lanes of the commune: repair, snow clearing, upkeep of ditches and verges.

canut.label: Canut
canut.summary: In Lyon, a worker in the silk industries.
canut.text: In Lyon, the canut is a worker in the silk industries; the term "ferrandinier" was adopted by silk workers after the canut uprisings of 1831 and 1834, in reaction to the word's increasingly derogatory connotation.

caoutchoutier.label: Caoutchoutier
caoutchoutier.summary: Factory worker coating fabrics with rubber to waterproof them.
caoutchoutier.text: The caoutchoutier works in a factory where he coats fabrics and other objects with rubber to make them waterproof or airtight.

caparaconniere.label: Caparaçonnière
caparaconniere.summary: Maker of caparisons, cloths protecting horses from the weather and insects.
caparaconniere.text: The caparaçonnière makes caparisons, cloths used to cover horses to protect them from the weather or insects.

capitaine.label: Capitaine (captain)
capitaine.summary: Military officer or commander of a ship.
capitaine.text: The capitaine commands a company of troops or a ship, depending on the military or maritime context of the record. An intermediate officer rank, frequently cited in records concerning soldiers and sailors.

caporal.label: Caporal (corporal)
caporal.summary: Non-commissioned officer of the first rank, at the head of a squad.
caporal.text: The caporal is the first non-commissioned rank in the infantry, commanding a squad of soldiers. A rank frequently mentioned in military records.

carabinier.label: Carabinier
carabinier.text: The carabinier is a horseman armed with a carbine, a light cavalry unit attested as early as the 17th century.

caravanseraskier.label: Caravanseraskier
caravanseraskier.summary: Person responsible for receiving and watching over travellers at a caravanserai.
caravanseraskier.text: The caravanseraskier manages a caravanserai, an establishment offering lodging to travellers and their pack animals along the trade routes of the Near and Middle East. A rare term in French, Gallicized to denote this function of Eastern origin.

carcanier.label: Carcanier
carcanier.summary: Rare term of uncertain occupational use, possibly linked to making iron collars.
carcanier.text: The little-attested term carcanier may denote a maker of carcans (iron collars used as an instrument of punishment) or another activity close to it by the word's root. Its precise use remains uncertain.

carcassier.label: Carcassier
carcassier.summary: Craftsman making carcasses, internal structures serving as a support for various manufactured objects.
carcassier.text: The carcassier makes carcasses, frames or support structures (wood, metal, wicker) intended to receive a covering or trim, for example in hat-making, saddlery or furniture-making.

cardeur.label: Cardeur (carder)
cardeur.summary: Textile worker teasing out and aligning fibres of wool, cotton or flax using cards.
cardeur.text: The cardeur teases out, cleans and aligns textile fibres (wool, cotton, flax) using cards, tools fitted with metal points, preparing the raw material for spinning. An essential and very common step of craft textile-making.

cardeur_de_filouzelle.label: Cardeur de filoselle
cardeur_de_filouzelle.summary: Carder specialized in processing filoselle, silk waste or tow.
cardeur_de_filouzelle.text: The cardeur de filoselle cards filoselle, a coarse thread drawn from silk waste and tow unfit for fine spinning, used for lower-quality fabrics. A carding specialty linked to the silk industry.

cardeur_de_soye.label: Cardeur de soie
cardeur_de_soye.summary: Worker carding silk to prepare the fibres before spinning.
cardeur_de_soye.text: The cardeur de soie ("soye", old spelling) teases out and aligns silk fibres before spinning, a preparatory step specific to the silk industry, notably developed in the Lyon region.

cardier.label: Cardier
cardier.summary: Craftsman making cards, boards fitted with points used to tease out textile fibres.
cardier.text: The cardier makes cards, boards bristling with metal points used by carders to prepare textile fibres. A trade distinct from the carder, who uses these tools rather than making them.

carillonneur.label: Carillonneur (bell-ringer)
carillonneur.summary: Musician playing the carillon, a set of tuned bells.
carillonneur.text: The carillonneur plays the carillon, an instrument made of several tuned bells, installed in a bell tower or belfry, a tradition especially alive in northern France, Flanders and the Netherlands.

carreleur.label: Carreleur (tiler)
carreleur.summary: Craftsman laying terracotta, stone or ceramic tiles on floors or walls.
carreleur.text: The carreleur lays tiles — terracotta, stone or ceramic — to cover floors and walls. The variant "carlier" denotes the same trade in certain regions.

carrelier.label: Carrelier (tile-maker)
carrelier.summary: Craftsman making terracotta, faience or ceramic tiles.
carrelier.text: The carrelier makes tiles intended for floor or wall covering, to be distinguished from the carreleur, who lays them. A trade linked to local tileworks and faience workshops.

carrie.label: Carrié
carrie.summary: Cemetery keeper responsible for its upkeep and burials; the closest modern equivalent is the monumental mason.
carrie.text: The carrié maintains a cemetery and takes part in burials, a modest function whose closest equivalent today would be the funerary monumental mason, responsible for monuments and graves.

carrier.label: Carrier (quarryman)
carrier.summary: Worker or operator specialized in extracting stone in a quarry.
carrier.text: The carrier extracts stone in a quarry, by hand or with explosives depending on the period, to supply building sites with rubble stone or ashlar. The regional variants "carreur", "carriéreur", "pierrieur" or "quarriereur" denote the same trade.

carronier.label: Carronier
carronier.summary: Itinerant brickmaker making bricks directly on the building site.
carronier.text: The carronier is an itinerant brickmaker who makes bricks ("carrons") directly on the construction site, rather than running a fixed brickworks, thereby avoiding the transport of heavy materials.

carrossier.label: Carrossier (coachbuilder)
carrossier.summary: Craftsman making, repairing and decorating vehicle bodywork.
carrossier.text: The carrossier builds, repairs and decorates vehicle bodywork — coaches and horse-drawn carriages originally, then automobiles from the 20th century. A demanding art trade, combined with joinery, saddlery and painting.

carruyer.label: Carruyer
carruyer.summary: Porter loading and unloading goods, notably on quays or in warehouses.
carruyer.text: The carruyer is a porter, a worker responsible for loading and unloading solid goods on his own back, an activity close to that of the hook-porter or unloader in ports and market halls.

cartier.label: Cartier (card-maker)
cartier.summary: Maker of playing cards and, sometimes, cartographer.
cartier.text: The cartier makes playing cards, printed and coloured according to techniques codified by guild as early as the 15th century. The term could also, by extension, denote a drawer of geographical maps.

carton.label: Carton
carton.summary: Driver of covered, horse-drawn wagons used to transport goods.
carton.text: The carton drives vehicles fitted with tarpaulins and drawn by horses, used to transport goods by road. A regional term related to the trade of carter.

cartonneur.label: Cartonneur
cartonneur.summary: Worker making cardboard and cardboard packaging.
cartonneur.text: The cartonneur makes cardboard and cardboard packaging, in an industrial cardboard mill, an activity booming from the 19th century with the development of packaging.

cartonnier.label: Cartonnier
cartonnier.summary: Craftsman making objects out of cardboard by assembly and decoration (boxes, cases).
cartonnier.text: The cartonnier assembles and decorates cardboard objects — boxes, cases, various cardboard items — unlike the cartonneur, who produces the cardboard itself in large industrial quantities.

caseyeur.label: Caseyeur
caseyeur.summary: Fisherman using pots or traps to catch shellfish and fish.
caseyeur.text: The caseyeur fishes using pots or traps, a technique used notably to catch shellfish (lobsters, crabs, spiny lobsters) along the coast.

casquetier.label: Casquetier (cap-maker)
casquetier.summary: Craftsman making caps and peaked headwear.
casquetier.text: The casquetier makes caps, soft headwear fitted with a peak, whose use spread notably in the 19th century among working-class and military circles.

casse_moute.label: Casse-moute
casse_moute.summary: Itinerant miller collecting grain at people's homes to grind it.
casse_moute.text: The casse-moute travels from farm to farm to collect grain to be ground, bringing back the flour in exchange for a milling fee. An itinerant variant of the miller's trade, in regions lacking a nearby mill.

casseur_de_voitures.label: Casseur de voitures
casseur_de_voitures.summary: Forerunner of the modern car breaker, specialized in dismantling and salvaging parts from horse-drawn vehicles.
casseur_de_voitures.text: The casseur de voitures dismantles worn-out horse-drawn vehicles to salvage and resell reusable parts — wood, ironwork, wheels — an activity that is the direct forerunner of the modern car breaker.

catisseur.label: Catisseur
catisseur.summary: Textile worker handling the glazing and finishing of fabrics through catissage.
catisseur.text: The catisseur practises catissage, a finishing operation that smooths and glazes a fabric (notably wool) under a hot press, to give it a shiny, even appearance.

caucheteur.label: Caucheteur
caucheteur.summary: Craftsman who made stockings and tall shoes of cloth or soft leather.
caucheteur.text: The caucheteur made hose or ankle boots, a term derived from "chausse" used in certain regions of northern and western France. He is close to the hosier or the shoemaker depending on whether he worked cloth or leather. The word occasionally appears in civil records to denote a craftsman of leg and foot wear.

caussetier.label: Caussetier
caussetier.summary: Farmer working the arid limestone lands of the Causses, notably in the Quercy.
caussetier.text: The caussetier is a farmer adapted to the poor, stony soils of the causses, those limestone plateaus of southwestern France (Quercy, Larzac). Farming there was traditionally geared toward sheep raising and drought-resistant crops. The term, regional, is found mainly in the records of parishes located on these plateaus.

cavalier.label: Cavalier (horseman)
cavalier.summary: Man fighting or travelling on horseback, in the military or civil sense.
cavalier.text: The term cavalier most often denotes a soldier serving in a mounted unit (cavalry), but it can also simply describe a man riding a horse in civilian life. In old records, it generally indicates mounted military service, as opposed to the foot soldier. The word is also sometimes used as a courtesy title for a gentleman.

cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.label: Cavalier dans une Compagnie de Remonte
cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.summary: Cavalry soldier assigned to buying and training troop horses.
cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.text: The cavalier dans une compagnie de remonte is a soldier of a cavalry regiment assigned to the unit responsible for buying and training the mounts intended for the troops.

cavelier.label: Cavelier
cavelier.summary: Keeper of an establishment offering food and drink for payment.
cavelier.text: The cavelier kept an inn, a tavern or an alehouse, offering food and drink to travellers and local residents. The term is a regional variant close to cabaretier or tavernier. It appears in some records from western and central France.

cavetonnier.label: Chavetonnier
cavetonnier.summary: Shoemaker specialized in making shoes from sheepskin.
cavetonnier.text: The chavetonnier (sometimes spelled cavetonnier or çavetonnier) is a leather craftsman close to the cobbler, specialized in shoes made from sheepskin, a less costly leather than calf or cattle hide. This regional term is found in some records from western and central France, often under fluctuating spellings.

caveur.label: Caveur
caveur.summary: Docker responsible for lowering casks with pulleys into the holds of ships.
caveur.text: The caveur worked on the quays and in ports, operating the pulleys and tackle needed to load or lower casks and heavy goods into the holds ("caves") of ships. A demanding port trade, related to that of the stevedore.

cazerotier.label: Cazerotier
cazerotier.summary: Craftsman making the wooden moulds and forms used to drain and shape cheese.
cazerotier.text: The cazerotier made "cazerottes" or "cazes", perforated moulds of wood or rush used by cheesemakers to drain the curd and give the cheese its shape. This craft trade, linked to the regional cheese industry, is found mainly in dairy-farming areas.

ceinturier.label: Ceinturier (belt maker)
ceinturier.summary: Leather craftsman specialized in making belts and matching accessories.
ceinturier.text: The ceinturier made belts, civilian waist-belts and small leather accessories, a craft close to saddlery and fine leatherwork. He is distinct from the ceinturonnier, who was geared more towards military equipment.

ceinturonnier.label: Ceinturonnier
ceinturonnier.summary: Maker of military belts and leather equipment for soldiers.
ceinturonnier.text: The ceinturonnier made the belts and leather equipment worn by soldiers (baldrics, pouches, scabbards), linked to military supply. This trade is distinguished from the civilian ceinturier by its essentially military clientele.

cellerier.label: Cellerier (cellarer)
cellerier.summary: Monk responsible for managing the monastery's provisions and material goods.
cellerier.text: The cellerier held one of the most important monastic offices after that of the abbot: he administered the provisions, cellars, lands and revenues of the community, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict. The term is also found more broadly to denote a steward responsible for provisions in a great household or a chapter.

cendrier.label: Cendrier
cendrier.summary: Craftsman who recovered and processed wood ash for the soap and glass industries.
cendrier.text: The cendrier collected wood ash from domestic hearths to resell it to makers of lye, potash, soap or glass, who needed it as an alkaline raw material. This recycling trade was an important link in pre-industrial craft production.

cendrilleur.label: Cendrilleur
cendrilleur.summary: Worker responsible for removing the ash produced by hearths, forges and industrial plant.
cendrilleur.text: The cendrilleur carried out the regular cleaning and removal of ash accumulated in forge hearths, kilns and boilers, an arduous but necessary task for the proper running of the plant. He differs from the cendrier, who valorized ash as raw material rather than simply removing it.

censal.label: Censal
censal.summary: Financial broker trading in annuities and credit operations, a Mediterranean-usage term.
censal.text: The censal is a financial intermediary, attested notably in Mediterranean ports such as Marseille, who traded in constituted annuities ("censales") and various credit instruments, on the model of the well-documented Catalan censal in Barcelona's trade. The term reflects the influence of Catalan and Provençal commercial practices on the financial vocabulary of the Midi.

censeur.label: Censeur
censeur.summary: Officer or official responsible for examining and controlling writings, morals or seigneurial rights depending on context.
censeur.text: The term censeur covers several realities depending on period and context: a royal official responsible for approving publications before printing, but also, in an older sense linked to the word "cens", one who assesses or collects a due. In schools, it also denotes a supervisor responsible for discipline. The precise meaning thus depends heavily on the source document.

censeur_royal.label: Censeur royal (royal censor)
censeur_royal.summary: Royal official responsible for examining manuscripts and authorizing their publication.
censeur_royal.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the censeur royal (or censeur des livres) was a man of letters appointed by the crown to examine manuscripts before granting the royal privilege, a necessary condition for their legal printing. This function of prior control over publishing, entrusted to specialists recognized in their field, structured the whole of the French book world until the Revolution.

censier.label: Censier
censier.summary: Holder or collector of the cens, an annual due owed to the landed lord.
censier.text: The censier collected, or owed, the cens, a fixed due paid annually by the tenant (censitaire) to his lord in recognition of the latter's eminent ownership of the land. This system, inherited from the medieval cens-based tenure, durably structured land relations in the French countryside until its abolition in 1789-1793.

cercayres.label: Cercayrès
cercayres.summary: Professional mushroom gatherer, notably in the Périgord.
cercayres.text: The cercayrès (or cercaïre) denotes, in the Périgord and neighbouring regions, a professional gatherer of mushrooms — ceps chief among them — resold at local markets. This small seasonal gathering trade often supplemented other farming activities.

cercleur.label: Cercleur (hooper)
cercleur.summary: Coopering worker who fits and adjusts wooden or metal hoops onto casks.
cercleur.text: The cercleur takes part in making casks and barrels by fitting and tightening the hoops — bands of split wood and, later, iron — that hold the staves together. He is distinct from the cerclier, who shapes the hoops themselves, fitting and manufacture being two separate steps in the cooper's trade.

cerclier.label: Cerclier
cerclier.summary: Maker of wooden or metal hoops used to hold casks and barrels together.
cerclier.text: The cerclier shapes the hoops — rings of split wood (hazel, chestnut) and, from the 19th century, iron — that encircle casks and barrels to hold the staves together. The trade is distinct from that of the cercleur, who fits the hoops onto the cask rather than making them. The term is found under many dialectal spellings (cercillier, cerqueleur, cerquelier, cerquemaneur), all formed on the root "cercle" (hoop).

cerenceresse.label: Cerenceresse
cerenceresse.summary: Regional synonym for filassière, a female worker who combed tow to prepare it for spinning.
cerenceresse.text: The cerenceresse is a female worker who combs tow (flax or hemp fibres) with a hackle, a comb with iron points, to disentangle it and make it fit for spinning. The term, with the "-eresse" ending characteristic of feminine occupational names in Old French, is attested as a regional synonym for filassière.

cerisier.label: Cerisier
cerisier.text: The cerisier is a fruit grower devoted to growing cherry trees and selling their fruit. The term denotes either a specialized grower or simply a farmer owning a cherry orchard in certain producing regions.

cerusier.label: Cérusier
cerusier.summary: Maker of ceruse, a white lead-based pigment used in paint.
cerusier.text: The cérusier produces ceruse (basic lead carbonate), a highly opaque white pigment used in paint and formerly in cosmetics to whiten the complexion. Its manufacture, by exposing sheets of lead to vinegar fumes, exposed workers to severe lead poisoning, making it a notoriously dangerous trade before its regulation and gradual prohibition.

cervoisier.label: Cervoisier
cervoisier.summary: Brewer of cervoise, a fermented grain beverage, ancestor of beer.
cervoisier.text: The cervoisier brews cervoise, an unhopped beer made from barley or other grains, consumed since Gaulish antiquity and throughout the Middle Ages. The term gradually gave way to "brasseur" as hops became widespread from the late Middle Ages onward.

cetereau.label: Cétéreau
cetereau.summary: Pit-saw sawyer working in the Forez region, cutting tree trunks into planks.
cetereau.text: The cétéreau is a pit-saw sawyer of the Forez region: he cuts tree trunks into planks with a saw, work carried out in a team of two, one sawyer (the "chevrier") standing on the trunk itself set on a trestle (the "chèvre"), the other (the "renard" or "renardier") pulling the saw from below.

chableur.label: Chableur
chableur.summary: Forest worker who fells or moves trees using a cable and a winch.
chableur.text: The chableur uses a "chable" (cable or winch) to fell trees in a controlled manner or to move them to points of floating, a technique used notably in forestry and in transporting timber by water. The term also gave rise to "chablis", denoting trees felled by wind.

chableur_de_pertuis.label: Chableur de Pertuis
chableur_de_pertuis.summary: Worker responsible for handling cables at the pertuis, narrow passages of navigable rivers.
chableur_de_pertuis.text: The chableur de pertuis worked at the "pertuis", the narrow passes or sluices of rivers developed for navigation or timber floating, where he handled cables and ropes to get boats or timber rafts through. This specialized river trade was particularly present on the rivers of the Massif Central and the Paris Basin developed for floating.

chabretaire.label: Chabretaire
chabretaire.summary: Player of the chabrette, a traditional bagpipe of the Limousin, often an itinerant musician.
chabretaire.text: The chabretaire plays the chabrette, a traditional mouth-blown bagpipe of the Limousin and Poitou, fitted with a bone blowpipe mount. He livened up dances, weddings and village festivals, often travelling from town to town for his performances.

chagrinier.label: Chagrinier
chagrinier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making shagreen, a grained leather used in luxury fine leather goods.
chagrinier.text: The chagrinier works shagreen, a grained leather obtained from goat, sheep or ray skin, treated to achieve its characteristic granular texture. This leather was highly prized for luxury bookbinding, cases and small leather goods in the 18th and 19th centuries.

chaideur.label: Chaideur
chaideur.summary: Metalworker responsible for crushing iron ore before processing.
chaideur.text: The chaideur works in a metallurgical operation, where he crushes and grinds iron ore to prepare it for smelting in the blast furnace or forge. This trade belongs to the pre-industrial iron-production chain.

chainetier.label: Chaînetier
chainetier.summary: Maker of chains and small chains, often for decorative or light use.
chainetier.text: The chaînetier makes small chains, notably fine chains used in jewellery, clockmaking or light domestic use. He is distinct from the chaînier, who is geared toward producing heavier metal chains for industrial or maritime use.

chainier.label: Chaînier
chainier.summary: Maker of metal chains, notably for industrial, agricultural or maritime use.
chainier.text: The chaînier forges or assembles larger metal chains intended for heavy uses: mooring, lifting, agricultural traction. The trade developed particularly with the industrialization of the 19th century.

chainiste.label: Chaîniste
chainiste.summary: Worker specialized in making or maintaining chains and chain mechanisms.
chainiste.text: The chainiste works on chains and chain mechanisms, a term that covers both the traditional craft of the forged chain and, more recently, mechanical and industrial applications (transmission chains, for example).

chaintrier.label: Chaintrier
chaintrier.summary: Medieval craftsman specialized in setting up fences and trellises around plots of land.
chaintrier.text: The chaintrier takes his name from the "chaintre", an Old French term for the strip of unploughed land bordering a field. He would have been responsible for laying out and marking these agricultural borders and fences, a role close to that of the fence-maker in medieval countryside.

chaisier.label: Chaisier (chairmaker)
chaisier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making chairs, stools and seats of wood and straw.
chaisier.text: The chaisier makes chairs and various seats, assembling a turned-wood frame fitted with a woven-straw, rush or solid-wood seat. This trade long constituted an important local craft specialty in certain rural regions of France.

chalandon.label: Chalandon
chalandon.summary: Boatman driving a chaland, a flat-bottomed craft used for river transport.
chalandon.text: The chalandon (also spelled chalandou in certain regions, notably on the Loire) drives a chaland, a flat-bottomed boat typical of French river navigation, used to carry goods and materials along rivers. This river trade declined with the rise of the railway in the 19th century.

chaliste.label: Châliste
chaliste.text: The châliste weaves shawls, those large pieces of cloth worn over the shoulders, whose fashion boomed considerably in the 19th century with the craze for cashmere-style shawls. This specialized textile trade developed notably in wool- and silk-producing centres.

chalmandrier.label: Chalmandrier
chalmandrier.summary: Weaver specialized in making glazed woollen fabrics with a satin finish.
chalmandrier.text: The chalmandrier wove woollen fabrics called "chalmandes" or "calmandes", glazed fabrics with a satin-like finish obtained by a particular pressing, used notably for clothing and furnishings in the 17th and 18th centuries.

chaloupier.label: Chaloupier
chaloupier.summary: Builder and repairer of longboats, small craft used at sea or on rivers.
