copiste.text: The copiste reproduces texts by hand — manuscripts, legal deeds, musical scores — before printing and then the typewriter became widespread. In medieval monasteries, copyists, often monks, ensured the transmission of ancient texts in the scriptoria.

coq.label: Coq
coq.summary: Cook aboard a ship, responsible for preparing the crew's meals.
coq.text: The coq is a ship's cook, a term borrowed from the Dutch "kok". Aboard merchant or warships, he prepares the crew's meals under often rudimentary conditions, with limited provisions during long voyages.

coqueleux.label: Coqueleux
coqueleux.text: The coqueleux raises cocks intended for cockfighting, a traditional practice in certain regions of northern France.

coquetier.label: Coquetier
coquetier.summary: Itinerant merchant collecting eggs, poultry and small farm produce to resell in town.
coquetier.text: The coquetier is a merchant, often itinerant, who collects eggs and poultry from surrounding farms to resell them at urban markets. The term, not to be confused with the object of the same name (the small egg cup), is attested in many regions under varied dialectal forms.

corailleur.label: Corailleur
corailleur.summary: Person who harvests or works coral.
corailleur.text: The corailleur harvests coral at sea, notably in the Mediterranean, or works it in a workshop to make jewellery and ornamental objects.

corbelier.label: Corbelier
corbelier.text: The corbelier is a basket-maker specialized in making willow-woven baskets.

cordelier.label: Cordelier
cordelier.summary: Craftsman making ropes and cordage from plant fibres.
cordelier.text: The cordelier, or cordier, makes ropes, twine and cordage by twisting together fibres of hemp, flax or esparto. The trade was often practised outdoors, in long walkways called ropewalks, where the craftsman walked backward while twisting his thread. Not to be confused with the Cordeliers, the Franciscan religious order bearing the same name because of the triple-knotted cord girding their habit.

cordoneuse.label: Cordoneuse
cordoneuse.summary: Openwork embroiderer tracing the curved shapes of the work with a small cord.
cordoneuse.text: The cordoneuse is an openwork embroiderer who traces, using a small cord, the curved shapes to be given to the work before the openwork proper.

cordonnier.label: Cordonnier (shoemaker)
cordonnier.text: The cordonnier makes new leather shoes, to be distinguished from the cobbler, who only repairs them. The term comes from "cordouan", a tanned goatskin originating from Cordoba much used for fine footwear. It is one of the most common craft trades in civil records; old spelling and surname variants such as Corvisier, Courvisier or Courvoisier are found.

cordouannier.label: Cordouannier
cordouannier.summary: Shoemaker working cordovan, goatskin leather from Cordoba.
cordouannier.text: The cordouannier is a shoemaker specialized in working cordovan, goatskin leather from Cordoba, a noble material of old shoemaking.

cornet.label: Cornet
cornet.summary: Musician playing the cornet, a wind instrument used notably in brass bands and orchestras.
cornet.text: Cornet denotes the musician playing the cornet à pistons, or, more anciently, the cornett ("cornet à bouquin"), a wind instrument used in municipal brass bands, orchestras and sometimes military bands, notably from the 19th century.

cornetier.label: Cornetier
cornetier.summary: Craftsman working cattle horn to make combs, buttons or lanterns.
cornetier.text: The cornetier prepares and works cattle or other animal horn, softened by heat and then moulded or cut, to make combs, buttons, powder flasks, knife handles or lantern panes, before horn was supplanted by other materials such as celluloid.

corratier.label: Corratier
corratier.summary: In Haute-Loire, a wine broker and merchant checking quality, quantity and provenance.
corratier.text: The corratier is, in Haute-Loire, a wine broker and merchant responsible for checking the quality, quantity and provenance of wine.

corroyeur.label: Corroyeur (currier)
corroyeur.summary: Craftsman who softens and finishes leather after tanning.
corroyeur.text: The corroyeur takes over after the tanner: he softens, thins, smooths and dyes tanned leather to make it usable by leatherworkers (shoemakers, saddlers, glovers). Currying comprises beating, degreasing and smoothing operations that determine the final quality of the leather.

corsetier.label: Corsetier
corsetier.text: The corsetier makes corsets, a boned undergarment intended to shape and slim the figure.

cotier.label: Côtier
cotier.summary: Agent helping omnibus or stagecoach teams climb hills.
cotier.text: The côtier assisted horse-drawn teams — omnibuses, stagecoaches — on difficult climbs, by temporarily adding reinforcing horses (the reinforcing team generally numbered three horses) for the duration of the hill. The term derives from "côte" (hill), and is found mainly in towns with marked relief in the 19th century.

cotonier.label: Cotonier
cotonier.summary: Textile worker employed at the various stages of preparing and spinning cotton.
cotonier.text: The cotonier works cotton from raw material to thread: carding, combing, spinning, then weaving depending on the workshop. The term spread with the rise of the French cotton industry from the 18th century, particularly in Normandy and the Vosges.

cotrier.label: Cotrier
cotrier.summary: Worker who carries cotrets — small bundles of wood — from the cutting site to the forest edge.
cotrier.text: The cotrier removes the wood and bundles (cotrets) felled by woodcutters and carries them to the edge of the forest, where they are piled before being loaded by carters for transport to town or points of sale. The name derives from "cotret", a small bundle of firewood.

coulie.label: Coulie
coulie.summary: Small shopkeeper practising high-interest lending to miners.
coulie.text: The coulie keeps a shop near mining operations and practises credit or usury toward mine workers, often as wage advances repayable in kind or in labour. This rare term reflects the debt practices common in mining basins.

coulier.label: Coulier
coulier.summary: Porter of the Garonne river ports, responsible for loading and unloading boats.
coulier.text: The coulier is a porter working in the river ports of the Garonne, responsible for loading and unloading gabares and other trading boats. This handling trade, sometimes organized into a port guild, declined with falling river traffic in the face of the railway.

coulissier.label: Coulissier
coulissier.summary: Unofficial broker operating at the Paris Bourse, on the margins of licensed stockbrokers.
coulissier.text: The coulissier trades securities at the Paris Bourse without holding the official office of stockbroker, operating "à la coulisse", that is, in the corridors and outside the official trading floor. This parallel market, tolerated and then regulated, notably handled securities not listed on the official floor, until the two markets merged in the 20th century.

coultre.label: Coultre
coultre.summary: Sacristan responsible for the upkeep of the church and sacristy.
coultre.text: The coultre, or coutre, is a sacristan, responsible for the upkeep of the place of worship, the keeping of sacred objects and assisting the priest during services. The term derives from the Old French "costre" (keeper, then sacristan), of which "coltre"/"coultre" is an attested variant.

coupeur_de_cheveux.label: Coupeur de cheveux
coupeur_de_cheveux.summary: Itinerant craftsman who bought peasant women's hair to resell it to wigmakers.
coupeur_de_cheveux.text: The coupeur de cheveux travelled the countryside to buy and cut women's hair, often in exchange for small change or ribbons, in order to resell it to makers of wigs and hairpieces. This trade, attested mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly affected the poorest peasant families.

coureur.label: Coureur
coureur.summary: Messenger travelling fast on foot to carry news or letters.
coureur.text: The coureur is a foot messenger, responsible for quickly carrying news, letters or small parcels over short or medium distances, before the horse post and then modern means of transport became widespread.

coureur_de_chien.label: Coureur de Chien
coureur_de_chien.summary: Miner responsible for pushing mine carts, called "dogs".
coureur_de_chien.text: The coureur de chien pushes mine carts, nicknamed "mine dogs" because of the noise they made, reminiscent of barking.

couronnier.label: Couronnier
couronnier.summary: Craftsman making wreaths, notably for religious or funeral ceremonies.
couronnier.text: The couronnier makes wreaths intended for ceremonies: bridal wreaths, funeral wreaths, or religious ornaments. This trade, often linked to floristry or passementerie, gained importance with the fashion for mourning wreaths in the 19th century.

courratier.label: Courratier
courratier.summary: Broker specialized in negotiating and trading wine.
courratier.text: The courratier is a wine broker, an intermediary between producers and merchants, responsible for tasting, appraising and bringing buyers and sellers together. The term, a regional variant of "courtier", is particularly attested in the Bordeaux vineyard, where the wine-broker function remains regulated today.

courrier.label: Courrier
courrier.summary: Official carrier of messages, dispatches or mail.
courrier.text: The courrier officially carries messages, dispatches or correspondence, on foot, on horseback or by relay of post horses. Under the Ancien Régime, royal couriers ensured the fast transmission of orders and information over the network of post relays, the forerunner of the modern postal administration.

courrier_de_cabinet.label: Courrier de cabinet
courrier_de_cabinet.text: The courrier de cabinet is a royal courier responsible for carrying the sovereign's official correspondence.

courtaut.label: Courtaut
courtaut.summary: Shop employee occupied with sedentary work, by ellipsis of "courtaud de boutique".
courtaut.text: The courtaut is a journeyman employed in a shop for sedentary work, a term formed by ellipsis of the expression "courtaud de boutique". The word "courtaud" originally evokes clothing shorter than that worn by nobles and the wealthy bourgeoisie, hence the idea of a modest status.

courtepointier.label: Courtepointier
courtepointier.summary: Craftsman making courtepointes, quilted and padded coverlets.
courtepointier.text: The courtepointier makes courtepointes, ceremonial quilted and padded coverlets intended to adorn beds, as well as hangings and caparisons for ceremonies. The trade, regulated by guilds under the Ancien Régime, is sometimes denoted by the spelling variant "coutepointier".

courtier.label: Courtier (broker)
courtier.summary: Licensed intermediary bringing sellers and buyers together for a commission.
courtier.text: The courtier acts as an intermediary in a commercial transaction — goods, real estate, insurance, securities — bringing sellers and buyers together for a commission, without becoming the owner of the goods traded. Under the Ancien Régime, many brokerages were venal royal offices regulated by trade body (wine brokers, horse brokers, goods brokers).

courtier_en_marchandises.label: Courtier en marchandises (commodity broker)
courtier_en_marchandises.summary: Broker specialized in negotiating goods between merchants.
courtier_en_marchandises.text: The courtier en marchandises brings together buyers and sellers of commercial goods — foodstuffs, raw materials, manufactured products — for a commission, without trading on his own account.

courtillier.label: Courtillier
courtillier.summary: Gardener cultivating a courtil, a small enclosed garden for vegetables and fruit.
courtillier.text: The courtillier cultivates a courtil, a modest enclosed garden located on the outskirts of villages or towns, devoted to vegetables, fruit and sometimes a little livestock. This type of small market-garden supplied local markets, notably around towns such as Paris.

couseur.label: Couseur
couseur.summary: Worker specialized in sewing work, notably in garment-making or bookbinding.
couseur.text: The couseur performs sewing work by hand or machine, whether in garment-making (assembling clothes), shoemaking (sewing shoe uppers) or bookbinding (sewing a book's gatherings). The precise sense depends on the field of activity mentioned in the record.

couseuse_en_lainges.label: Couseuse en lainges
couseuse_en_lainges.summary: Seamstress of household linen: sheets, towels, dishcloths.
couseuse_en_lainges.text: The couseuse en lainges makes and repairs household linen: sheets, towels, dishcloths and other domestic linen pieces.

coussier.label: Coussier
coussier.summary: Craftsman making hose, a garment covering the legs.
coussier.text: The coussier makes hose, a medieval and early-modern garment covering the legs, ancestor of trousers and stockings, before this term came to denote more specifically, from the 16th century, only the part covering the foot and calf.

coustier.label: Coutier
coustier.summary: Maker or merchant of ticking, a tightly woven cloth used for mattresses and cushions.
coustier.text: The coutier works ticking, a tightly woven linen or cotton cloth, resistant to feathers or horsehair working through it, used to make mattresses, cushions and bolsters. The term is found under several related spellings (coustier, coutière) depending on region and record.

coutal.label: Coutal
coutal.summary: Driver of mules for transporting goods.
coutal.text: The coutal (or coutaud) drives loaded mules for transporting goods, notably in mountainous or foothill areas where these pack animals were better suited than horses to steep paths. The term, of Occitan origin, is found mainly in the south of France.

coutelier.label: Coutelier (cutler)
coutelier.summary: Craftsman making knives and other cutting instruments.
coutelier.text: The coutelier forges and shapes knives, scissors and cutting instruments, a trade organized into a guild as early as the Middle Ages and particularly flourishing in towns such as Thiers or Nogent. The term sometimes appears in the old form "coustelier", from the Old French "coustel" or "coutel" (knife).

coutilier.label: Coutillier
coutilier.summary: 14th–15th-century foot soldier armed with a lance and a coutille (a broad dagger).
coutilier.text: The coutillier, or coutilier, is a late-medieval foot soldier (14th–15th centuries), fitted with a mail hauberk topped by a brigandine, fighting with lance and coutille, a short, broad dagger with an "ox-tongue" blade. He formed the light infantry of feudal armies and mercenary companies, charging with the lance in melees, finishing off fallen combatants with the dagger, defending positions and taking part in sieges.

couturier.label: Couturier
couturier.summary: Craftsman responsible for sewing pieces of cloth or leather cut by others.
couturier.text: In the division of labour of Ancien Régime guilds, the couturier is responsible for sewing and assembling pieces of cloth or leather previously cut by the tailor or the shoemaker, a specialization that faded over time to more broadly denote one who makes clothes. The old spelling "cousturier" is common in old records.

couturier_de_livre.label: Couturier de Livre
couturier_de_livre.summary: Printing employee responsible for sewing a book's pages before binding.
couturier_de_livre.text: The couturier de livre works in printing, where he sews the gatherings of pages together before the binding operation proper.

couverturier.label: Couverturier
couverturier.summary: Craftsman or merchant making and selling bed blankets.
couverturier.text: The couverturier makes or sells woollen blankets intended for bedding, a trade linked to working cloth and carded wool, often practised in regions with a textile tradition.

couvreur.label: Couvreur (roofer)
couvreur.summary: Craftsman who builds and repairs roofs.
couvreur.text: The couvreur builds and maintains roofs, using materials available depending on the region: tile, slate, wood shingles, thatch or stone slabs. A trade worked at height, regulated by guild in towns, whose specialties (slate roofer, thatcher) are sometimes distinguished in records.

couvreur_d_ardoise.label: Couvreur d'ardoise
couvreur_d_ardoise.summary: Roofer specialized in laying slate roofs.
couvreur_d_ardoise.text: The couvreur d'ardoise lays and repairs slate roofs, a material characteristic of regions such as Anjou, Brittany or the Ardennes, where slate extraction fed a whole craft chain linked to construction.

couvreur_de_lauzes.label: Couvreur de lauzes
couvreur_de_lauzes.summary: Roofer using flat stones (lauzes) for roofing.
couvreur_de_lauzes.text: The couvreur de lauzes lays roofs of flat stones called lauzes, a traditional technique of certain mountainous regions (Cévennes, Quercy).

couvreur_en_chaume.label: Couvreur en chaume (thatcher)
couvreur_en_chaume.summary: Roofer specialized in laying thatched roofs.
couvreur_en_chaume.text: The couvreur en chaume lays thatched roofs (rye straw, reed or rushes depending on the region), a traditional technique widespread in the French countryside until its gradual decline in favour of tile and slate from the 19th century.

couvreur_en_esseurions.label: Couvreur en esseurions
couvreur_en_esseurions.summary: In the Nièvre, a roofer using wooden shingles (oak or chestnut).
couvreur_en_esseurions.text: In the Nièvre, the couvreur en esseurions lays wooden shingles of a particular species, perhaps oak or chestnut, to cover roofs.

coyratier.label: Coyratier
coyratier.summary: Craftsman who prepares and finishes leather after tanning.
coyratier.text: The coyratier takes part in leather-working after tanning, a function close to that of the currier. The term, of rare and probably regional spelling, remains little documented in genealogical sources.

craquelinier.label: Craquelinier
craquelinier.summary: Baker-pastry cook specialized in making craquelins, small crisp breads or dry cakes.
craquelinier.text: The craquelinier makes craquelins, small breads or dry biscuits of boiled and then baked dough, braided or knotted, a specialty attested notably in northern France, Belgium and Alsace, close to the pretzel in certain traditions.

craquelottiere.label: Craquelottière
craquelottiere.summary: Preparer of craquelots, lightly salted and smoked herring.
craquelottiere.text: The craquelottière prepares craquelots, fresh herring lightly salted and then hot-smoked, a specialty of Normandy fishing ports such as Dieppe and Fécamp, where herring preparation employed a large female workforce as soon as the boats landed.

crazalher.label: Crazalher
crazalher.summary: Craftsman making wooden troughs for agricultural or domestic use.
crazalher.text: The crazalher makes wooden troughs, used for feeding livestock or various domestic and craft uses. This rare and probably regional term is little documented in general genealogical sources.

credencier.label: Crédencier
credencier.summary: Person in charge of distributing provisions within a community or institution.
credencier.text: The crédencier is responsible for distributing food and provisions in a community — convent, school, hospital — a role close to that of the steward or bursar, often practised within religious institutions.

cremier.label: Crémier (dairyman)
cremier.summary: Merchant of fresh dairy products: milk, butter, cream, cheese.
cremier.text: The crémier sells fresh dairy products — milk, cream, butter, fresh cheese — often collected directly from surrounding farms. The dairy-shop trade developed particularly in towns from the 19th century, with the rise of organized milk collection.

crepinier.label: Crépinier
crepinier.summary: Maker of crépine, a woven fringe trimming beds and canopies.
crepinier.text: The crépinier makes crépine, a kind of fringe woven and worked at the top, used to trim beds and canopies.

crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.label: Crépinier de fil et de soie
crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.summary: Passementerie craftsman making crépines, ornamental fringes of thread or silk.
crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.text: The crépinier de fil et de soie makes crépines, passementerie works made of an openwork woven band from which short, dense fringes hang, often made of gold or silver thread. Highly prized in the 18th century to adorn royal and bourgeois furnishings, crépines were also used to trim hangings, clothing and harness.

crespinier.label: Crespinier
crespinier.summary: Weaving craftsman making light, sheer fabrics: crepe, gauze, fine silk.
crespinier.text: The crespinier makes light fabrics of silk, crepe or gauze, a textile trade distinct from the crépinier, who works in passementerie. The term derives from "crespe", an old form of the word crêpe denoting a light, rippled cloth.

criblier.label: Criblier
criblier.summary: Craftsman making sieves and screens to sort grain.
criblier.text: The criblier makes sieves, open-mesh instruments, often of woven willow, perforated skin or pierced sheet metal, used to sort grain, separate wheat from chaff or grade various materials. Crubelier and cruvelier are regional variants of the same trade, the word "cruvèl" being an Occitan form of "crivèl" (sieve).

crieur.label: Crieur (town crier)
crieur.summary: Person responsible for publicly announcing news, notices and goods aloud.
crieur.text: The public crieur announces aloud, in the streets and squares, official notices, sales, found or lost items, and goods for sale (wine crier, fish crier). An old function, regulated in many towns, the crieur was the main channel of information before the press.

crinier.label: Crinier
crinier.summary: Craftsman who prepares and works animal hair for various uses.
crinier.text: The crinier prepares horsehair — from the mane and tail of horses, or cattle hair — used to stuff seats and mattresses, to make fabric (woven horsehair), brushes or bow hair.

crinquallier.label: Crinquallier
crinquallier.summary: Merchant of hardware and metal objects.
crinquallier.text: The crinquallier sells hardware — nails, tools, metal implements — the term being an old variant of "quincaillier", itself derived from "clinquaille", formerly denoting scrap iron and small metal items.

cristallier.label: Cristallier
cristallier.summary: Prospector and cutter of rock crystal, notably in the Alpine ranges.
cristallier.text: The cristallier searches for and extracts rock crystal (quartz) from rock fissures, a traditional activity of Alpine massifs such as Mont Blanc, before also more broadly denoting the craftsman who cuts and shapes crystal objects.

crocheteur.label: Crocheteur
crocheteur.summary: Porter using a hook or a basket to carry loads.
crocheteur.text: The crocheteur carries heavy loads using a hook worn over the shoulder or a basket, notably in the markets and ports of Paris (the crocheteurs of Les Halles). This trade of strength, often organized into a sworn guild, was one of the most gruelling in urban handling.

crochetier.label: Crochetier
crochetier.summary: Craftsman making hooks for carrying or various uses.
crochetier.text: The crochetier makes metal hooks used for carrying loads (by porters), hanging goods, or other domestic and craft uses.

crocteur_de_gres.label: Crocteur de grès
crocteur_de_gres.summary: Worker extracting and breaking sandstone in a quarry.
crocteur_de_gres.text: The crocteur de grès (also called croqueteur or croqueur in dialect) breaks sandstone extracted in a quarry into small pieces, a material used for paving, construction and millstones. This gruelling quarry work is found in regions rich in sandstone deposits, such as northern France.

croise.label: Croisé
croise.summary: Combatant who took part in a crusade, enlisted under the sign of the cross.
croise.text: The croisé is one who has "taken the cross", that is, vowed to take part in a crusade, a religious military expedition organized between the 11th and 13th centuries toward the Holy Land or other targets designated by the Church. The term may appear in noble genealogies claiming crusader ancestry, often difficult to establish with certainty.

croquetier.label: Croquetier
croquetier.summary: Itinerant merchant related to the coquetier, collecting eggs, butter, cheese and poultry to resell in town.
croquetier.text: The croquetier is an itinerant merchant related to the coquetier: he travels farms to buy fresh produce — eggs, butter, cheese, poultry — then carries it to urban markets to resell it retail. This rural intermediary trade vanished with the development of modern distribution networks.

crossier.label: Crossier
crossier.text: The crossier makes stocks, the wooden parts, of firearms, a trade linked to gunsmithing that combines woodworking with knowledge of the dimensions required to fit the barrel and the weapon's mechanism.

cruysier.label: Cruysier
cruysier.summary: Potter making terracotta objects, notably jugs.
cruysier.text: The cruysier shapes terracotta objects, notably jugs and utilitarian vessels, a trade related to that of the potter. The term probably derives from "cruche" (jug).

cto.label: CTO
cto.summary: Executive responsible for a company's technology strategy and choices.
cto.text: The CTO (Chief Technology Officer), or technical director, is the executive responsible for technology choices, systems architecture and innovation within a company, particularly in the digital and technology sectors. A contemporary function, with no equivalent among old trades.

cubillier.label: Cubillier
cubillier.summary: Cooper specialized in making buckets and vats of various sizes.
cubillier.text: The cubillier makes wooden buckets and vats of various sizes, intended for storing liquids, winemaking or domestic and craft uses, a specialty close to that of the cooper.

cueilleur.label: Cueilleur
cueilleur.summary: Person responsible for harvesting natural produce: fruit, plants, or other resources.
cueilleur.text: The cueilleur harvests natural produce by hand — fruit, flowers, medicinal plants, mushrooms or other wild or cultivated resources — often seasonal work supplementing other farm activities.

cueilleur_de_jambe.label: Cueilleur de Jambe
cueilleur_de_jambe.summary: Glassworker who gathers the viscous glass forming the stem of a glass from the furnace.
cueilleur_de_jambe.text: The cueilleur de jambe is a glassworker who gathers from the furnace, using a punty, the viscous glass that will form the stem of the glass, and presents it to the stem-setter.

cueilleur_de_pied.label: Cueilleur de Pied
cueilleur_de_pied.summary: Glassworker who gathers the viscous glass forming the foot of a glass piece from the furnace.
cueilleur_de_pied.text: The cueilleur de pied is a glassworker who gathers from the furnace, using a punty, the viscous glass that will form the foot of the glass piece, and presents it to the foot-setter.

cueilleur_de_simples.label: Cueilleur de simples
cueilleur_de_simples.summary: Gatherer of food or medicinal plants.
cueilleur_de_simples.text: The cueilleur de simples harvests plants ("simples") intended for food or medicinal use.

cuilleriste.label: Cuilleriste
cuilleriste.summary: Craftsman making spoons and other wooden table utensils.
cuilleriste.text: The cuilleriste makes spoons and small table utensils, mainly of wood, a craft often practised in rural or forested areas where wood was readily available. The term is also found in the accented spelling "cuillériste".

cuilleronnier.label: Cuilleronnier
cuilleronnier.text: The cuilleronnier, also called cuillerier, makes tableware, particularly spoons of metal (tin, silver) or horn, a trade distinct from the cuilleriste, who works wood more.

cuiratier.label: Cuiratier
cuiratier.summary: Craftsman working leather, whose guild held a leading rank among municipal trades.
cuiratier.text: The cuiratier is a worker who works leather. According to Littré, the cuiratiers held first rank in the municipal body among the trade guilds of certain towns, a sign of the economic importance of leather preparation and trade under the Ancien Régime.

cuireur.label: Cuireur
cuireur.summary: Saddlery worker responsible for covering the wooden frames of saddles with leather.
cuireur.text: The cuireur takes part in saddle-making: he covers the saddle tree, a wooden structure previously shaped by the saddle-tree maker, with leather, a specialized step of traditional saddlery.

cuironnier.label: Cuironnier
cuironnier.summary: Craftsman working leather to make various objects, related to the cuilleronnier.
cuironnier.text: The cuironnier shapes various leather objects, a trade related to the cuilleronnier, sometimes combining leatherwork with that of other materials to make utensils or accessories.

cuiseur.label: Cuiseur
cuiseur.summary: Worker responsible for firing or cooking materials: charcoal, metals or other substances.
cuiseur.text: The cuiseur carries out firing operations requiring controlled heat treatment: charring wood to produce charcoal, heating metals at the forge, firing lime or brick depending on context.

cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.label: Cuiseur de Paquest de Fer
cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.summary: Cutlery worker responsible for forging raw iron bars to preform them.
cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.text: The cuiseur de paquest de fer is a cutlery worker responsible for forging raw iron bars to preform them before their final shaping.

cuisinier.label: Cuisinier (cook)
cuisinier.summary: Person responsible for preparing meals, professionally or domestically.
cuisinier.text: The cuisinier prepares meals, whether in a bourgeois or noble household, an inn, or on his own account. Under the Ancien Régime, great households employed a "queux" or "oyer" (kitchen officer) responsible for organizing meals, while in towns, caterers and roast-meat sellers sold cooked meat and prepared charcuterie.

culler.label: Culler
culler.summary: Port inspector responsible for setting the sale price of cod.
culler.text: The culler is a port official responsible for assessing and setting the price of landed cod, a role linked to cod-fishing ports such as those of Brittany or Normandy.

culotteur_de_pipes.label: Culotteur de Pipes
culotteur_de_pipes.summary: Person who seasons new pipes before their sale by tobacconists.
culotteur_de_pipes.text: The culotteur de pipes seasons (progressively smokes to blacken the bowl of) new pipes, which are then sold thus seasoned by the tobacconists he works for.

culottier.label: Culottier
culottier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making leather breeches.
culottier.text: The culottier makes exclusively leather breeches, a men's garment of leather or chamois-dressed skin covering the lower body to the knee, particularly worn by soldiers and horsemen before trousers became widespread.

culottiere.label: Culottière
culottiere.summary: Seamstress specialized in making men's clothing, notably breeches.
culottiere.text: The culottière makes breeches and other men's clothing, a sewing specialty distinct from the leather breeches worked by the culottier, geared toward cloth rather than leather.

cultivateur.label: Cultivateur
cultivateur.summary: Farmer who works his own land himself.
cultivateur.text: The cultivateur farms land, whether as owner, tenant or sharecropper, a term that became widespread in the 19th century, gradually replacing "laboureur" to denote the farmer, regardless of wealth.

cure.label: Curé (parish priest)
cure.summary: Priest responsible for a parish, in charge of religious services and keeping the registers.
cure.text: The curé is the priest in charge of a parish, responsible for celebrating services, administering the sacraments and, until the Revolution, keeping the parish registers of baptisms, marriages and burials — the main genealogical source before civil registration was established in 1792.

curial.label: Curial
curial.summary: Officer or secretary attached to a court of law.
curial.text: The curial is an officer attached to a court or jurisdiction, performing secretarial or registry functions, the term deriving from the Latin "curia" (court, tribunal).

custos.label: Custos
custos.summary: Keeper and sacristan of a church, often mentioned in its Latin form in old records.
custos.text: Custos is the Latin term, common in parish registers written in Latin, denoting the keeper or sacristan of a church, responsible for guarding sacred objects and maintaining the place of worship.

cuvelier.label: Cuvelier
cuvelier.summary: Craftsman making vats and wooden containers, spelling variant: cuvetier.
cuvelier.text: The cuvelier (or cuvetier) makes large wooden vats and containers, intended for winemaking, brewing or various industrial and domestic uses, a trade related to coopering and largely vanished with industrialization and the replacement of wood by other materials.

cylindreur.label: Cylindreur
cylindreur.summary: Worker using a roller to soften leather or glaze fabrics.
cylindreur.text: The cylindreur runs leather or fabrics between rollers to soften, smooth or glaze them, a finishing operation used in currying and the textile industry.

dactylographe.label: Dactylographe (typist)
dactylographe.summary: Person responsible for typing texts on a typewriter.
dactylographe.text: The dactylographe, commonly shortened to "dactylo", types letters, reports and documents on a typewriter. This profession, largely female-dominated, developed from the late 19th century with the spread of typewriters in administrations, notarial offices and companies, before declining with the computerization of clerical work.

damasquineur.label: Damasquineur
damasquineur.summary: Craftsman inlaying threads of gold or silver into iron or steel.
damasquineur.text: The damasquineur practises damascening, a technique of inlaying fine threads of gold or silver into an iron or steel surface previously notched, to adorn weapons, armour or art objects. The technique takes its name from the city of Damascus, where this art was renowned.

dame_de_confiance.label: Dame de confiance
dame_de_confiance.summary: Lady's companion occupying a position of trust with the mistress of a household.
dame_de_confiance.text: The dame de confiance accompanies and assists a lady of the household, occupying a position intermediate between domestic service and kinship, often entrusted with delicate tasks or the management of certain aspects of domestic life.

dardier.label: Dardier
dardier.summary: Craftsman making scythes and other sharp farm tools.
dardier.text: The dardier makes scythes and cutting tools for farm work, a forge trade linked to the mowing of hay and grain.

daubiste.label: Daubiste
daubiste.summary: Seller of lower-grade meat, a term attested in the Lyon region.
daubiste.text: The daubiste sells second-choice meat, notably intended for daube (stew), a regional term attested in the Lyon area and distinct from the butcher, who handles higher-quality cuts.

dauraire.label: Dauraire
dauraire.summary: Term from southern France for a gilding goldsmith, from the Latin daurator/deaurator.
dauraire.text: Dauraire (with the variant dauradier) is the term used in the south of France to denote a goldsmith specialized in gilding, derived from the Latin daurator or deaurator. In the 14th and 15th centuries, goldsmiths who practised gilding were commonly called "doriers" or "dorers"; the term was later supplanted by "doreur".

debardeur.label: Débardeur (stevedore)
debardeur.summary: Worker responsible for unloading boats and port handling.
debardeur.text: The débardeur unloads boats and handles goods in ports, a physical trade particularly present in the great river and sea ports. Originally, the term also denoted one who moves timber out of the forest, that is, out of the felling areas.

debassier.label: Débassier
debassier.text: The débassier, or débasière in the feminine, knits wool stockings, a textile craft widespread in the countryside before hosiery was industrialized, notably in specialized regions such as Berry or Auvergne.

debitant.label: Débitant
debitant.summary: Merchant selling goods retail, notably drink or tobacco.
debitant.text: The débitant sells goods retail directly to the consumer, the term being used mainly for regulated businesses such as drink or tobacco shops, subject to a licence since the 19th century.

debitant_d_eau_de_vie.label: Débitant d'eau-de-vie
debitant_d_eau_de_vie.summary: Café-keeper or itinerant merchant specialized in selling brandy and spirits.
debitant_d_eau_de_vie.text: The débitant d'eau-de-vie sells brandy and other spirits, either in a fixed shop (tavern, café) or on an itinerant round. This strong-alcohol trade was subject to specific regulations under the Ancien Régime and then to a licensing system after the Revolution.

decalabreur.label: Décalabreur
decalabreur.summary: Mine worker cleaning the roofs of slate quarries after blasting.
decalabreur.text: The décalabreur cleans the roofs of slate extraction chambers after mine blasts, clearing unstable rocks liable to collapse. This dangerous trade is specific to slate-quarry basins such as those of Anjou or the Ardennes.

decatisseur.label: Décatisseur
decatisseur.summary: Textile worker who removes the sheen given to fabrics by finishing treatments.
decatisseur.text: The décatisseur treats fabrics to remove the artificial sheen left by finishing operations, using steam or hot water, in order to obtain a matte, more natural-looking finish — a finishing step in the textile industry, notably wool.

dechargeur_a_dos.label: Déchargeur à dos
dechargeur_a_dos.summary: Porter who carries goods on his back, notably for unloading ships and vehicles.
dechargeur_a_dos.text: The déchargeur à dos carries goods directly on his back, a mode of portage used for unloading ships and vehicles in ports and on quays, before handling was mechanized.

dechargeur_de_vin.label: Déchargeur de vin
dechargeur_de_vin.summary: Handler specialized in unloading wine and other drinks delivered by boat.
dechargeur_de_vin.text: The déchargeur de vin unloads casks of wine, cider and other drinks from ships arriving in port, specialized handling work in wine-trading ports.

dechiffreur.label: Déchiffreur
dechiffreur.summary: Postal employee responsible for deciphering illegible addresses to allow mail delivery.
dechiffreur.text: The déchiffreur works in postal services, responsible for interpreting badly written or incorrect addresses so as to ensure mail reaches its recipient, a function that arose with the development of the modern postal service.

dechireur.label: Déchireur
dechireur.summary: Worker specialized in scrapping worn-out boats.
dechireur.text: The déchireur dismantles ships that have reached the end of their life to recover reusable materials and parts (wood, metal, rope, ironwork), an activity linked to ports and shipyards.

decimateur.label: Décimateur
decimateur.summary: Person or institution having the right to collect the tithe, an ecclesiastical tax on harvests.
decimateur.text: The décimateur is one who has the right to levy the tithe, a levy in kind, generally a tenth, on harvests, owed to the Church or, by agreement, sometimes shared with the local lord. This right could be exercised directly by the parish priest, by an abbey, or leased to a third party for a fee. The tithe was abolished along with feudal privileges on the night of 4 August 1789.

decolleteur.label: Décolleteur
decolleteur.summary: Worker lathe-machining small, high-precision metal parts.
decolleteur.text: The décolleteur, or décolleteuse in the feminine, lathe-machines small parts requiring great precision — screws, spindles, clockmaking components — an industrial specialty particularly developed in the Arve valley, in Haute-Savoie, the French cradle of screw-machining.

decolleur.label: Décolleur
decolleur.summary: Cod-preparation worker responsible for removing the liver, entrails and head of the fish.
decolleur.text: The décolleur cuts freshly caught cod to remove the liver, entrails and head, an essential step in preparing the fish before salting, carried out aboard cod-fishing vessels or in fishing ports.

decoupeur.label: Découpeur
decoupeur.summary: Craftsman who cuts decorative motifs into fabric or paper using specialized irons.
decoupeur.text: The découpeur makes ornaments by cutting, using specialized irons or punches to create decorative motifs on fabric, paper or leather.

decoupeuse.label: Découpeuse
decoupeuse.summary: Textile worker who cuts the floating threads between the decorative motifs of a fabric.
decoupeuse.text: The découpeuse handles finishing on figured fabrics, notably gauze, cutting the weft threads that float between the decorative motifs to give the fabric its finished look.

decouvreur.label: Découvreur
decouvreur.summary: Explorer who revealed new territories, resources or trade routes.
decouvreur.text: The découvreur is one who explores and reveals unknown territories, natural resources or trade routes, a term used for explorers of the great maritime and colonial expeditions.

decrotteur.label: Décrotteur (bootblack)
decrotteur.summary: Person who cleans and polishes passers-by's shoes, or sweeps mud from the streets.
decrotteur.text: The décrotteur practises one of two related trades: either he cleans and polishes passers-by's shoes on the street or at a fixed stand, or he sweeps the mud accumulated on roadways after rain. Shoe-blacks, often young boys, were a familiar figure of the streets of large towns in the 19th century.

decurion.label: Décurion
decurion.summary: Roman officer commanding a decury, a unit of ten soldiers.
decurion.text: The décurion commands a decury, a unit of ten men, in the Roman army or organizations inspired by it. The term sometimes appears in learned or heraldic contexts evoking an ancient ancestry or reference.

defaiseur.label: Défaiseur
defaiseur.summary: Worker specialized in dismantling structures and salvaging reusable materials.
defaiseur.text: The défaiseur dismantles structures or works to recover reusable materials and elements, a controlled demolition trade practised notably in building or carpentry.

deformeur.label: Déformeur
deformeur.summary: Shoemaking worker responsible for giving soles their final gloss and stamping patterns on them.
deformeur.text: The déformeur handles finishing in shoemaking, responsible for polishing soles and stamping decorative patterns on them, a specialty of industrial shoemaking.

defricheur.label: Défricheur
defricheur.summary: Person who clears land by felling trees and brush to make it arable.
defricheur.text: The défricheur fells trees and clears brush from a forested or fallow plot to make it arable, essential work during the great phases of land improvement, notably in the Middle Ages and during the rural land-settlement movements of later centuries.

defroisseur.label: Défroisseur
defroisseur.summary: Textile worker responsible for removing creases and wrinkles from fabrics and clothing.
defroisseur.text: The défroisseur irons and smooths fabrics and clothing to remove creases, a finishing operation in the textile or garment industry.

degaineur.label: Dégaineur
degaineur.summary: Swashbuckler, quick to draw the sword to duel or brawl.
degaineur.text: The dégaineur, according to Littré, denotes a swashbuckler or a brawler, that is, a person inclined to draw the sword and fight in a duel or a fray. This is not a trade in the strict sense but a term, formed on the verb "dégainer" (to draw a weapon), that describes a quarrelsome behaviour characteristic of certain gentlemen or soldiers of the Ancien Régime.

degorgeur.label: Dégorgeur
degorgeur.summary: Worker responsible for unclogging and cleaning pipes and drainage systems.
degorgeur.text: The dégorgeur cleans and unclogs blocked pipes, sewers and sanitation systems. The term is also used in wine vocabulary to denote the disgorging operation of champagne, unrelated to this plumbing trade.

degrafeuse.label: Dégrafeuse
degrafeuse.summary: Female worker responsible for removing staples from documents, fabrics or packaging.
degrafeuse.text: The dégrafeuse removes staples used to temporarily hold together documents, fabrics or packaging, a workshop or office task depending on context.

degraisseur.label: Dégraisseur
degraisseur.summary: Worker specialized in removing stains and grease from fabrics or leather.
degraisseur.text: The dégraisseur removes grease and oil stains from fabrics, clothing or leather, a trade at the origin of modern dry cleaning, practised in a specialized workshop from the 19th century.

degrossisseur.label: Dégrossisseur
degrossisseur.summary: Worker who does the first rough shaping of a piece before its finishing.
degrossisseur.text: The dégrossisseur roughs out a piece — wood, metal, stone — giving it its general shape before other craftsmen carry out precise finishing.

deicier.label: Déicier
deicier.text: The déicier is a maker of dice for games, an old trade now vanished, attested in dictionaries of old trades. He shapes and sells his dice, in the manner that a clog-maker shapes and sells his clogs. The spelling "deessier" is a spelling variant.

dejarreuse_de_chapeaux.label: Déjarreuse de chapeaux
dejarreuse_de_chapeaux.summary: Female worker separating coarse hairs from fine fur on rabbit skins intended for hat-making.
dejarreuse_de_chapeaux.text: The déjarreuse de chapeaux prepares rabbit or hare skins intended for making hat felt, separating the "jarres" (long, coarse hairs) from the fine fur usable for felting, a step upstream of the hatter's work.

delateur.label: Délateur
delateur.summary: Person who denounces offences or reprehensible behaviour to the authorities.
delateur.text: The délateur denounces, officially or secretly, offences, crimes or suspicious behaviour to the authorities, often for a reward. The term takes on a particularly negative connotation during periods of organized denunciation, such as the Revolution or the Occupation.

delegue_cantonal.label: Délégué cantonal
delegue_cantonal.summary: Volunteer representative responsible for overseeing a canton's primary schools.
delegue_cantonal.text: The délégué cantonal is, under the Third Republic, a volunteer notable appointed to visit and oversee the primary schools of his canton, working with the academy inspector, within the framework of primary-school organization set up by the Ferry laws.

delesteur.label: Délesteur
delesteur.summary: Port worker responsible for removing ballast from ships before loading.
delesteur.text: The délesteur removes ballast (stones, sand or gravel) from ships arriving empty, an operation necessary before loading new goods in trading ports.

deliesseur.label: Déliésseur
deliesseur.summary: Worker responsible for untying the bindings and ropes holding various objects or materials together.
deliesseur.text: The déliésseur unties the ropes, bindings or string used to hold objects or materials together, an ancillary task in trade, transport or craft work.

delisseur.label: Délisseur
delisseur.summary: Paper-mill worker responsible for finishing: sizing, folding, smoothing and cutting paper.
delisseur.text: The délisseur carries out the final finishing operations in a paper mill: sizing, gathering into reams, folding, smoothing, drying and cutting sheets before sale.

delivreur.label: Délivreur
delivreur.summary: Person responsible for transporting and handing over goods, parcels or mail to recipients.
delivreur.text: The délivreur handles the last link of the distribution chain by directly handing over goods, parcels or mail to their recipients.

demagnetiseur.label: Démagnétiseur
demagnetiseur.summary: Technician responsible for removing residual magnetism from metal parts.
demagnetiseur.text: The démagnétiseur removes residual magnetism built up in metal parts or sensitive equipment, a modern technical function linked to industry and electronics.

demeloir.label: Démêloir
demeloir.summary: Textile worker responsible for disentangling tangled fibres before spinning or weaving.
demeloir.text: The démêloir separates and disentangles tangled textile fibres, a preparatory step necessary before carding, spinning or weaving.

demineur.label: Démineur
demineur.summary: Specialist responsible for locating and neutralizing mines and explosive devices.
demineur.text: The démineur locates, identifies and neutralizes mines, bombs and other explosive devices in order to make contaminated areas safe, a profession born of the need for demining after the two world wars.

demoiselle_de_confiance.label: Demoiselle de confiance
demoiselle_de_confiance.summary: Young woman employed as a lady's companion to the women of the household.
demoiselle_de_confiance.text: The demoiselle de confiance accompanies and assists the ladies of a household in their social activities, a function close to that of a lady's companion, reserved for a younger or unmarried woman.

demonstrateur.label: Démonstrateur
demonstrateur.summary: Teacher illustrating a course through experimental demonstration, notably in the sciences.
demonstrateur.text: The démonstrateur teaches through practice and experimentation, in physics, anatomy or botany, often supporting a tenured professor in Ancien Régime faculties or botanical gardens.

denombriliste.label: Dénombriliste
denombriliste.summary: Person responsible for carrying out censuses of population, property or resources.
denombriliste.text: The dénombriliste carries out censuses and enumerations — population, property, resources — for administrative or statistical purposes.

dentateur.label: Dentateur
dentateur.summary: Old term for one who pulls and treats teeth, often a barber, before the word dentist appeared.
dentateur.text: The dentateur practises tooth extraction and dental care, an old term attested as early as the 16th century: Ambroise Paré warns against "the barbers and dentateurs" who are too hasty to pull teeth. These practitioners were most often barbers practising this activity alongside their main trade, before dentistry became a medical discipline in its own right in the 18th and 19th centuries.

dentelliere.label: Dentellière (lace maker)
dentelliere.summary: Craftswoman specialized in making lace by interlacing threads.
dentelliere.text: The dentellière makes lace, a delicate, openwork textile made by interlacing threads with bobbins or a needle according to complex patterns. Haute-Loire, around Le Puy-en-Velay, as well as Normandy (Alençon, Bayeux) and Flanders, are among the great historic centres of this craft, which supported many rural families from the 16th to the 20th century.

dentier.label: Dentier (denturist)
dentier.summary: Craftsman making artificial teeth and dental prostheses.
dentier.text: The dentier makes artificial teeth and prostheses intended to replace missing teeth, an old craft at the origin of the modern denturist profession.

dentiste.label: Dentiste (dentist)
dentiste.summary: Practitioner specialized in caring for and treating teeth.
dentiste.text: The dentiste cares for teeth and treats dental conditions. The profession gradually became structured from the 18th century, notably with the work of Pierre Fauchard, before its modern regulation in the 19th century.

depeceur.label: Dépeceur
depeceur.summary: Butcher specialized in butchering animals and cutting carcasses.
depeceur.text: The dépeceur cuts up animal carcasses, separating the different pieces of meat according to traditional cuts, a specialty of the butcher's trade.

depeceur_de_carrosses.label: Dépeceur de carrosses
depeceur_de_carrosses.summary: Specialist in dismantling worn-out horse-drawn carriages, forerunner of the car breaker.
depeceur_de_carrosses.text: The dépeceur de carrosses dismantles worn-out carriages and horse-drawn vehicles to recover reusable parts and materials, an activity that can be seen as the forerunner of the modern car breaker.

depensier.label: Dépensier
depensier.summary: Financial manager of a religious or maritime institution, equivalent of the steward.
depensier.text: The dépensier manages the expenses and supply of an institution — convent, hospital, ship — a role close to that of the steward, requiring accounting skills.

depileur.label: Dépileur
depileur.summary: Tanning worker responsible for removing hair from hides before tanning.
depileur.text: The dépileur removes hair and fur from animal hides during the first steps of leather preparation, generally by soaking in a lime bath, before tanning proper.

depisteur.label: Dépisteur
depisteur.summary: Person responsible for detecting and reporting the presence of specific people, animals or problems.
depisteur.text: The dépisteur detects and reports the presence of people, animals, diseases or anomalies depending on his field of activity, a term with varied uses (health, safety, hunting).

depoussiereur.label: Dépoussiéreur
depoussiereur.summary: Worker responsible for removing dust in industrial or work spaces.
depoussiereur.text: The dépoussiéreur removes dust and suspended particles in workshops and industrial spaces, a function linked to occupational hygiene and safety.

dequilleur.label: Déquilleur
dequilleur.summary: Textile worker responsible for removing the pins used to hold the spacing of warp threads.
dequilleur.text: The déquilleur removes the pins, small rods used during weaving to hold the spacing of the warp threads, a finishing operation on the loom.

deratiseur.label: Dératiseur
deratiseur.summary: Specialist responsible for eliminating rats, mice and other harmful rodents.
deratiseur.text: The dératiseur eliminates rats, mice and other harmful rodents in homes, warehouses and public spaces, a profession that became structured with growing awareness of the health risks linked to rodents, such as plague or the contamination of foodstuffs.

deriveur.label: Dériveur
deriveur.summary: Worker creating diversions of watercourses for irrigation or industry.
deriveur.text: The dériveur builds diversions of watercourses intended for irrigating land, feeding mills or factories, or draining water, important hydraulic know-how in agricultural or industrial regions.

desaireux.label: Désaireux
desaireux.summary: Sanitary agent responsible for disinfecting places contaminated by plague.
desaireux.text: The désaireux disinfects houses and places contaminated during plague epidemics, purifying the air and goods by fumigation or fire, an emergency sanitary function that appeared during the great epidemics of the Ancien Régime.

desossateur.label: Désossateur (deboner)
desossateur.summary: Butcher specialized in deboning cuts of meat.
desossateur.text: The désossateur removes the bones from pieces of meat to ease their culinary preparation and presentation, a specialty of the butcher's trade, particularly developed in the modern food-processing industry.

dessecheur.label: Dessécheur
dessecheur.summary: Specialist in draining marshes to turn them into farmland.
dessecheur.text: The dessécheur drains and dries marshy areas to turn them into productive land, large-scale hydraulic work carried out notably in the marshes of western and northern France since the 17th century, a period of great drainage works supported by the monarchy.

dessinateur.label: Dessinateur (draughtsman)
dessinateur.summary: Person who designs technical or artistic drawings.
dessinateur.text: The dessinateur produces drawings, whether technical (plans, machines, buildings) or artistic (illustrations, textile designs). The term covers both the artist and the industrial draughtsman, whose trade developed with industrialization in the 19th century.

detableur.label: Détableur
detableur.summary: Worker responsible for dismantling tables and workbenches to salvage reusable elements.
detableur.text: The détableur dismantles worn-out tables and workbenches to recover reusable elements, a salvage trade linked to woodworking.

detaillant.label: Détaillant (retailer)
detaillant.summary: Merchant who sells goods retail, in small quantities, to the consumer.
detaillant.text: The détaillant sells goods retail, as opposed to the wholesaler, who sells in large quantities, directly to the end consumer.

detailleur.label: Détailleur
detailleur.text: The détailleur sells fish retail at markets, sourcing it from fish wholesalers or directly from fishermen.

detailleur_de_chair.label: Détailleur de chair
detailleur_de_chair.summary: Butcher selling meat retail directly to consumers at markets.
detailleur_de_chair.text: The détailleur de chair sells meat retail at markets, a specialty of the butcher's trade geared toward direct sale to the consumer rather than slaughter or wholesale.

detective.label: Détective
detective.summary: Private investigator conducting inquiries on behalf of individuals or companies.
detective.text: The private détective conducts inquiries on behalf of individuals, companies or lawyers, a profession that developed from the late 19th century with the rise of private-investigation agencies.

detouilleur.label: Détouilleur
detouilleur.summary: Textile worker specialized in the first combing of wool.
detouilleur.text: The détouilleur carries out the first disentangling and combing of raw wool, a preparatory step before carding and spinning.

detricheur.label: Détricheur
detricheur.summary: Textile worker specialized in carding wool fibres before spinning.
detricheur.text: The détricheur cards wool and other textile fibres, disentangling and aligning the fibres to prepare the material for spinning.

devalleur.label: Dévalleur
devalleur.summary: Carrier of liquid goods, notably a boatman steering boats out of port.
devalleur.text: The dévalleur transports liquid goods and handles casks and other containers; the term also denotes bargemen responsible for steering boats out of port, work linked to the river and sea trade of wine, oil or other foodstuffs.

devideur.label: Dévideur (winder)
devideur.summary: Textile worker responsible for winding thread, an organizing step for spun yarn.
devideur.text: The dévideur, or dévuideur, winds spun thread, that is, transfers it from the spinning bobbin onto bobbins or skeins suited to the following steps of weaving or sale.

diacre.label: Diacre (deacon)
diacre.summary: Ordained minister of the Church, an intermediate degree before the priesthood or a ministry in its own right.
diacre.text: The diacre is an ordained minister of the Catholic Church, historically a step before priestly ordination, responsible for assisting the priest in the liturgy and charitable service. Since the Second Vatican Council, the permanent diaconate also exists as a ministry in its own right, including for married men.

dimeur.label: Dîmeur
dimeur.summary: Tenant who leased the right to collect tithes on a parish.
dimeur.text: The dîmeur leases the right to collect the tithe on a given parish or territory, paying a fixed fee to the décimateur (the right-holder, often the Church) in exchange for the right to collect its yield, hoping for a profit if the harvest is good.

dimier.label: Dîmier
dimier.summary: Person responsible for the physical collection of tithes on behalf of the décimateur or the dîmeur.
dimier.text: The dîmier carries out the concrete collection of tithes on the ground, assessing and levying a tenth of the harvests on behalf of the right-holder (décimateur) or his tenant (dîmeur), a task often entrusted to a day-labourer or a local employee.

dinandier.label: Dinandier
dinandier.summary: Coppersmith working brass to make utensils.
dinandier.text: The dinandier works brass to make household utensils, candlesticks or decorative objects, an art called dinanderie after the town of Dinant, in Belgium, a historic centre of this metalwork since the Middle Ages.

directeur.label: Directeur
directeur.summary: Person responsible for directing an establishment, a company or an institution.
directeur.text: The directeur runs an establishment, a company, a school or an institution, a generic term whose exact scope depends on the context mentioned in the record.

directeur_d_ecole.label: Directeur d'école (headmaster)
directeur_d_ecole.summary: Person responsible for the educational and administrative direction of a school.
directeur_d_ecole.text: The directeur d'école runs a school, ensuring educational and administrative coordination, a function that became institutionalized with the development of public primary education from the Ferry laws of the 1880s.

directeur_de_banque.label: Directeur de banque (bank manager)
directeur_de_banque.summary: Person responsible for managing and running a banking establishment.
directeur_de_banque.text: The directeur de banque runs a banking establishment or one of its branches, a function that developed with the rise of the modern banking system in the 19th century.

directeur_de_conscience.label: Directeur de conscience (spiritual director)
directeur_de_conscience.summary: Cleric guiding a person's or a community's spiritual life.
directeur_de_conscience.text: The directeur de conscience is a priest or religious who accompanies and guides an individual's spiritual life, often that of an influential figure or a religious community, through counsel and regular confession.

disquaire.label: Disquaire (record dealer)
disquaire.text: The disquaire sells music records (vinyl and then CD), a trade that appeared with the spread of the phonograph in the 20th century.

distillateur.label: Distillateur (distiller)
distillateur.summary: Craftsman or industrialist making spirits by distillation.
distillateur.text: The distillateur produces spirits and brandies by distillation, turning fermented wine, fruit or grain into spirits, an activity regulated by guilds and then by a licensing system (bouilleurs de cru) from the 19th century.

dizainier.label: Dizainier
dizainier.summary: Local officer responsible for a group of ten residents, notably for the watch or the militia.
dizainier.text: The dizainier, or dixainier, leads a "dizaine", a group of ten men responsible for the watch, urban security or the local militia, a neighbourhood organization inherited from the Middle Ages present in many towns.

docker_portuaire.label: Docker portuaire
docker_portuaire.summary: Port worker responsible for stowing, loading and unloading ships.
docker_portuaire.text: The docker portuaire loads and unloads ships, notably handling the hooking and unhooking of loads with cranes and lifting gear, a profession organized into powerful unions in the great ports such as Marseille or Le Havre.

docteur.label: Docteur (doctor)
docteur.summary: Holder of a doctorate, physician or scholar recognized in his discipline.
docteur.text: The docteur is either a physician or, more broadly, the holder of a university doctorate in a discipline (theology, law, medicine), the oldest university degree awarded in France as early as the Middle Ages.

docteur_en_theologie.label: Docteur en théologie (doctor of theology)
docteur_en_theologie.summary: Holder of the highest university degree in theology.
docteur_en_theologie.text: The docteur en théologie has earned the doctorate, the highest degree awarded by a faculty of theology, a long and prestigious course of study under the Ancien Régime, often followed by members of the clergy destined for high ecclesiastical or teaching responsibilities.

docteur_regent.label: Docteur régent
docteur_regent.summary: Professor holding a chair in a university faculty.
docteur_regent.text: The docteur régent is a tenured professor teaching in an Ancien Régime university faculty, a member of the permanent teaching staff as opposed to non-regent doctors, who did not teach.

doigtier.label: Doigtier
doigtier.summary: Craftsman making finger guards for delicate work.
doigtier.text: The doigtier makes finger guards of leather, metal or textile intended to protect the fingers during delicate or dangerous work, such as sewing, harvesting or precision craft work.

doleur.label: Doleur
doleur.summary: Worker wielding the doloire, experienced head of a pit-sawing team or cask-stave cutter.
doleur.text: The doleur is a worker specialized in wielding the doloire, a heavy axe whose use requires as much skill as strength: cask staves are cut with the doloire. Within a pit-sawing team, the doleur is the most experienced: he recruits the team, negotiates with owners and rates, and barks and squares the log before sawing.

domestique.label: Domestique (servant)
domestique.summary: Person employed in the domestic service of a noble or bourgeois household.
domestique.text: The domestique is employed in the service of a noble or bourgeois household, for housework, cooking, upkeep or attending the masters. Under the Ancien Régime, the term covers a hierarchy of functions ranging from the simple valet to positions of trust such as the steward.

dominotier.label: Dominotier
dominotier.summary: Craftsman making and selling wallpaper and printed prints.
dominotier.text: The dominotier makes and sells "dominos", decorated papers printed using engraved wooden blocks, used as wallpaper, poor man's tapestry, or for printing popular prints and playing cards, a craft that flourished from the 16th to the 18th century.

dompteur.label: Dompteur
dompteur.summary: Specialist in taming wild animals, notably for circuses and shows.
dompteur.text: The dompteur trains wild animals — big cats, bears, elephants — to perform acts in circus shows or itinerant menageries, a profession that developed with the rise of the modern circus in the 19th century.

donneur.label: Donneur
donneur.summary: Textile worker responsible for preparing and setting up looms.
donneur.text: The donneur prepares and sets up looms, ensuring their proper functioning for production, an important technical function in weaving workshops.

donneur_d_eau.label: Donneur d'eau
donneur_d_eau.summary: Employee distributing spa water to bathers at a spa establishment.
donneur_d_eau.text: The donneur d'eau distributes spa water to bathers at a thermal establishment, a job linked to the development of spa resorts and spa medicine in France from the 19th century.

doreur.label: Doreur (gilder)
doreur.summary: Craftsman specialized in gilding wood, metal or plaster objects.
doreur.text: The doreur applies fine sheets of gold, or a gilded metal, to supports of wood, metal, leather or plaster, to adorn frames, furniture, bookbindings or religious objects, a precision craft organized into a guild under the Ancien Régime.

doridier.label: Doridier
doridier.summary: Gilder and goldsmith, a regional term related to the doreur.
doridier.text: The doridier practises the combined trades of gilder and goldsmith, applying gilding to precious metal objects, a rare term probably related to "doreur".

dorissier.label: Dorissier
dorissier.summary: Cod fisherman aboard a dory, a small boat launched from the cod-fishing vessel.
dorissier.text: The dorissier line-fishes for cod from a dory, generally in a team of two (the skipper and his "avant"), rowing for long hours to set lines under often perilous conditions (storms, icebergs, fog). He is part of the cod-fishing vessel's crew alongside the splitters, salters and "bulotiers", and returns to the mother ship to have his catch unloaded, salted and dried. This trade marked the great cod fishery on the Newfoundland banks, practised notably by Norman and Saint-Malo sailors from the 19th century.

dorlotier.label: Dorlotier
dorlotier.summary: Craftsman making ribbons, braid and passementerie, a regional variant of the rubanier.
dorlotier.text: The dorlotier, or dorelotier, makes ribbons, braid and other passementerie items, a regional term equivalent to rubanier depending on the production area, notably around Saint-Étienne, a great French centre of ribbon-making.

doubleur_de_laine.label: Doubleur de laine
doubleur_de_laine.summary: Textile worker who doubles and twists wool yarn on the spinning wheel to strengthen it.
doubleur_de_laine.text: The doubleur de laine is a worker in wool mills responsible for combining several strands of yarn on the spinning wheel or the doubling mill, in order to obtain a stronger yarn before weaving. This doubling operation follows spinning proper and prepares the yarn for the stresses of the loom.

doubleur_de_soie.label: Doubleur de soie
doubleur_de_soie.summary: Silk-mill worker who doubles silk thread on reels after throwing.
doubleur_de_soie.text: The doubleur de soie works downstream of the throwster: he combines and twists several strands of silk on reels to strengthen the thread before weaving. The trade is typical of French silk-manufacturing towns, where silk work is broken down into many specialized steps entrusted to distinct workers.

doucisseur_de_glace.label: Doucisseur de glace
doucisseur_de_glace.summary: Worker in a mirror-glass manufactory responsible for the final polishing of the glass.
doucisseur_de_glace.text: The doucisseur de glace works in a plate-glass and mirror manufactory (such as Saint-Gobain): after casting and rough-grinding, he polishes the glass surface to make it perfectly smooth and transparent, the last step before the mirror is silvered.

douilleur.label: Douilleur
douilleur.summary: Worker who prepares hair intended for wigmakers and hairpiece makers.
douilleur.text: The douilleur prepares natural hair bought in bundles for resale to wigmakers and hairpiece makers: sorting, disentangling and preparing the hair before it is mounted on hairpieces and wigs.

douvelier.label: Douvelier
douvelier.summary: Craftsman who makes douvelles, small curved boards used to build casks.
douvelier.text: The douvelier makes douvelles, those split and curved wooden boards which, assembled in a circle, form the wall of casks and barrels. He works upstream of, or as a complement to, the cooper, who then assembles these pieces to build the cask.

drapier.label: Drapier (draper)
drapier.summary: Maker or merchant of woollen cloth.
drapier.text: The drapier makes and/or sells woollen cloth, one of the most widespread fabrics of the Ancien Régime. The term covers both the merchant-drapier, who has craftsmen work to order and sells the finished cloth, and the weaver-drapier, who weaves his own cloth himself; cloth towns (Elbeuf, Louviers, Sedan, Carcassonne) organized the trade into powerful guilds subject to very strict manufacturing regulations.

drapier_drapant.label: Drapier drapant
drapier_drapant.summary: Draper who weaves and makes his own cloth himself, as opposed to the merchant-drapier.
drapier_drapant.text: The drapier drapant is distinguished from the simple merchant-drapier in that he himself practises the weaver's trade: he makes the cloth he sells, rather than having it made to order by other craftsmen or merely trading in it. The distinction, common in guild regulations, marks the craftsman's economic and technical status.

draveur.label: Draveur (log driver)
draveur.summary: Forest worker who floated timber down rivers to sawmills.
draveur.text: The draveur practised timber floating ("la drave"): he guided logs cut in the forest along waterways to sawmills or points of sale, clearing log jams with a pike pole, often walking on the logs themselves. This particularly dangerous trade remained alive in Quebec into the mid-20th century and also existed in France in forest and floating regions (Morvan, Vosges).

drayeur.label: Drayeur
drayeur.summary: Currier who works leather with the drayoire.
drayeur.text: The drayeur is a currier who uses the drayoire, a curved-blade tool, to stretch and soften tanned hides and give them their final grain before the leather is sold.

dreigeur.label: Dreigeur
dreigeur.summary: Shellfish gatherer on the coast of the Pays de Caux.
dreigeur.text: The dreigeur is a shore gatherer who collects shellfish and crustaceans on the tidal flat, a term attested in the Pays de Caux (Normandy) where this activity often supplemented the income of fishing families.

dresseur.label: Dresseur
dresseur.summary: Person responsible for training domestic or performing animals.
dresseur.text: The dresseur trains animals according to their purpose: riding or draught horses, hunting or guard dogs, circus or fairground animals. The term applies both to a traditional rural trade and to 19th-century fairground performers.

dresseur_charbonnier.label: Dresseur charbonnier
dresseur_charbonnier.summary: Charcoal burner who builds the wood stack before firing the charcoal.
dresseur_charbonnier.text: The dresseur charbonnier is the charcoal-burning worker responsible for "building" the stack: methodically piling and arranging the logs into a mound covered with earth and moss, ready to be lit for the long firing that produces charcoal.

drilleur.label: Drilleur
drilleur.summary: Needle-making worker who polishes the eye of needles.
drilleur.text: The drilleur takes part in needle-making: he polishes and finishes the eye (the hole the thread passes through), a delicate operation requiring great precision so as not to weaken the needle.

drogman.label: Drogman (dragoman)
drogman.summary: Official interpreter in Oriental languages for embassies and consulates.
drogman.text: The drogman is an interpreter-translator employed by European embassies, consulates and trading companies in the Ottoman Empire and the Levant, indispensable to diplomatic and commercial relations with local authorities. The word comes from the Arabic "tarjumān" ("translator") via Turkish and Italian; the great powers maintained "jeunes de langues" (young interpreters) trained specifically for this role.

droguetier.label: Droguetier
droguetier.summary: Maker of droguet, a fabric mixing wool with thread or silk.
droguetier.text: The droguetier weaves droguet, a light patterned fabric often mixing wool with linen or silk, as well as tiretaine, a coarse fabric of wool and linen worn by people of modest condition.

droguiste.label: Droguiste (druggist)
droguiste.summary: Merchant of medicinal products, dye and fine grocery.
droguiste.text: The droguiste sells "drogues" in the old sense of the term: raw medicinal products, dyeing substances, spices and cleaning products. Before the regulation of the modern pharmacy, he played a role close to that of the apothecary for everyday remedies, while also trading in grocery and various chemical products.

drosseur.label: Drosseur
drosseur.summary: Wool-mill worker who greases and cards wool on the "drossettes".
drosseur.text: The drosseur works in wool mills: he greases the wool and then runs it through the "drossettes", large cards that disentangle and prepare the fibres before spinning. The term is also found in the form "drousseur" in Belgian and northern French wool-manufacturing regions.

drouineur.label: Drouineur
drouineur.summary: Small itinerant tinker repairing kitchen utensils from village to village.
drouineur.text: The drouineur is an itinerant tinker who travels the countryside to repair pots, pans and other metal utensils, often by tin soldering, in the manner of itinerant re-tinners.

duegne.label: Duègne (duenna)
duegne.summary: Elderly woman responsible for watching over the conduct and honour of young women.
duegne.text: The duègne (from the Spanish "dueña", "mistress of the house") is a governess or lady's companion responsible for watching over and accompanying a young woman of good family, particularly in Spanish custom and then, by literary extension, in Ancien Régime French society.

duranguier.label: Duranguier
duranguier.summary: Basque craftsman who wove thick woollen fabrics called marègues or mandilars.
duranguier.text: The duranguier made very thick woollen fabrics, called "marègues" or "mandilars", highly protective against the cold. The trade thrived in the Basque Country, particularly at Hasparren (Pyrénées-Atlantiques) where a street still bears the name "rue des Duranguiers"; it is attested as early as the 17th century and declined at the end of the 19th.

ebeniste.label: Ébéniste (cabinetmaker)
ebeniste.summary: Craftsman of luxury furniture, master of veneering and marquetry.
ebeniste.text: The ébéniste is a woodworking craftsman who, unlike the joiner, works mainly by veneering and marquetry: he applies fine sheets of precious wood (including ebony, which gave the trade its name) onto a solid-wood structure to make prestigious furniture. The trade became a distinct guild in Paris in the 17th century, notably around the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, and reached its peak with the great cabinetmakers of royal furniture in the 17th and 18th centuries.

eboueur.label: Éboueur
eboueur.summary: Worker responsible for collecting rubbish and keeping the streets clean.
eboueur.text: The éboueur is responsible for removing household waste and street mud (the word comes from "boue"/"boue de voirie", road mud). The trade became structured into an organized municipal service as towns, from the 19th century, adopted public-hygiene and waste-collection regulations.

ebougeuse.label: Ébougeuse
ebougeuse.summary: Textile worker who removes knots and impurities from fabrics with tweezers.
ebougeuse.text: The ébougeuse is a textile-finishing worker: using iron tweezers, she meticulously removes from fabrics the knots, straw bits and fluff that would impair their quality, before the cloth is sold.

ebrancheur.label: Ébrancheur
ebrancheur.summary: Woodcutter specialized in the preventive cutting of branches before felling.
ebrancheur.text: The ébrancheur climbs trees to cut large branches before the trunk is felled, so as to prevent them from damaging neighbouring trees or injuring woodcutters as they fall.

ecacheur.label: Écacheur
ecacheur.summary: Worker who flattens metal wire between two grindstones, or a wax-chandler's worker who kneads wax.
ecacheur.text: The écacheur has several attested senses: in metalworking, he is the worker who flattens metal wire by running it between two grindstones, or one who sets files and billhooks on the grindstone; at the wax chandler's, he is one who kneads wax to make it perfectly even, without lumps harder than the rest.

ecailler.label: Écailler
ecailler.summary: Merchant who sells and opens oysters and other shellfish.
ecailler.text: The écailler sells oysters and other shellfish, which he opens ("écaille") himself using a special knife. The term, still in use today to denote the oyster-opener of markets and brasseries, appears in old records under related forms such as "écailleur".

ecailliste.label: Écailliste
ecailliste.summary: Craftsman who works tortoiseshell to make decorative objects.
ecailliste.text: The écailliste shapes tortoiseshell, a precious material malleable when heated, to make missal covers, spectacle frames, combs and small art objects, a luxury craft close to that of the fancy-goods maker.

ecaillon.label: Écaillon
ecaillon.summary: Slate-quarry worker who extracts and cuts slate in the quarries.
ecaillon.text: The écaillon works in slate quarries: extracting the slate schist and then splitting and sizing the sheets to produce roofing slate, a trade attested in slate-quarry basins such as those of Anjou or the Ardennes.

ecangueur.label: Écangueur
ecangueur.summary: Textile worker who breaks flax and hemp stalks to separate the fibres.
ecangueur.text: The écangueur prepares textile fibres by breaking flax or hemp stalks using the "écang", a wooden tool that separates the tow from the straw and woody parts. This trade is also found in the form "échangueur" in some regions.

echalasseur.label: Échalasseur
echalasseur.summary: Craftsman who cuts and makes vine stakes.
echalasseur.text: The échalasseur cuts and prepares vine stakes, the wooden posts planted to support vine stocks or trellised crops, a trade linked to wine-growing regions.

echantilleur.label: Échantilleur
echantilleur.summary: Official inspector of the weights and measures used by merchants and craftsmen.
