fermailler.text: The fermailler shapes clasps and hooks, often of brass or precious metal, used to fasten clothing, belts, books or purses. This small-goldsmith or coppersmith work overlaps with that of the button-maker and the goldsmith depending on the richness of the materials used.

fermier.label: Fermier
fermier.summary: Farmer who works land in exchange for paying rent to the owner.
fermier.text: The fermier farms land he does not own, in exchange for a fixed rent ("fermage") paid to the owner, unlike the sharecropper, who shares the harvest. This status, more favourable to the tenant since independent of harvest fluctuations, spread mainly in the north and the Paris basin, while sharecropping dominated in the south and centre of France.

fermier_general.label: Fermier général (farmer-general)
fermier_general.summary: Private financier who advances tax to the king and reimburses himself by collecting indirect taxes himself.
fermier_general.text: The fermier général belongs to the Ferme générale, a company of financiers who leased from the king the collection of indirect taxes (gabelle, traites, aides) in exchange for an advance lump-sum payment. This system, a source of immense fortunes but also of intense unpopularity, ended with the French Revolution — several fermiers généraux, including Lavoisier, were guillotined in 1794.

ferrailleur.label: Ferrailleur (scrap dealer)
ferrailleur.summary: Merchant and salvager of scrap metal, buying and reselling used metal objects and debris.
ferrailleur.text: The ferrailleur collects, sorts and resells scrap — worn-out iron or steel objects and debris — to supply foundries and forges with recycled raw material. This itinerant or fixed trade, often associated with ragpickers, is an old form of metal recycling.

ferrandinier.label: Ferrandinier
ferrandinier.summary: Weaver making ferrandine, a fabric mixing silk and wool (or thread), woven notably in Lyon.
ferrandinier.text: The ferrandinier weaves ferrandine, a light fabric mixing a silk warp with a wool or thread weft, whose manufacture developed in Lyon in the 17th century under the impetus of a weaver named Ferrand. Less costly than pure silk, it enjoyed great popular success before declining in the face of competition from other mixed fabrics.

ferratier.label: Ferratier
ferratier.summary: Regional term for scrap dealer: merchant who salvages and resells iron and used metal objects.
ferratier.text: The ferratier is a regional variant of the scrap dealer, denoting one who collects and resells scrap and old iron objects for reuse or remelting. The word is also attested as the name of a farrier's tool, reflecting the closeness between working iron and its salvage trade.

ferreur.label: Ferreur
ferreur.summary: Synonym for hemp-beater: worker who breaks hemp stalks with a flail or brake.
ferreur.text: The ferreur, a regional term equivalent to "batteur de chanvre" or "chanvrier", works to separate hemp's textile fibre from the woody part of the stalk (the "chènevotte"), using iron tools — hence the name — such as the brake or flail. This step follows the retting of the stalks and precedes the combing of the tow.

ferreur_d_aiguillettes.label: Ferreur d'aiguillettes
ferreur_d_aiguillettes.summary: Craftsman who fits the metal tip (the "fer") onto the end of aiguillettes, clothing cords.
ferreur_d_aiguillettes.text: The ferreur d'aiguillettes fixes a small metal tip (iron, brass or tin) to the end of aiguillettes — laces or cords used to fasten certain garment pieces before the button became widespread — to ease their passing through eyelets and prevent fraying. "Esguillettes" is the old spelling of "aiguillettes".

ferreur_de_formes.label: Ferreur de formes
ferreur_de_formes.summary: Shoemaking worker who nails and firmly fixes the sole to the shoe last.
ferreur_de_formes.text: The ferreur de formes takes part in shoemaking: he fixes the sole to the last (the wooden mould that gives the shoe its shape) using small nails, a step decisive for the shoe's sturdiness and comfort before industrial stitching or gluing developed.

ferrier.label: Ferrier
ferrier.summary: Iron worker, a generic term denoting one who works metal in a forge or an iron mine.
ferrier.text: "Ferrier" broadly denotes an iron worker, whether a blacksmith, an iron miner or a foundry worker depending on region and period. The term, vaguer than "forgeron" or "maréchal-ferrant", appears notably in old records of mining and iron-working regions.

ferron.label: Ferron
ferron.summary: Old term for a blacksmith or iron merchant, the origin of the surname Ferron.
ferron.text: "Ferron" is an old French word for a blacksmith or iron worker, now vanished from everyday use but fossilized in the surname Ferron, very common in western France. It shares its Latin root ("ferrum", iron) with "ferronnier" and "ferrailleur".

ferronnier.label: Ferronnier
ferronnier.summary: Craftsman who shapes wrought iron into utilitarian or decorative objects: railings, banisters, signs.
ferronnier.text: The ferronnier works iron with hammer and anvil to produce railings, balconies, staircase banisters, signs or art objects, in a tradition that distinguishes his decorative work from that of the more functional blacksmith or farrier. Art ironwork enjoyed a golden age in the Art Nouveau period, with figures such as Hector Guimard.

ferrotier.label: Ferrotier
ferrotier.summary: Glassworker responsible for gathering molten glass on the end of an iron rod to give it to the blower.
ferrotier.text: The ferrotier works within a glassworks team: using a "ferret", an iron rod, he gathers a mass of molten glass (the parison) from the furnace, which he then hands to the blower responsible for shaping it. This supporting trade, now vanished with the mechanization of the glass industry, illustrates the highly specialized organization of work in old glassworks.

ferteur.label: Ferteur
ferteur.summary: Textile worker who combs fibres (hemp or flax) to disentangle and align them before spinning.
ferteur.text: The ferteur combs hemp or flax tow using a hackle (a board bristling with iron points) to disentangle the fibres, remove impurities and align the strands for spinning. This step, between breaking and spinning proper, determines the fineness of the resulting thread.

feseresse_de_chapeaux_d_orfroi.label: Feseresse de chapeaux d'orfroi
feseresse_de_chapeaux_d_orfroi.summary: Luxury hat-maker embroidering orfroi (gold-thread) headwear for an aristocratic clientele.
feseresse_de_chapeaux_d_orfroi.text: The feseresse de chapeaux d'orfroi makes headwear adorned with orfroi embroidery — bands of fabric embroidered with gold or silver thread, also used on liturgical vestments — intended for a wealthy clientele. The term "orfroi" comes from the Latin "aurum phrygium", "gold of Phrygia", a region renowned in antiquity for its gold embroidery.

fesseresse_d_aumoniere_sarrazinoise.label: Fesseresse d'aumonière sarrazinoise
fesseresse_d_aumoniere_sarrazinoise.summary: Maker of richly adorned purses or bags.
fesseresse_d_aumoniere_sarrazinoise.text: The fesseresse d'aumônière sarrazinoise makes richly adorned purses or bags, called "à la sarrazinoise", a medieval term from Étienne Boileau's Book of Trades.

feuillagiste.label: Feuillagiste
feuillagiste.summary: Person who makes artificial flowers and foliage.
feuillagiste.text: The feuillagiste makes artificial flowers and foliage, a craft close to that of the florist-plumassier.

feuillardier.label: Hoop-wood cutter (feuillardier)
feuillardier.summary: Forest craftsman who shapes wooden circles from chestnut wood (hoop-wood) intended for cask binding.
feuillardier.text: The feuillardier exploits chestnut coppices — especially in Charente, Limousin, and northern Dordogne — to produce hoop-wood: stems split then bent into circles, used by the cooper to bind barrels and baskets. The term appeared only around 1850, though the trade is older; the number of feuillardiers, which reached 1,280 in 1906, later declined with competition from iron hoop-wood.

feutier.label: Felt maker (feutier)
feutier.summary: Maker of felt, a non-woven fabric obtained by fulling and pressing wool or hair fibres.
feutier.text: The feutier produces felt by fulling and pressing damp wool or animal-hair fibres (often rabbit or beaver hair) without passing through weaving. This material served notably in hat-making, which sometimes made this trade overlap with that of the felt-hat maker.

fevre_marechal.label: Smith-farrier (fèvre maréchal)
fevre_marechal.summary: Craftsman combining the skills of blacksmith and farrier, serving a rural community.
fevre_marechal.text: The fèvre-maréchal combined general iron work — tools, fittings, various repairs — with farrier work shoeing horses, two activities often distinct in towns but merged in small rural communities where a single craftsman had to answer all metallurgical needs. "Fèvre" comes from Latin faber, craftsman.

fidelier.label: Pasta maker (fidelier)
fidelier.summary: Provençal craftsman who produces food pasta, particularly fidéou (fine vermicelli), from durum wheat.
fidelier.text: The fidelier makes food pasta, particularly fidéou or fidés — fine vermicelli — typical of Provençal and more broadly Mediterranean cuisine (the word fideos is found in Catalan and Spanish). This artisanal activity, ancestor of industrial pasta factories, allowed long-term wheat preservation when transformed.

fifre.label: Fifer (fifre)
fifre.summary: Musician playing the fife, a small shrill flute used for military and naval signals and ceremonies.
fifre.text: The fifer is a musician who plays the fife, a small high-pitched wind instrument, employed aboard ships and in regiments to pace marching, transmit signals or animate ceremonies, often in a pair with a drummer. The role remained attested in sailing navies into the 19th century.

figuriniste.label: Figurine maker (figuriniste)
figuriniste.summary: Creator of figurines or miniature costumes, for theatre, cinema or decorative sculpture.
figuriniste.text: The figuriniste (or figuriste) designs and creates figurines — small sculptures representing characters or scenes — or designs costume designs for spectacles, depending on context. The term covers both ancient art craftsmanship (nativity-figure maker, religious-figure sculptor) and contemporary theatre craft.

filandiere.label: Hemp/linen spinner (filandière)
filandiere.summary: Spinner specialized in spinning linen or hemp, a term also at the origin of the expression 'spider-spinner.'
filandiere.text: The filandière spins linen or hemp tow with a spindle or spinning wheel, work traditionally female and often practised at home to supplement agricultural income. The word also gave rise to the expression "araignée filandière" (spinner spider), naming certain web-spinning spiders, by analogy with the thread produced. "Filandier" is its masculine form, rarer.

filassier.label: Flax/hemp preparer (filassier)
filassier.summary: Textile worker who prepares flax (linen or hemp fibre) by breaking then combing, before spinning.
filassier.text: The filassier transforms retting-treated linen or hemp stems into flax (fibre): he breaks them to separate the textile fibre from the woody part, then combs it with a hackle to untangle and align the strands. The feminine "filassière" denoted more specifically the workers responsible for fine combing, the step following before spinning proper.

filateur.label: Spinning-mill owner (filateur)
filateur.summary: Industrialist directing a spinning mill, factory for transforming textile fibres into thread.
filateur.text: The filateur owns or directs a spinning mill, an industrial establishment equipped with spinning machines (mechanized from the late 18th century onward) transforming cotton, wool or linen into thread. The term thus designates rather an industrial entrepreneur than a simple spinner worker.

filatier.label: Sayette-thread merchant (filatier)
filatier.summary: Amiens merchant who sells sayette thread, supplying sayette weavers with fibre.
filatier.text: The filatier commercializes sayette thread — worsted wool thread mixed with a silk thread — used in sayette-making, a textile industry that developed in Amiens from the 16th century onward thanks to the arrival of reformed artisans. He often distributed carded wool to home spinners before collecting and reselling the thread obtained.

filatrice.label: Silk thread-winder (filatrice)
filatrice.summary: Worker who unwinds thread from silk cocoons by immersion in hot water.
filatrice.text: The filatrice works in a silk-spinning mill: she plunges cocoons in hot water to soften the gum binding the fibres, then unwinds several strands simultaneously to form a continuous, regular silk thread. This trade, essentially female, supported the rise of sericulture in south-eastern France, notably around Lyon.

fileresse.label: Silk spinner (fileresse)
fileresse.summary: Worker spinner unwinding and spinning silk, named according to the spindle size employed.
fileresse.text: The fileresse is a worker spinner unwinding and spinning silk, her designation varying according to the spindle size she employed.

aliases: Silk thread spinner with large and small spindles
fileresse_de_soie_a_grands_et_petits_fus.label: Silk spinner with various spindle sizes (fileresse de soie à grands et petits fuseaux)
fileresse_de_soie_a_grands_et_petits_fus.summary: Silk spinner using different spindle sizes to produce silk threads of varying qualities.
fileresse_de_soie_a_grands_et_petits_fus.text: The silk spinner with various spindle sizes adapted her tool to the result sought: the large spindle gave a thicker thread for common uses, the small spindle a finer thread reserved for precious fabrics. "Fileresse" is an old feminine form of "fileur," now replaced by "fileuse."

filetier.label: Fishing-net maker (filetier)
filetier.summary: Craftsman making fishing nets, by knotting threads according to the mesh suited to each use.
filetier.text: The filetier knots and assembles threads (hemp, then cotton or nylon) to make fishing nets, whose mesh and size vary according to the species sought and the fishing technique employed. This know-how, long transmitted in fisherman families of Breton and Norman ports, has largely disappeared with industrialized net-making.

filetoupier.label: Hemp beater (filetoupier)
filetoupier.summary: Farm worker who beats hemp to separate seeds and prepare stems for retting.
filetoupier.text: The filetoupier participated in the first stages of hemp work: beating dried stems to detach seeds (hemp seed), before the stems themselves were retting in water to free the textile fibre. The word seems composed of "fil" (thread) and "étoupe" (coarse fibre residue of hemp or linen).

fileur.label: Rope spinner (fileur)
fileur.summary: Cordage worker who regularly supplies the rope-works with fibres, controlling thread tension and regularity.
fileur.text: The fileur works in a rope-works: he supplies fibres (most often hemp) to the spinning mechanism, ensuring regular supply to obtain cordage of constant cross-section. This post, exercised walking backward along the rope-works over long distances, gave its name to the elongated "rope-works" typical of ports (such as that at Rochefort).

fileur_d_or.label: Gold-thread spinner (fileur d'or)
fileur_d_or.summary: Craftsman who stretches and winds a gold thread over a textile core, for embroidery and braid-making.
fileur_d_or.text: The gold-thread spinner makes the gold thread used in embroidery and braid-making: he winds in spiral a fine gold leaf or gilt-metal around a silk or linen core, obtaining a supple thread that keeps the sheen of precious metal. This precision work, close to goldsmithing, served to ornament liturgical vestments, military uniforms and ceremonial dress.

fileuse.label: Spinner (fileuse)
fileuse.summary: Worker who spins a textile fibre (wool, linen, hemp, cotton) with a spindle or spinning wheel.
fileuse.text: The spinner transforms raw textile fibre into continuous thread, by progressively twisting it with a hand spindle then, from the 16th century onward, with a pedal-driven wheel that greatly speeds the work. An essentially domestic activity, spinning occupied many rural women during long winter evenings, often in collective vigils.

fileuse_de_coton.label: Cotton spinner (fileuse de coton)
fileuse_de_coton.summary: Worker who spins cotton, an activity that mechanized early with the rise of industrial spinning mills.
fileuse_de_coton.text: The cotton spinner spins imported cotton fibre, an activity that shifted very early from domestic craft to mechanized mill work from the late 18th century onward, notably in Normandy and northern France, birthplaces of the French textile industrial revolution.

fileuse_de_laine.label: Wool spinner (fileuse de laine)
fileuse_de_laine.summary: Worker who spins wool, transforming it into thread for weaving or knitting.
fileuse_de_laine.text: The wool spinner cards then spins sheep's fleece to make a thread used in weaving (cloth, fabrics) or knitting. This work, one of the oldest and most widespread in French countryside, long preceded and supplied local wool weavers before the era of mechanical mills.

fileuse_de_lin.label: Linen spinner (fileuse de lin)
fileuse_de_lin.summary: Worker who spins linen fibres with a spinning wheel, to obtain thread for linen weaving.
fileuse_de_lin.text: The linen spinner transforms flax — fibre obtained after hackling linen stems — into regular thread by means of a spinning wheel, thread then woven into linen. This activity was particularly developed in linen-producing regions such as Normandy, Brittany and Flanders, birthplace of the linen and lace industries.

fileuse_de_soie.label: Silk spinner (fileuse de soie)
fileuse_de_soie.summary: Worker who spins silk by unwinding cocoons of silkworms to form continuous thread.
fileuse_de_soie.text: The silk spinner works in a silk mill: she immerses cocoons in hot water then unwinds simultaneously several strands to form a continuous, strong raw silk thread. This activity strongly marked the economy of south-eastern France, particularly around Lyon and in the Cévennes, regions of intensive sericulture in the 18th–19th centuries.

fille_de_confiance.label: Trusted servant (fille de confiance)
fille_de_confiance.summary: Domestic servant occupying a privileged position in the household, entrusted with delicate tasks.
fille_de_confiance.text: The trusted servant enjoyed a privileged position among domestics: her masters entrusted her with sensitive tasks (handling money, supervising children, overseeing other domestics) supposing tested loyalty and discretion, often after many years of service in the same household.

fille_de_friture.label: Fish fryer (fille de friture)
fille_de_friture.summary: Worker specialized in frying fish, in a cannery or in a popular eating-house.
fille_de_friture.text: The fish fryer prepares and fries fish, whether in a small popular-eating establishment or in a cannery, where frying could precede canning. This work was found notably in fishing ports and popular quarters near market halls.

fille_de_peine.label: Drudge (fille de peine)
fille_de_peine.summary: Servant assigned to the most taxing domestic work: heavy cleaning, water-carrying, physical labour.
fille_de_peine.text: The drudge occupied the lowest rung of the domestic hierarchy: entrusted with the hardest and least valued work — laundry, water-carrying, floor and privy maintenance — as opposed to the chambermaid or trusted servant, closer to household masters.

fille_de_quartier.label: Cleaning servant (fille de quartier)
fille_de_quartier.summary: Belgian domestic employee responsible for maintaining an apartment or part of a large dwelling, often temporarily.
fille_de_quartier.text: The cleaning servant, a term mainly used in Belgium, maintains an apartment or section of a large house, frequently part-time or seasonally, unlike a servant permanently attached to a single household.

fille_de_salle.label: Hospital cleaner (fille de salle)
fille_de_salle.summary: Housemaid and nursing aide in a hospital.
fille_de_salle.text: The hospital cleaner ensures housekeeping and assists carers in a hospital ward, an old function at the origin of the nursing aide profession.

finisseur.label: Finisher (finisseur)
finisseur.summary: Worker responsible for finishing operations on a product, the last step before sale.
finisseur.text: The finisher intervenes at the end of the manufacturing chain to perfect a product — polishing, checking, retouches, assembling final details — according to the quality requirements of the sector concerned (textiles, metallurgy, furniture, etc.). The term is thus generic and found in many occupations.

finisseuse.label: Finisher (finisseuse)
finisseuse.summary: Worker responsible for finishing operations on a product, notably in textiles or clothing-making.
finisseuse.text: The finisher performs final retouches on a product before sale: in textiles and clothing-making in particular, she ensures finishing (hems, buttonholes, quality checks) after main assembly by other workers.

fioutier.label: Petty merchant (fioutier)
fioutier.summary: Small trader or regional artisan selling miscellaneous goods and everyday objects.
fioutier.text: The term fioutier, rare and little documented, seems to denote a small trader or itinerant artisan offering miscellaneous goods and everyday objects to a local clientele, as a settled peddler might. Its precise regional origin and exact field of activity remain uncertain due to lack of reliable sources.

flaconnier.label: Bottle maker (flaconnier)
flaconnier.summary: Maker of glass or metal bottles, for goldsmithing or perfume trade.
flaconnier.text: The flaconnier makes bottles in glass or metal, generally intended for goldsmithing or perfume trade.

flanellier.label: Flannel weaver (flanellier)
flanellier.summary: Weaver of flannel, a lightweight woollen fabric.
flanellier.text: The flannel weaver weaves flannel, a lightweight carded-wool fabric, used for clothing and linen making.

fletayeur.label: Ferry operator (flétayeur)
fletayeur.summary: Ferry operator, named after his boat the flette.
fletayeur.text: The ferry operator is a ferry operator whose boat, called "flette," gave him his name.

fletteur.label: Glass edge finisher (fletteur)
fletteur.summary: Glass worker who smooths glass edges with an abrasive band.
fletteur.text: The glass edge finisher is a glassworker who smooths glass edges using an abrasive band, a finishing step in glassmaking.

fleuriste.label: Florist (fleuriste)
fleuriste.summary: Seller or seller of flowers, grown or bought wholesale for retail sale.
fleuriste.text: The florist sells cut or potted flowers, which he sometimes grows himself or buys at market halls and flower markets. The trade was organized into a corporation from the 17th century and remains today one of the few ancient occupational names to have kept its original meaning without notable change.

flotteur.label: Log driver (flotteur)
flotteur.summary: Worker who conveys wood down rivers, from forest to towns or ports.
flotteur.text: The log driver conveys wood on waterways, either in assembled log trains guided with poles, or in loose-log floating, to transport logs from distant forests to sawmills, shipyards or wood-consuming cities. The floating of wood for Paris from the Morvan, via the Yonne, is the most famous example, active until mid-19th century.

fluqueur.label: Waggon loader (fluqueur)
fluqueur.summary: In the Amiens region, a waggon hand loading and unloading goods vehicles.
fluqueur.text: In the Amiens region, the fluqueur is a waggon hand charged with loading and unloading waggons and carts of goods.

fonctionnaire.label: Civil servant (fonctionnaire)
fonctionnaire.summary: Holder of a permanent post in a public administration.
fonctionnaire.text: The civil servant holds a statutory post in a state administration, local authority or public establishment, governed in France by a law distinct from private labour law. The term, in older documents, may also denote more widely a holder of a public office or charge.

fondeur.label: Founder (fondeur)
fondeur.summary: Metallurgical worker who melts metal and casts it in moulds to form pieces.
fondeur.text: The founder melts metal (iron, bronze, tin, copper) in a furnace then casts it in a mould to obtain pieces of varying shapes: statues, bells, cannons, utensils. Founding forms a key step of metallurgy, distinct from cold or hammer work practised by the blacksmith.

fondeur_de_cloches.label: Bell founder (fondeur de cloches)
fondeur_de_cloches.summary: Craftsman founder specialized in making bells for churches and religious buildings.
fondeur_de_cloches.text: The bell founder casts bronze (an alloy of copper and tin) in a complex mould of earth and lost wax to produce bells, whose sound depends on precise alloy dosing and careful geometry. Founder families, such as the Cornille-Havard in Normandy, passed on this know-how generation after generation until today.

fondeur_de_suif.label: Tallow melter (fondeur de suif)
fondeur_de_suif.summary: Founder of animal fats intended for candles and soap.
fondeur_de_suif.text: The tallow melter melts animal fats used for making candles and soap.

fondeur_en_caracteres.label: Type founder (fondeur en caractères)
fondeur_en_caracteres.text: The type founder makes printing type by casting lead in matrices, an occupation essential to printing before mechanical composition.

forcat.label: Galley slave (forçat)
forcat.summary: Criminal sentenced to the galleys then to deportation.
forcat.text: The galley slave is a criminal sentenced by justice to serve in the galleys, then later to deportation to a colonial penal colony; he is related to the galley rower and the transported prisoner.

forcetier.label: Tool maker (forcetier)
forcetier.summary: Maker of large iron tools, notably shears (forces) for cloth-shearers.
forcetier.text: The tool maker fabricates large iron tools, in particular shears (large scissors) used by cloth-shearers.

forestier.label: Forester (forestier)
forestier.summary: Agent or worker responsible for the management, exploitation or surveillance of a forest.
forestier.text: The forester worked at the upkeep, exploitation or surveillance of wooded areas, a function covering both the woodcutter worker and the agent charged with enforcing forestry regulations depending on era and context. Under the Ancien Régime, management of royal forests fell under a specific administration, that of Waters and Forests.

foreur.label: Cannon borer (foreur)
foreur.summary: Worker in a boring-mill charged with boring cannon barrels from the foundry.
foreur.text: The cannon borer works in a boring-mill where he is charged with boring cannon barrels from the foundry, an operation that could be hand-worked or mechanically powered.

foreur_de_bateaux.label: Boat borer (foreur de bateaux)
foreur_de_bateaux.summary: Shipwright boring holes intended for wooden pegs and dowels.
foreur_de_bateaux.text: The boat borer is a shipwright charged with boring, using an auger or hand-drill, holes intended to receive the wooden pegs and dowels assembling the hull.

forgeron.label: Forgeron (blacksmith)
forgeron.summary: Craftsman working iron at the forge fire to make tools and fittings.
forgeron.text: The blacksmith heated and hammered iron to make or repair farm tools, cart fittings and horseshoes. A central village figure, he was sometimes also the farrier when he shod horses and oxen as well.

forgeur_de_baionnette.label: Bayonet maker (forgeur de baïonnette)
forgeur_de_baionnette.summary: Weapon craftsman forging bayonets, blades meant to be fixed to a rifle barrel.
forgeur_de_baionnette.text: The bayonet maker shapes by hammer and file the blade and socket of the bayonet, a white weapon fixed to the rifle barrel's end for close combat, generalized in European armies from the 17th century onward. This work fell under royal then national arms manufactories.

forgeur_de_fiches.label: Hinge maker (forgeur de fiches)
forgeur_de_fiches.summary: In 18th-century Loire, maker of window and door hinges.
forgeur_de_fiches.text: In 18th-century Loire, the hinge maker fabricates hinges (fiches) for windows and doors.

formier.label: Hat-form maker (formier)
formier.summary: Craftsman preparing wooden forms used to shape hats.
formier.text: The hat-form maker prepares wooden forms on which hat-makers shape hats.

formiere.label: Mould maker (formière)
formiere.summary: Worker who makes moulds (forms), notably in shoemaking or hat-making.
formiere.text: The mould maker shapes forms — wooden or metal moulds that give finished objects their geometry, whether the form of a shoe in shoemaking or of a hat in hat-making. The precise term depends on the context of the document where it appears, as several trades employed "forms" as basic tools.

forneleur.label: Lime-kiln worker (forneleur)
forneleur.text: The lime-kiln worker works in a lime-kiln, where he ensures the cooking of limestone to extract lime.

fort_des_halles.label: Market porter (fort des Halles)
fort_des_halles.summary: Warehouse hand of the Paris market halls, charged with carrying and unloading goods on his back.
fort_des_halles.text: The market porter unloaded and transported on his back crates, sacks and meat quarters in great Parisian markets, particularly the central Halles. Organized in a corporation with their own costume and rules, these porters renowned for their strength formed a popular figure of Paris until the Halles' closing in 1969.

fossoyeur.label: Gravedigger (fossoyeur)
fossoyeur.summary: Worker in funeral services who digs graves and performs burials of the dead.
fossoyeur.text: The gravedigger digs the grave in the cemetery, lowers the coffin into it then fills it after the ceremony, an essential and permanent task of every parish or municipality. Often attached to the church or parish vestry under the Ancien Régime, he could combine this function with that of bell-ringer or beadle.

fou_du_roi.label: Royal jester (fou du Roi)
fou_du_roi.summary: Official fool at the court of French kings, from Charles V to Louis XIV.
fou_du_roi.text: The royal jester is the official fool at the court of French kings, an office attested from Charles V until Louis XIV, who abolished it.

fouacier.label: Bread maker (fouacier)
fouacier.summary: Merchant and/or maker of fouaces, dense-dough bread in star shape.
fouacier.text: The fouace maker makes and/or sells fouaces, a kind of very dense-dough bread, of long shelf-life, traditionally shaped as a six-pointed star.

foubier.label: Regional artisan (foubier)
foubier.summary: Regional artisan whose exact activity remains uncertain, probably linked to a local craft transmitted orally.
foubier.text: The term foubier is not reliably documented in consulted genealogical and lexicographic sources; it would denote an artisan practising a traditional trade using techniques specific to his region, without the exact nature of this activity being establishable with certainty.

foudroyeur.label: Large-cask maker (foudroyeur)
foudroyeur.summary: Cooper specialized in making foudres, large storage and wine-aging casks.
foudroyeur.text: The large-cask maker builds foudres, casks of very large capacity (sometimes exceeding several thousand litres) used for wine or other liquid storage and aging in cellars, a technique close to coopering but adapted to much more massive wood pieces.

fouleur.label: Leather soaker (fouleur)
fouleur.summary: Tawer who spreads and soaks hides in treatment vats.
fouleur.text: The leather soaker is a tawer who spreads hides in vats where they undergo treatment, soaking them to arrange and work them thoroughly.

foulon.label: Fuller (foulon)
foulon.summary: Worker who fulls wool fabrics, beating and pressing them to tighten and thicken the cloth.
foulon.text: The fuller submits wool cloth to mechanical hammering (at a fulling mill, powered by hydraulic force) or hand beating, in soapy or clay water, to tighten fibres and make the fabric denser, warmer and more resistant. This step, essential in cloth-making, gave its name to many "fulling mills" along rivers.

fourbisseur.label: Sword-maker (fourbisseur)
fourbisseur.summary: Armourer in white arms, who garnishes, mounts and sells sabres and swords.
fourbisseur.text: The sword-maker is an armourer specialized in white arms: he garnishes, mounts and sells all sorts of sabres and swords.

fourbisseur_d_haubergeons.label: Mail-coat maker (fourbisseur d'haubergeons)
fourbisseur_d_haubergeons.summary: Armourer specialized in making sleeveless, unhooded mail coats.
fourbisseur_d_haubergeons.text: The mail-coat maker is an armourer specialized in making haubergeons, short mail coats without sleeves or hood.

fourboutier.label: Vegetable merchant (fourboutier)
fourboutier.text: The vegetable merchant is a market gardener, vegetable seller whom he sometimes grew himself.

fourgonnier.label: Baker (fourgonnier)
fourgonnier.summary: Baker in charge of the oven and bread baking.
fourgonnier.text: The baker is a baker charged with the oven and bread baking, wielding for this the fourgon, a kind of iron scraper used to rake the embers.

fournier.label: Miller/Baker (fournier)
fournier.summary: Baker or oven operator, often a manorial oven where villagers baked their bread.
fournier.text: The miller/baker operated a bread oven, whether his own business or the manorial oven where villagers were obliged, under the Ancien Régime, to bake their dough in exchange for a fee. The word is at the origin of many surnames (Fournier, Fornier) very common in France.

fourreur.label: Furrier (fourreur)
fourreur.summary: Craftsman who dresses and works furs, from raw skins to finished garments and trimmings.
fourreur.text: The furrier dressed skins (tanning, dyeing) then assembled them into coats, collars or trimmings, a luxury activity strictly regulated by its corporation under the Ancien Régime. Distinct from the pelterer who handled more the raw skin trade, the furrier intervened more in final transformation and making.

fourreux.label: Fur merchant (fourreux)
fourreux.text: The fur merchant sells furs, to be distinguished from the furrier who works and makes them.

foyalier.label: Hearth/chimney artisan (foyalier)
foyalier.summary: Regional artisan linked to the building or upkeep of hearths and chimneys, according to local usage.
foyalier.text: The term foyalier, little attested in old occupational dictionaries, would denote an artisan intervening in the building, upkeep or repair of domestic hearths and chimneys using techniques and needs specific to his region; its exact field of activity cannot be established with certainty due to lack of reliable sources.

fraisier.label: Butcher (fraisier)
fraisier.text: The fraisier is a butcher, probably specialized in offal sales, to be linked with the tripe-seller.

frangeur.label: Fringe maker (frangeur)
frangeur.summary: Craftsman specialized in making fringes, textile ornaments with hanging threads.
frangeur.text: The fringe maker weaves or knots fringes — ornamental bands ending in hanging threads — used to border curtains, hangings, uniforms or liturgical ornaments. This trade falls under passementerie, like that of the braid-maker, but differs by the specific production of fringes rather than flat braids.

frappeur.label: Hammer-man (frappeur)
frappeur.summary: Blacksmith who hammers the piece to be forged while another worker holds it.
frappeur.text: The hammer-man is a blacksmith worker who hammers the piece to forge with a sledge or hammer at the forge exit, while another worker holds it with tongs.

freineur.label: Brake operator (freineur)
freineur.summary: Miner responsible for operating brakes on ore cars on inclined planes.
freineur.text: The brake operator is a miner responsible for operating the brakes on ore cars or wagons on mine inclined planes.

fremailler.label: Clasp maker (frémailler)
fremailler.summary: Maker of fermaux: hooks, brooches, clasps fastening clothing.
fremailler.text: The clasp maker makes fermaux (fermails), that is, clasps such as hooks, brooches and clasps, used for fastening clothing.

fresquiste.label: Fresco painter (fresquiste)
fresquiste.text: The fresco painter paints frescoes, a technique of mural painting executed on fresh plaster.

fretier.label: Barrel-lath cutter (frétier)
fretier.summary: Cutter of chestnut laths intended for barrel-making.
fretier.text: The barrel-lath cutter cuts chestnut laths intended for barrel-making, preparatory work for coopering.

fretteur.label: Hemp fiber cleaner (fretteur)
fretteur.summary: Worker who clears hemp flax of the woody residue remaining after hackling.
fretteur.text: The hemp fiber cleaner cleans hemp flax by beating or shaking it to detach the chènevotte, the brittle woody residues of the stem, to keep only the usable textile fibre for spinning. This step follows hackling and precedes combing with a hackle.

fripier.label: Second-hand clothes dealer (fripier)
fripier.summary: Dealer in clothes, furniture or second-hand objects, resold after refurbishment.
fripier.text: The second-hand dealer bought and resold second-hand clothing and objects, refurbished if needed, an activity essential before the era of cheap ready-to-wear for clothing the common classes. Organized into a corporation in Paris from the Middle Ages, second-hand dealing formed an important economic link, notably in reselling inheritances and seized goods.

friteur.label: Fish fryer (friteur)
friteur.summary: Person keeping a fry house, selling fried fish and potatoes.
friteur.text: The fish fryer kept a fry house, stand selling fried fish and potatoes, the French equivalent of English "fish and chips."

friteuse.label: Fish fryer (friteuse)
friteuse.text: The fish fryer worked in a fish cannery, where she was charged with frying fish before canning.

friturier.label: Fried fish seller (friturier)
friturier.text: The fried fish seller sold fried fish, often at markets or seaside.

froctier.label: Froc fabric weaver (froctier)
froctier.summary: Weaver or merchant of froc, coarse woollen fabric made notably in the Caux country (Normandy).
froctier.text: The froc fabric weaver (or froquier) worked froc, a coarse woollen fabric made in Bolbec, Gruchet and other Caux localities in Normandy. The term is attested in Seine-Maritime and Eure documents from the 18th century; it should not be confused with froc denoting monastic habit, though both words share the same root evoking rough woollen cloth.

fromager.label: Cheesemaker (fromager)
fromager.summary: Maker or merchant of cheeses, transforming milk or ensuring aging and sale.
fromager.text: The cheesemaker transforms milk into cheese (curdling, moulding, aging) or, depending on the region, specializes in its trade and cave aging. The diversity of French terroirs gave birth to hundreds of regional varieties, each linked to distinct local know-how and corporations.

frotteur_de_lunettes.label: Spectacle polisher (frotteur de lunettes)
frotteur_de_lunettes.summary: Optician who smooths and polishes lens surfaces of spectacles and mirrors.
frotteur_de_lunettes.text: The spectacle polisher is an optician worker charged with smoothing and polishing lens surfaces of spectacles and mirrors.

fruitier.label: Fruit seller / Cheese coop manager (fruitier)
fruitier.summary: Fruit merchant, or, in the Alps and Jura, head of a fruitière, collective cheese cooperative.
fruitier.text: The fruit seller vends fruits at market or in shop; but in Jura, Alpine and Franche-Comté massifs, the word also denotes one managing a "fruitière," a cooperative where several producers pooled their milk to collectively make large cheese wheels (Comté, Gruyère), a tradition dating to the Middle Ages.

fumiste.label: Chimney specialist (fumiste)
fumiste.summary: Craftsman who builds and maintains fireplaces, stoves and smoke ducts.
fumiste.text: The chimney specialist installed and repaired fireplaces, stoves and smoke-duct outlets, a technical trade essential before the spread of central heating. The modern figurative sense of the word ("unreliable person") might come from a joke on itinerant chimney specialists of the 19th century, reputed sometimes unreliable in repair promises.

fuselier.label: Spindle maker (fuselier)
fuselier.summary: Maker of wooden spindles and distaffs from holly and other woods.
fuselier.text: The spindle maker made spindles from holly wood and distaffs, tools used by spinners.

fustier.label: Wood worker (fustier)
fustier.summary: In the Middle Ages, any person working wood (carpenter, cooper, turner, joiner).
fustier.text: In the Middle Ages, the fustier denotes any wood worker: carpenter, cooper, turner, joiner, etc.

futainier.label: Fustian maker (futainier)
futainier.summary: Maker or merchant of fustian, a thread-and-cotton fabric.
futainier.text: The fustian maker makes or sells fustian, a twilled fabric of linen thread and cotton, used for clothing and linings.

futier.label: Barrel maker (fûtier)
futier.summary: Cooper specialized in making barrels, wooden containers for liquid storage.
futier.text: The barrel maker assembled wooden staves bound with hoops to make sealed barrels, intended to store and transport wine, cider, eau-de-vie or other liquids. The term is close to "cooper," of which it often forms a regional synonym or specialization in large-capacity pieces.

gabarier.label: Barge operator (gabarier)
gabarier.summary: Bargeman driving a gabare, flat-bottomed boat used to transport goods on rivers.
gabarier.text: The barge operator navigated a gabare, a flat-bottomed boat suited to shallow rivers, to transport goods (wood, wine, stone, salt) between inland and sea ports. This river transport, essential before railway development, marked rivers like the Loire, Dordogne and Charente.

gabeleur.label: Salt-tax collector (gabeleur)
gabeleur.summary: Officer charged with collecting the gabelle, the royal salt tax, under the Ancien Régime.
gabeleur.text: The salt-tax collector levied the gabelle, an indirect tax on salt established in the 14th century and one of the most unpopular of royal taxes until its abolition in 1790. He also often managed the distribution of salt in salt-stores, where each household was obliged to buy a minimum quantity (the "salt of duty").

gabelou.label: Salt-tax enforcer (gabelou)
gabelou.summary: Officer charged with suppressing salt smuggling and collecting gabelle tax, a term now pejorative for 'customs officer.'
gabelou.text: The salt-tax enforcer patrolled roads and fiscal borders to track salt smugglers, and levied taxes due on this commodity. Very unpopular under the Ancien Régime, the word survived in modern familiar speech as a pejorative synonym for "customs officer."

gabian.label: Provençal tax officer (gabian)
gabian.summary: Provençal slang term designating, derisively, the customs officer or indirect-tax agent (salt tax, tolls).
gabian.text: Gabian (or gapian) is an Provençal slang term designating the customs officer, the salt-tax enforcer or more broadly the employee of indirect tax and toll administration. The word would play on a double origin: derived from "gabelle," it also evokes the gabian, the Provençal name for a gull or gannet, by mocking analogy between the thick-necked bird and the tax agent.

gabier.label: Topman (gabier)
gabier.summary: Sailor specialized in handling high sails, working from the ship's tops.
gabier.text: The topman climbed the rigging to handle high sails and survey the horizon from the tops (platforms high on the masts), work requiring agility and lack of vertigo. On large sailing ships, topmen formed a distinct corps of specialists separate from deck sailors.

gabier_brevete.label: Certified topman (gabier breveté)
gabier_brevete.summary: Topman who obtained a certificate attesting to his qualifications, a rank above simple topman in the navy.
gabier_brevete.text: The certified topman had undergone specific training and obtained an official certificate sanctioning his mastery of sail and rigging handling, which distinguished him from the simple or novice topman and opened access to greater responsibility aboard.

gacheur.label: Mortar mixer (gâcheur)
gacheur.text: The mortar mixer is a mason worker charged with preparing mortar (the mixing), related to the mortar worker and mortar maker.

gadouard.label: Scavenger (gadouard)
gadouard.summary: Worker charged with collecting and transporting gadoue, mud and waste matter from urban streets and pits.
gadouard.text: The scavenger collected gadoue — mixture of mud, garbage and waste matter — from streets and cesspits of cities, before installation of modern sewer networks. This unhealthy work, often done at night, played an essential sanitary role in Ancien Régime and 19th-century cities.

gager.label: Pawnbroker (gager)
gager.summary: Lender who advances money against the deposit of a valuable object as pledge.
gager.text: The pawnbroker granted loans in exchange for the deposit of a valuable object (jewel, tool, garment) left as pledge, which he returned upon repayment or resold in case of default. This activity, ancestor of the pawn-shop and modern pawnbrokers, was sometimes practised outside official corporations.

gagiste.label: Salaried employee (gagiste)
gagiste.summary: Employee paid a fixed wage, notably in the military or civil administration of the Ancien Régime.
gagiste.text: The salaried employee received gages, a fixed remuneration paid by an administration, a noble house or a military institution, as opposed to income derived directly from exploitation of property or trade. The term covers very diverse functions, from simple domestic to certain junior officers.

gagne_deniers.label: Day laborer (gagne-deniers)
gagne_deniers.summary: Unskilled worker toiling by the day for modest wages, at the bottom of the social ladder.
gagne_deniers.text: The day laborer hired out his labour day-to-day, without particular qualification or job security, for various tasks of loading or heavy work. This term, close to "labourer" or "day-worker," designates the most precarious fringe of the Ancien Régime working world.

gailloteur.label: Cargo rigger (gailloteur)
gailloteur.summary: Port worker responsible for attaching and detaching cargo loads during ship loading and unloading.
gailloteur.text: The term gailloteur, little documented elsewhere, would denote a dock worker charged with attaching and detaching loads (nets, pulleys) during ship loading and unloading operations, a function close to that of the docker or stevedore.

gainier.label: Sheath maker (gaînier)
gainier.summary: Craftsman who makes rigid sheaths and cases to protect precious objects, tools or instruments.
gainier.text: The sheath maker shapes sheaths and cases, often of wood covered in leather or shagreen, to protect and display precious objects: jewels, scientific instruments, cutlery, weapons. This fine woodworking and leather-work combined relates to Parisian luxury craftsmanship.

gainier_de_fourreaux.label: Scabbard maker (gaînier de fourreaux)
gainier_de_fourreaux.summary: Sheath craftsman specialized in making scabbards for swords and white arms.
gainier_de_fourreaux.text: The scabbard maker makes scabbards — rigid cases in wood, leather or metal — intended to protect sword blades and other white arms, ensuring perfect fit to facilitate drawing while assuring the wearer's safety.

galerien.label: Galley slave (galérien)
galerien.summary: Convict sentenced to forced labour, rowing chained on royal galleys until this punishment ended in the 18th century.
galerien.text: The galley slave is sentenced, for crime or misdemeanor (including salt smuggling), to row chained on the king's galleys, a sentence particularly dreaded for its physical hardship. The Toulon penal colony, where convicts continued to be called "galériens" by habit, took over from the galleys after their decommissioning in the early 18th century.

galibot.label: Mine boy (galibot)
galibot.summary: Young mine worker, often adolescent, charged with support tasks and underground assistance.
galibot.text: The mine boy is a young miner, sometimes barely twelve years old in the 19th century, employed underground for assistance tasks: setting support timbers, driving ore cars pulled by horses or dogs, before achieving the rank of full underground miner. The term is emblematic of the coal basins of northern France and the Pas-de-Calais.

galochier.label: Clog maker (galochier)
galochier.summary: Craftsman who makes galoches, shoes with leather upper mounted on wooden sole.
galochier.text: The clog maker makes galoches, mixed shoes with leather upper and thick wooden sole, more comfortable than the all-wood clog while resisting moisture better than leather alone. Very worn by rural working classes until the early 20th century, galoches gradually gave way to all-leather then rubber shoes.

galonnier.label: Braid weaver (galonnier)
galonnier.summary: Passementerie craftsman specialized in making braids, narrow bands serving as decoration or insignia.
galonnier.text: The braid weaver weaves braids — narrow, rigid ribbons, often enhanced with gold, silver or coloured thread — used to ornament military uniforms, servant liveries or ceremonial clothing, and to indicate ranks. This passementerie trade particularly developed with the codification of military uniforms from the 17th century onward.

galvacher.label: Teamster (galvacher)
galvacher.summary: Morvan or Nivernais peasant who hired out his oxen and cart for seasonal transport work.
galvacher.text: The teamster left his Morvan or Nivernais farm with his ox team to hire out his transport services elsewhere in France, notably for wood hauling or earthwork, before returning for agricultural work. This seasonal migration, typical of these poor regions, supplemented meagre income from small-scale farming.

gantelier.label: Gauntlet maker (gantelier)
gantelier.summary: Weapon-craftsman who makes gauntlets, armour pieces protecting the hand and forearm.
gantelier.text: The gauntlet maker forges and articulates gauntlets, armour elements made of moveable metal plates protecting the hand while preserving its mobility, indispensable to the equipment of the knight then of the armoured soldier until plate armour's decline in the 17th century.

gantier.label: Glove maker (gantier)
gantier.summary: Craftsman who makes gloves in leather or other materials, for protection or elegance.
gantier.text: The glove maker cuts and sews gloves, in fine leather (kid, lamb) for elegant uses or in sturdier materials for professional and agricultural uses. Grasse, in the Alpes-Maritimes, established itself from the 16th century as a major centre of luxury glove-making, linked to its perfumery tradition (perfumed gloves). "Ganteur" is an old variant.

garagiste.label: Garage owner (garagiste)
garagiste.summary: Operator of an automobile garage, ensuring vehicle repair, maintenance or sale.
garagiste.text: The garage owner repairs and maintains automobiles, and often also runs a business selling new or second-hand vehicles and fuel. This trade appears with automobile democratization in the early 20th century and becomes one of the characteristic professions of modern rural and urban life.

garanier.label: Warren keeper (garanier)
garanier.summary: Keeper of a private game warren.
garanier.text: The warren keeper ensures guard of a private warren, a game-filled reserve enclosed and belonging to a private person or lord.

garcon_baigneur.label: Bath attendant (garçon baigneur)
garcon_baigneur.summary: Public bath employee charged with assisting bathers: bath preparation, towels, supervision.
garcon_baigneur.text: The bath attendant works in a public bathing establishment, very widespread in cities before the generalization of private bathrooms, where he prepares hot water, supplies linen and assists patrons. This trade gradually disappears in the 20th century with sanitary equipment in dwellings.

garcon_d_entrepot.label: Warehouse hand (garçon d'entrepôt)
garcon_d_entrepot.summary: Junior employee charged with handling and arranging goods in a warehouse.
garcon_d_entrepot.text: The warehouse hand receives, arranges and prepares goods stored in a commercial warehouse, a handling task requiring no particular qualification. The term "garçon" commonly denoted, in old documents, a junior employee regardless of his actual age.

garcon_de_cafe.label: Waiter (garçon de café)
garcon_de_cafe.summary: Server employed in a café, providing customer service and serving drinks.
garcon_de_cafe.text: The waiter welcomes patrons, takes orders and serves drinks in a café or brasserie, a trade that developed with the rise of these establishments in French cities from the 19th century onward, notably in Paris where the "café waiter" in apron and waistcoat becomes a typical urban figure.

garcon_de_grave.label: Fishing apprentice (garçon de grave)
garcon_de_grave.summary: Young apprentice sailor aboard a cod ship to learn the cod-fishing trade.
garcon_de_grave.text: The fishing apprentice (not to be confused with the "gravier," who dries fish on the shore) is a young apprentice sailor aboard a cod ship, performing the simplest tasks aboard to gradually learn deep-sea fishing techniques.

garcon_de_lavoir.label: Washhouse worker (garçon de lavoir)
garcon_de_lavoir.summary: Water carrier supplying a public washhouse with hot water to facilitate laundry work.
garcon_de_lavoir.text: The washhouse worker transports the hot water needed for a public washhouse operation, where laundresses came to beat and rinse private laundry. This supplementary work, often entrusted to a young employee, complemented the collective organization of laundry before home washing machines arrived.

garcon_serger.label: Weaver's apprentice (garçon serger)
garcon_serger.summary: Apprentice to the serge-weaver trade, learning to weave serge, a twilled woollen fabric.
garcon_serger.text: The weaver's apprentice is a young apprentice placed with a serge-weaver — a weaver specialized in serge, a woollen fabric woven in twilled weave recognizable by its diagonal ribs — to gradually learn the trade's gestures before becoming journeyman then master.

garde.label: Guard (garde)
garde.summary: Generic term designating an agent charged with surveillance of a place, property or activity.
garde.text: Garde, used alone, is a generic term covering very many surveillance functions — gamekeeper, forest warden, rural constable, property guard — whose precise sense can only be established by the context of the document where it appears, often supplemented by a qualifier.

garde_barriere.label: Gate keeper (garde-barrière)
garde_barriere.summary: Railway employee charged with operating barriers at level crossings.
garde_barriere.text: The gate keeper opens and closes a level-crossing barrier as trains pass, a watchpost often occupied by an entire family housed in the nearby gatehouse. This trade, appearing with railway development in the 19th century, gradually automated in the 20th century.

garde_ceinture_a_l_aqueduc.label: Canal guard (garde-ceinture à l'aqueduc)
garde_ceinture_a_l_aqueduc.summary: Guard charged with surveillance of border canals surrounding dikes in the Poitevin Marshes, Vendée.
garde_ceinture_a_l_aqueduc.text: The canal guard supervises and maintains a border canal, a hydraulic structure running along a dike or levee to ensure its drainage and stability, as in the dike system of the Poitevin Marshes in Vendée. Landowner societies, such as that of Vix-Maillezais from 1697, employed permanent guards for these water-works surveillance missions.

garde_champetre.label: Rural constable (garde-champêtre)
garde_champetre.summary: Municipal official charged with enforcing rural regulations and recording agricultural violations.
garde_champetre.text: The rural constable, officially instituted in 1791, ensures compliance with municipal regulations in rural matters: crop protection, road and water-course protection, and hunting and fishing police at the municipal level. Sworn in, he can issue violation reports, unlike a simple private guard.

garde_chasse_royal.label: Royal gamekeeper (garde-chasse royal)
garde_chasse_royal.summary: Officer charged with supervising and protecting the hunting territories reserved for the sovereign.
garde_chasse_royal.text: The royal gamekeeper protects the game and hunting terrain belonging to the king against poaching, a function attached under the Ancien Régime to the administration of the "King's Pleasures," which managed notably the great hunting captaincies around royal residences like Versailles or Fontainebleau.

garde_couches.label: Lying-in attendant (garde-couches)
garde_couches.summary: Woman employed to assist a mother during lying-in and help with initial care of the newborn.
garde_couches.text: The lying-in attendant assists a woman during her confinement (recuperation period following childbirth), helping with domestic tasks and initial newborn care, complementing or following the midwife proper who performed the delivery.

garde_de_bois.label: Woodland warden (garde de bois)
garde_de_bois.summary: Agent charged with surveying a forest and ensuring compliance with wood-exploitation regulations.
garde_de_bois.text: The woodland warden (or forest warden) patrols a wooded area to prevent illegal cutting, poaching and fires, and ensure compliance with exploitation rules set by the owner or the Waters and Forests administration. A function distinct from the woodcutter, it involves surveillance rather than wood work itself.

garde_de_sel.label: Salt warehouse keeper (garde du sel)
garde_de_sel.summary: Officer charged with surveillance and management of salt stocks in royal granaries.
garde_de_sel.text: The salt warehouse keeper supervises salt granaries, royal warehouses where salt was stored before mandatory sale to residents under the salt tax (gabelle), and ensures proper record-keeping and fraud prevention. An administrative function linked to salt taxation, it is distinct from the gabelou, a field agent tracking smuggling.

garde_de_troupeau.label: Herdsman (gardien de troupeau)
garde_de_troupeau.summary: Shepherd charged with supervising and driving a flock, most often of sheep, to pasture.
garde_de_troupeau.text: The herdsman (or flock guard) leads cattle to pasture, protects them from predators and accidents, and returns them to the fold or stable at day's end, a basic function of extensive raising practised in pasture or transhumance regions.

garde_des_bleds.label: Grain field guard (garde des blés)
garde_des_bleds.summary: Rural supervisor charged with protecting grain fields from damage before harvest.
garde_des_bleds.text: The grain field guard (or harvest guard) patrols grain fields during ripening to prevent damage from stray cattle, game or crop theft, a function often collectively assigned by a village community before the institution of the rural constable.

garde_des_cohues.label: Market hall guard (garde des cohues)
garde_des_cohues.summary: Municipal agent charged with surveillance of cohues, market halls or rooms hosting markets and assemblies.
garde_des_cohues.text: The market hall guard maintains order in the cohues — buildings hosting both market halls and sometimes judicial assemblies in certain western French towns (like Rennes or Vannes) — preventing disorder and theft on market days.

garde_des_gabelles.label: Salt tax guard (garde des gabelles)
garde_des_gabelles.summary: Officer charged with surveillance and control of salt trade under the salt tax (gabelle).
garde_des_gabelles.text: The salt tax guard enforces regulations on salt trade — exclusive sale in royal granaries, minimum quantities imposed, prohibition on circulation outside authorized roads — and participates in smuggling suppression alongside the gabelou and salt-tax collector.

garde_excentrique.label: Railway pointsman (garde-excentrique)
garde_excentrique.summary: Belgian railway signalman charged with operating switches to direct trains.
garde_excentrique.text: The railway pointsman operates railway switches to direct trains from one track to another, a function attested under this name in Belgian railways of the 19th century, where the "excentrique" denotes the switching mechanism control.

garde_forge.label: Forge overseer (garde-forge)
garde_forge.summary: Foreman of a metallurgical workshop charged with supplying and supervising a forge.
garde_forge.text: The forge overseer directs the daily work of a forge or metallurgical workshop: supplying ore and charcoal, supervising workers, managing production, under the authority of the master ironsmith who owns the establishment.

garde_fourneau.label: Furnace keeper (garde-fourneau)
garde_fourneau.summary: Iron-works worker assisting the founder in operating the blast furnace and fusion operations.
garde_fourneau.text: The furnace keeper constantly monitors furnace operation — temperature, ore supply, charcoal and flux — to assist the master founder in conducting metal fusion, a task requiring continuous presence day and night.

garde_frein.label: Brakeman (garde-frein)
garde_frein.summary: Railway employee charged with hand-operating wagon brakes before their automation.
garde_frein.text: The brakeman manually operated his wagon's brake handle, on the mechanic's order transmitted by whistle, before the generalization of automatic continuous braking at the late 19th century. This trade, exposed to weather and accidents, disappeared with railway equipment modernization.

garde_ligne.label: Track warden (garde-ligne)
garde_ligne.summary: Railway employee charged with surveillance and maintenance of a section of railway track.
garde_ligne.text: The track warden patrols and inspects a section of railway track in his charge, verifying the condition of rails, sleepers and structures to prevent any incident, a function essential to railway operational safety.

garde_marteau.label: Forest marking officer (garde-marteau)
garde_marteau.summary: Forest agent holding the hammer marking trees authorized for felling in a forest.
garde_marteau.text: The forest marking officer applies the official mark, using an engraved forest hammer, to trees selected for cutting, ensuring only hammer-marked trees are felled. This function, inherited from the Waters and Forests administration, remains practised today in national forest management by the National Forestry Office.

garde_messier.label: Harvest field guard (garde-messier)
garde_messier.summary: Rural supervisor charged with protecting harvests and ensuring village agricultural regulations are followed.
garde_messier.text: The harvest field guard (or harvest supervisor) is elected or appointed by the village community to watch crops before harvest and record damage caused by stray cattle or theft, an ancient function prefiguring the rural constable instituted in 1791.

garde_moulin.label: Mill guard (garde-moulin)
garde_moulin.summary: Supervisor charged with protection and maintenance of a mill's installations.
garde_moulin.text: The mill guard watches over a mill's installations — mechanism, sluice, mill-race — in the miller's absence or to supplement his activity, preventing damage and theft of flour or grain stored on site.

garde_note.label: Record keeper (garde-note)
garde_note.summary: Officer charged with preserving notarial records and registers, a function close to that of the notary.
garde_note.text: The record keeper (or records keeper) preserves the minutes — originals of documents drawn by a notary — and issues certified copies on request. The term, used in certain provinces (notably the south) as an old synonym for "notary," emphasizes the record-preservation function, essential before modern notarial archive organization.

garde_particulier.label: Private game warden (garde-particulier)
garde_particulier.summary: Sworn private guard employed by a property owner to protect his estate against poaching and violations.
garde_particulier.text: The private game warden is commissioned and sworn at a property owner's request to supervise his lands, woods or ponds, with power to record violations (poaching, wood theft) by report, unlike a simple guardian without police power.

garde_perles.label: Pearl warden (garde-perles)
garde_perles.summary: Lorraine officer charged with supervising and regulating freshwater pearl fishing in rivers.
garde_perles.text: The pearl warden controlled, for the account of the Dukes of Lorraine who had reserved the exclusive right, the fishing of pearls produced by freshwater mussels in rivers like the Vologne, in the Vosges. Fishing was permitted only in June, July and August; the resource eventually disappeared in the 20th century due to overfishing and industrial water pollution.

garde_police.label: Peace officer (garde-police)
garde_police.summary: Officer charged with surveillance and maintenance of public order under a police authority.
garde_police.text: The peace officer assures surveillance and public order-keeping missions in a town or quarter, under the authority of a commissioner or municipal administration, a function prefiguring modern municipal police corps.

garde_pompe.label: Fire pump keeper (garde-pompe)
garde_pompe.summary: Person charged with surveillance and maintenance of fire pumps before professional fire brigades were created.
garde_pompe.text: The fire pump keeper maintained and kept ready the fire pump of a town or quarter, a manual hand-pump device before mechanization, and intervened during fires pending the organization of professional fire brigades in the 19th century.

garde_port.label: Harbor warehouseman (garde-port)
garde_port.summary: Port employee charged with receiving, sorting and supervising goods unloaded.
garde_port.text: The harbor warehouseman organizes the reception of goods unloaded in a port, ensures their proper arrangement pending removal and prevents theft and damage on the quays, an administrative and surveillance function essential to good port commerce operation.

garde_riviere.label: River warden (garde-rivière)
garde_riviere.summary: Officer charged with surveillance, maintenance and police of a waterway.
garde_riviere.text: The river warden ensures compliance with regulations on a waterway: fishing, navigation, water drawing, bank maintenance, and can record violations by report. This function exists today in modernized form, attached to fishing federations or water police.

garde_salle.label: Hall guard (garde-salle)
garde_salle.summary: Employee charged with surveillance and management of a waiting room, arms room or assembly hall.
garde_salle.text: The hall guard watches over a public or official hall — arms room, waiting room of an administration, court room — ensuring its opening, cleanliness and order maintenance among its frequenters.

garde_scel.label: Seal keeper (garde-scel)
garde_scel.summary: Royal officer charged with preserving and affixing the official seal on acts of a chancellery or jurisdiction.
garde_scel.text: The seal keeper has material responsibility for the seal — an engraved matrix serving to authenticate official acts — which he preserves and affixes to documents produced by a royal, seigneurial or judicial chancellery. The most prestigious title issuing from this function, the Keeper of the Seals, remains today France's official title for the Minister of Justice.

garde_traversier.label: Forest road warden (garde-traversier)
garde_traversier.summary: Forest officer charged with maintaining roads and paths crossing a forest.
garde_traversier.text: The forest road warden ensures maintenance of cross-roads and paths allowing forest-area exploitation and surveillance, notably passage of wood-cart traffic, a function attached to the Waters and Forests administration.

garde_vente.label: Timber-sale warden (garde-vente)
garde_vente.summary: Forest warden charged with supervising a timber sale, the cutting plot allotted to an operator.
garde_vente.text: The timber-sale warden supervises a "sale" — name given to the forest plot whose cutting has been awarded to an operator — to ensure the operator respects boundaries and conditions set by the owner or forest administration, preventing abusive cutting or damage to neighbouring trees.

gardeur_de_forge.label: Metalworks overseer (gardeur de forge)
gardeur_de_forge.summary: Supervisor of a metallurgical workshop in the 16th-17th centuries, close to the role of forge overseer.
gardeur_de_forge.text: The metalworks overseer ensures, like the forge overseer, daily supervision of a metallurgical workshop — worker surveillance, supply, and proper production flow — a function attested in 16th and 17th century documents before the term gave way to other appellations.

gardien_de_caravanserail.label: Caravanserai keeper (gardien de caravansérail)
gardien_de_caravanserail.summary: Manager responsible for welcoming and securing travellers and their beasts in a caravanserai.
gardien_de_caravanserail.text: The caravanserai keeper manages a caravanserai — a vast way-station building along eastern and North African trade routes, offering lodging to travellers and shelter to their beasts of burden — ensuring welcome, security and sometimes collecting a sojourn fee.

gardien_de_phare.label: Lighthouse keeper (gardien de phare)
gardien_de_phare.summary: Employee charged with maintaining a lighthouse mechanism and ensuring continuity of its night signal.
gardien_de_phare.text: The lighthouse keeper maintained the lantern, rotary mechanism and optics of a lighthouse, and ensured the light remained lit all night to guide ships, often in isolated posts on an island or cape. This trade, overseen in France by the Lighthouse and Beacons administration since the 19th century, has virtually disappeared with complete lighthouse automation at the late 20th century.

garenceur.label: Madder dyer (garenceur)
garenceur.summary: Dyer using madder to dye fabrics red.
garenceur.text: The madder dyer is a dyer worker who uses madder, a plant whose root serves to dye fabrics red.

garennier.label: Rabbit-warren keeper (garennier)
garennier.summary: Keeper of a warren, an enclosed or reserved territory for semi-wild rabbit raising.
garennier.text: The rabbit-warren keeper supervises and exploits a warren — an enclosed or reserved territory where rabbits are raised in semi-liberty — protecting animals from poaching and predators, and regulating their population for hunting or sale. "Garandier" is an old spelling variant; "garde-garenne" and "rabbit guardian" designate the same function in a more descriptive form.

gargot.label: Pork wholesaler (gargot)
gargot.summary: Wholesale pork merchant, selling to butchers split pork carcasses prepared and halved.
gargot.text: The pork wholesaler bought pigs, had them slaughtered and sold them wholesale, usually halved in two quarters, to retail butchers and pork-dealers — a practice called "à la cheville," common in Ancien Régime slaughterhouses and butcher halls.

gargotier.label: Tavern keeper (gargotier)
gargotier.summary: Keeper of a gargote, a small cheap eating house for popular-class patrons.
gargotier.text: The tavern keeper kept a gargote, an often modest establishment offering simple and inexpensive food to workers, students and impoverished travellers. The word, long held derisively compared to more refined restaurants, designates an essential link in 19th-century urban popular eating.

garnisseur.label: Upholsterer (garnisseur)
garnisseur.summary: Craftsman who applies garnishes and ornaments to various objects: furniture, hats, harnesses, weapons.
garnisseur.text: The upholsterer adds final garnish to an object — padding a seat, lining a hat, ornaments on a harness or scabbard — the last step giving the piece comfort or aesthetic finish. The term, generic, appears in many craft occupations depending on the object garnished.

garnisseur_de_gaine.label: Scabbard finisher (garnisseur de gaîne)
garnisseur_de_gaine.summary: Craftsman who applies metal or decorative garnishes on sword and weapon scabbards.
garnisseur_de_gaine.text: The scabbard finisher adds finishing elements — ferrules, metal ornaments, linings — to weapon scabbards and sheaths, completing the work of the sheath-maker proper who shaped the structure of the case.

garnisseur_de_necessaires.label: Case maker (garnisseur de nécessaires)
garnisseur_de_necessaires.summary: Craftsman making and selling travel necessaire kits.
garnisseur_de_necessaires.text: The case maker makes and sells travel necessaires, fitted cases with toilet or writing accessories.

gastelier.label: Pastry maker (gastelier)
gastelier.summary: Merchant or maker of cakes and pastries, a medieval term formed on "gastel," ancestor of the word cake.
gastelier.text: The pastry maker makes and sells "gastels," pastries and cakes whose medieval name evolved into "gâteau." This ancient bakery-pastry trade appears in sources dating to the Middle Ages and experiences a resurgence of heritage interest, with contemporary bakers reusing the term for their signs.

gaudronneur.label: Rope tarrer (gaudronneur)
gaudronneur.summary: Rope-works worker charged with waterproofing cordage by coating it with tar.
gaudronneur.text: The rope tarrer (or coal-tarrer) coats cordage with vegetable tar to protect it from moisture and rot, treatment indispensable for marine cordage exposed constantly to sea water. This step follows rope-twisting in the rope-works manufacturing process.

gaufreur.label: Embosser (gaufreur)
gaufreur.summary: Textile worker who presses a relief pattern onto fabric through hot pressure.
gaufreur.text: The embosser presses fabric between engraved, heated plates or rollers to print a permanent relief pattern, a technique used notably on velvet, silk or leather to give them a decorative embossed appearance.

gauleyeur.label: Fruit knocker (gauleyeur)
gauleyeur.summary: Agricultural worker who harvests fruits by knocking them down with a pole (gaule).
gauleyeur.text: The fruit knocker beats branches of a fruit tree with a long pole, the gaule, to make fruits fall — walnuts, chestnuts, almonds or olives depending on region — a quick harvest method still practised today for certain tree nuts. The word comes from the verb "to gaule."

gazier.label: Gas worker (gazier)
gazier.summary: Worker or employee working in gas production, distribution or installation.
gazier.text: The gas worker worked in the gas industry: production of town gas in 19th-century gasworks, then distribution and hookup to private customers with natural gas generalization in the 20th century. The term commonly designates today the technician who installs and maintains gas installations.

geindre.label: Bread kneader (geindre)
geindre.summary: Bakery worker particularly charged with kneading dough.
geindre.text: The bread kneader is a bakery worker particularly charged with dough-kneading, a physically demanding task before mechanization.

gemmeur.label: Resin tapper (gemmeur)
gemmeur.summary: Forest worker who scores pine bark to harvest resin, called gemme.
gemmeur.text: The resin tapper practices tapping: he scores the bark of the maritime pine to provoke resin flow (the gemme), which he collects regularly in a pot fixed to the trunk. This activity made the wealth of the Gascony Landes forest from the 19th century until its decline after the Second World War, faced with synthetic resins and imports.

genevrier.label: Juniper liqueur maker (génevrier)
genevrier.text: The juniper liqueur maker makes juniper alcohol, an eau-de-vie flavoured with juniper berries.

gentiannaire.label: Gentian digger (gentiannaire)
gentiannaire.summary: In Auvergne, digger of gentian whose dried roots enter into aperitif preparation.
gentiannaire.text: In Auvergne, the gentian digger digs gentian, a plant whose dried roots are used in preparing aperitifs.

geographe.label: Cartographer (géographe)
geographe.summary: Person charged with drawing geographical maps.
geographe.text: The cartographer draws geographical maps, a learned craft linked to cartography and exploration.

gerlaire.label: Bucket maker (gerlaïre)
gerlaire.summary: In Auvergne, maker of gerles, large wooden pails for carrying milk from pastures.
gerlaire.text: In Auvergne, the bucket maker makes gerles, large wooden pails with a cover, used to carry milk from pastures to the farm.

gestionnaire_de_la_redaction.label: Editorial manager (gestionnaire de la rédaction)
gestionnaire_de_la_redaction.summary: Administrative and organizational head of a press editorial office or media.
gestionnaire_de_la_redaction.text: The editorial manager ensures the administrative and logistical organization of an editorial office — schedules, budgets, coordination of journalism teams — a modern function specific to press, radio, television or online media sectors.

gibecier.label: Pouch maker (gibecier)
gibecier.summary: Maker of gibecière, a flat, wide pouch worn at the belt.
gibecier.text: The pouch maker makes the gibecière, a flat, wide pouch once worn at the belt.

giboyeur.label: Game hunter (giboyeur)
giboyeur.summary: Foot hunter making a business of passing game, formerly with an arquebus.
giboyeur.text: The game hunter is a foot hunter making a business of passing game, which he shoots with a rifle; formerly he used an arquebus.

giletier.label: Waistcoat maker (giletier)
giletier.text: The waistcoat maker is a tailor specialized in making waistcoats.

gisseur.label: Plaster decorator (gisseur)
gisseur.summary: Craftsman decorating walls and ceilings with plaster motifs.
gisseur.text: The plaster decorator (or gypsum-worker) decorates walls and ceilings with plaster motifs; in the 18th century in Franche-Comté, the term designated more precisely the plasterer-stucco worker.

glaneuse.label: Gleaner (glaneuse)
glaneuse.summary: Woman recovering wheat ears left in a harvested field.
glaneuse.text: The gleaner recovers wheat ears forgotten in a field after harvest, an activity of subsistence more than a true trade, regulated by gleaning rights.

glypticien.label: Seal carver (glypticien)
glypticien.summary: Carver of small stones: ring stones, seals.
glypticien.text: The seal carver cuts small-volume stones such as ring-mounted stones, seals and other fine-engraving objects (glyptic).

gobeletier.label: Goblet maker (gobeletier)
gobeletier.summary: Maker of goblets, carafes, mugs and drinking glasses without stems.
gobeletier.text: The goblet maker makes goblets, carafes, mugs and drinking glasses without stems, in glass or metal.

godivellier.label: Cooper (godivellier)
godivellier.text: In Normandy, the godivellier denotes the cooper, maker of bushels and wooden vessels.

goemonier.label: Seaweed harvester (goémonier)
goemonier.summary: Gatherer of seaweed used dried as natural fertilizer.
goemonier.text: The seaweed harvester gathers seaweed, a marine plant that, once dried, was used as natural fertilizer on coastal lands.

gougeard.label: Servant (gougeard)
gougeard.text: The servant is a servant, a term attested in the Middle Ages.

gourdiec.label: Fisherman (gourdiec)
gourdiec.summary: At Belle-Île-en-Mer, a fishing sailor or landless day laborer.
gourdiec.text: At Belle-Île-en-Mer, the fisherman is a fishing sailor or a landless day laborer, living from occasional work.

gourmet.label: Wine merchant (gourmet)
gourmet.text: The wine merchant is a wine merchant, an old term distinct from the modern gastronomic sense.

gouvernante.label: Governess (gouvernante)
gouvernante.summary: Woman employed to direct a household or supervise the education of young girls within a family.
